(40)

which is conceptually similar to that in Eq. (
34
), visualizes the definition of the tangent vector pushforward’s coordinate expression.
It furthermore implies that the gauge transformations between different coordinatizations are given by

\displaystyle g_{\phi}^{B\widetilde{B}}\ =\ g_{\phi(p)}^{BA}\;g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}\mkern 1.0mu\big(g_{p}^{\widetilde{B}\widetilde{A}}\mkern 1.0mu\big)^{-1}\,,

(41)

which is the conceptual analog to Eq. (
35
).

3.4.2
Pushforward of reference frames and symmetries of the
G
-structure

Since reference frames are just
d
-tuples of linearly independent frame vectors, the pushforward of tangent vectors induces a pushforward of reference frames by
pushing the individual frame axes forward
.
Specifically, the pushforward of a frame
[e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}
at
p
is defined as the frame
\big[\phi_{*}|_{p}(e_{i})\big]_{i=1}^{d}
at
\phi(p)
.

This pushforward of frames is always well defined, however, it might not be compatible with the
G
-structure, that is, there is in general no guarantee that frames in
G\mkern-1.4muM
remain in
G\mkern-1.4muM
when being pushed forward.
Take for instance the
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
9
(top left), which is preserved by horizontal translations but not by vertical translations or any other isometry of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
.
Similarly, the
{R}
-structure in Fig.
9
(bottom left) is preserved by translations and horizontal reflections, but not by rotations.
We consider therefore the subgroup

\displaystyle\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\ :=\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\phi\in\Isom(\mkern-1.5muM\mkern-0.5mu)\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\ \big[\phi_{*}(e_{i})\big]_{i=1}^{d}\in G\mkern-1.4muM\quad\forall\ [e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\in G\mkern-1.4muM\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}\,\ \leq\ \Isom(\mkern-1.5muM\mkern-0.5mu)

(42)

of
isometries which are symmetries of the
G
-structure
, i.e. which are guaranteed to map any frame in
G\mkern-1.4muM
to another frame that is also contained in
G\mkern-1.4muM
.
22
22

22

More formally stated, such isometries are (or induce)
principal bundle automorphisms
of the
G
-structure.

Note that
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
depends in general on the specific choice of
G
-structure
G\mkern-1.4muM
, not only on the structure group
G
.
For the special case that
G\geq\operatorname{O}(d)
, it is guaranteed that
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\Isom(\mkern-1.5muM\mkern-0.5mu)
coincide since isometries are guaranteed to map orthonormal frames to orthonormal frames.
We are interested in the subgroup
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
since only those isometries will induce a well defined pushforward of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent feature vectors, as discussed further in the following section.

Before proceeding to the isometry action on feature vectors, we discuss what we call
isometry induced gauge transformations
.
For this purpose, let
\big[e_{i}^{\widetilde{A}}\big]_{i=1}^{d}
be that frame at
p
that corresponds to some source gauge
\psi_{p}^{\widetilde{A}}
and let
\big[e_{i}^{A}\big]_{i=1}^{d}
be that frame at
\phi(p)
that corresponds to some target gauge
\psi_{\phi(p)}^{A}
, as shown in Fig.
21
in red (left) and green (right), respectively.
The pushforward
\big[\phi_{*}|_{p}(e_{i}^{\widetilde{A}})\big]_{i=1}^{d}
of the source frame from
p
to
\phi(p)
(translucent red, right) does in general not coincide with the target frame.
However, as proven in Section
8.1.3
, the two frames are related by the isometry induced gauge transformation

\displaystyle\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\Big[$}}}}\phi_{*}|_{p}(e_{i}^{\widetilde{A}})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\rule{0.0pt}{12.0pt}_{i=1}^{d}$}\ =\ \big[e_{i}^{A}\big]_{i=1}^{d}\lhd g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\,,

(43)

where
g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)
is the group element from Eq. (
39
) and
\lhd
is the right action from Eq. (
11
).
The term “isometry induced gauge transformation” makes in so far sense that the geometries around
p
and
\phi(p)
are indistinguishable since
\phi
is an isometry, i.e. a symmetry of
M
.
Identifying the two points with each other, one can therefore reinterpret the
active
action of
\phi
on a geometric quantity as a
passive
gauge transformation, i.e. an induced change from the source to the target frame.

Theorem
8.3
in Section
8.1
asserts that
G
-structure preserving isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
and
G
-valued induced gauge transformations imply each other, that is,

\displaystyle\phi\in\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\in G\ \ \ \forall\ p\mkern-1.0mu\in\mkern-2.0muM

(44)

holds for arbitrary gauges
\psi_{p}^{\widetilde{A}}
and
\psi_{\phi(p)}^{A}
of the
G
-atlas.
The reader should verify these claims at our examples in Fig.
9
.

3.4.3
Pushforward of feature vectors

If (and only if) an isometry is a symmetry of the
G
-structure, it gives rise to a
pushforward of feature vectors
.
Intuitively, this pushforward moves feature vectors from points
p
to
\phi(p)
.
When being expressed relative to the two reference frames at
p
and
\phi(p)
, it is given by the induced gauge transformation

\displaystyle\rho\big(g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\big)\,.

(45)

Note that this transformation is well defined for any
\phi\in\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
, since the induced gauge transformations
g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)
will in this case take values in
G
and
\rho
is a
G
-representation.
In contrast, if
\phi
is not a symmetry of the
G
-structure, it is
impossible
to define a corresponding feature vector pushforward.
This statement relates to the fact that the features of conventional CNNs have no specified transformation behavior under rotations or reflections in the Euclidean group
\operatorname{E}(d)
.

The pushforward of individual feature vectors implies an action on the whole feature field
f
, which we denote by
\phi\rhd f
.
Relative to coordinates, this action is expressed as

\displaystyle\big[\phi\rhd f\big]^{A}(\phi(p))\ =\ \rho\big(g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\big)\,f^{\widetilde{A}}(p)\,.

(46)

We will later prove that coordinate independent CNNs are equivariant w.r.t. the action of isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
on feature fields; see Fig.
25
.
This property relies on the fact that the active isometry action on feature fields can by Eq. (
46
) be understood as a mere passive gauge transformation of feature vector coefficients.

4
Coordinate independent networks and
GM
-convolutions

Neural networks process data by applying a series of parameterized mappings (layers) to an input signal – in our case to a set of feature fields on a Riemannian manifold.
The
principle of covariance
requires thereby that the individual network layers should be
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent operations.
The coordinate representations of such layers will therefore have to transform such that they respect the transformation laws of their input- and output feature field.
Except form this consistency requirement, general coordinate independent layers remain
unconstrained
.

A common design principle of neural networks which operate on spatial signals (feature fields) is that they are in some generalized sense convolutional.
The main characteristic which most generalizations of the convolution operation share is that their inference is
position independent
.
This is achieved by
sharing template functions
, for instance convolution kernels or biases, between different locations.
Whenever the structure group
G
is non-trivial, the weight sharing process is ambiguous since template functions could be shared relative to different reference frames.
As we will argue in the following, this ambiguity is resolved by designing the shared template functions to be
equivariant under
G
-valued gauge transformations
.
Gauge equivariant template functions will be indifferent to the specific reference frame in which they are applied and therefore allow for a coordinate independent weight sharing.

In this section we will consider network layers which take fields
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
of type
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
as input and produce field
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}
of type
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
as output.
Section
4.1
discusses the specific case of layers which operate pointwise, that is, whose output
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)
at any
p\in M
depends only on the single input feature vector
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)
at the same location.
The practically relevant examples considered here are gauge equivariant
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolutions
in Section
4.1.1
, bias summation in Section
4.1.2
and nonlinearities in Section
4.1.3
.
The more complicated case of convolutions with spatially extended kernels is treated in Section
4.2
.
As a preparation, Section
4.2.1
discusses feature fields as seen from the viewpoints of local observers (reference frames), relative to which the (convolution) kernels will be applied.
Such observations are formalized as a pullback of the feature field to an observer’s tangent space; see Fig.
22
.
Section
4.2.2
introduces so called kernel field transforms, which are similar to convolutions but do not assume spatial weight sharing and are therefore parameterized by a (smoothly varying) kernel field on
M
.
The actual
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are in Section
4.2.3
defined as those kernel field transforms that are parameterized by a single, shared template kernel.
In order to ensure the coordinate independence of the weight sharing process, the convolution kernels are required to be
G
-
steerable
, i.e. to satisfy a gauge equivariance constraint.
Section
4.3
shows that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are automatically equivariant under those isometries that are symmetries of the
G
-structure (
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant).
This means that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions commute with the action of isometries on feature fields as visualized in Fig.
25
.

4.1
Pointwise gauge equivariant operations

To begin with, we consider some neural network operations for which the constraints coming from the required coordinate independence and weight sharing are particularly easy to derive.
All of these operations have in common that they act pointwise on feature vectors, that is, they compute output feature vectors
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)
at
p\in M
solely based on the input feature vectors
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)
at the same location.
In order to satisfy the principle of covariance, the coordinatizations of these operations are all required to transform according to a precomposition with
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
and a postcomposition with
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
.
When demanding that the operations are determined in terms of shared weights, these transformation laws imply a requirement for the gauge equivariance (or invariance) of the operations.

The derivations for the different pointwise operations in the following Sections
4.1.1
,
4.1.2
and
4.1.3
are in the first steps mostly analogous and lead to essentially the same covariance and equivariance constraints on the template functions.
They could therefore be treated together, keeping the particular operation (or template function) abstract.
However, since the implications of the resulting constraints differ for the particular instantiations, and since we want to keep the discussion close to the application, we will omit such an abstract formulation and directly consider particular instantiations.

4.1.1
Gauge equivariant
{\bf 1\mkern-5.0mu\bm{\times}\mkern-5.0mu1}
-convolutions

As a first example of pointwise operations, we consider the action of a family of
linear maps

\mathcal{C}_{p}
, which send the input feature vector
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)
at each
p\in M
to an output feature vector

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p):=\mathcal{C}_{p}\,f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)\,.

(47)

If we add the assumption of spatial weight sharing, the linear maps
\mathcal{C}_{p}
and
\mathcal{C}_{q}
at different locations
p
and
q
will be coupled, and the operation can be seen as a convolution with a linear operator-valued Dirac delta kernel.
This operation is quite common in computer vision, where it is usually denoted as
\mathit{{1\kern-2.75pt\times\kern-3.1pt1}}
-convolution
, since the spatial discretization of a linear Dirac kernel which operates on two-dimensional images is given by a (matrix-valued) kernel with a spatial extent of
1\!\times\!1
pixels.
We will in the following derive that the demand for spatial weight sharing will result in a constraint, which forces the matrix-valued template kernels to be
intertwiners
, that is, gauge equivariant matrices.

Prior to the assumption of weight sharing, the coordinate expressions of the linear maps
\mathcal{C}_{p}
and the gauge transformations between them behave very similar to those of the linear maps on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
, which we discussed in Section
3.1.2
.
Since the input and output feature vectors are in coordinates represented by coefficient vectors
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}
and
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}
, the linear map is naturally represented by that matrix
\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
that satisfies

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)=\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}\cdot f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\,.

(48)

This relation does of course hold for arbitrary coordinatizations, such that we have
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}(p)=\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\cdot f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{B}(p)
for any other gauge, labeled by
B
.
The transformation law which relates
\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}
to
\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}
follows by the principle of covariance from the transformation laws of the input and output features.
Since these are given by
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{B}(p)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)
and
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}(p)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)
, one has

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}(p)\

\displaystyle=\ \mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\cdot f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{B}(p)

\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\qquad

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\

\displaystyle=\ \mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)

\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\qquad

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\

\displaystyle=\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\,\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\,.

(49)

A comparison with Eq. (
48
) implies that the two coordinate expressions of
\mathcal{C}_{p}
are necessarily related by

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}

(50)

if they should respect the transformation laws of the feature vectors.
As usual, these considerations are concisely captured by a commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}\cdot}

(51)

The important practical implication of this result so far is that the linear map
\mathcal{C}_{p}
is not restricted in any way.
Differently formulated: as long as the coordinate expressions in different gauges are related by Eq. (
50
), one is free to parameterize
\mathcal{C}_{p}
in an arbitrary, fixed gauge
A
by an
unconstrained
matrix
\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}
.
As we will see, the situation changes when requiring the linear maps to share weights.

Consider now the case where the linear maps
\mathcal{C}_{p}
and
\mathcal{C}_{q}
share weights.
This means that we assume them to be parameterized by a shared set of parameters, given by a
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolution
template kernel
K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
.
The open question is how exactly the coordinate free maps should be parameterized in terms of this template kernel.
Our requirement for
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independence demands that we do not prefer any particular reference frame in the weight sharing process, that is, that we treat all coordinatizations in the same manner.
It is therefore necessary to
share the template kernel with all coordinatizations at the same time
, that is, to set

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{p}^{X}=K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\quad\textup{for \emph{any} gauge}\ \ \big(U^{X},\psi^{X})\in{A}^{G}\ \ \textup{with}\ \ p\in U^{X}\,,

(52)

where
{A}^{G}
is the (maximal)
G
-atlas corresponding to the considered
G
-structure; see Eq. (
25
).
As the covariance constraint in Eq. (
50
) needs to hold for arbitrary
G
-related gauges, and the coordinatizations
\mathcal{C}_{p}^{A}=\mathcal{C}_{p}^{B}=K_{\!1\!\times\!1}
of the linear maps do all coincide, the joint demand for weight sharing and
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independence is seen to imply a constraint

\displaystyle K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\,K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\qquad\forall\ g\in G

(53)

on the template kernel.
The corresponding adaptation of the commutative diagram in Eq. (
51
) with weight sharing is given by:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\cdot}

(54)

The conclusion of this analysis is that the template kernels which can be
unambiguously shared
are exactly those which are
invariant under the gauge action
.
The vector space of such gauge invariant
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolution
kernels is simply the space of
intertwining maps
between the representations
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
and
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
, that is,

\displaystyle\Hom_{G}(\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}},\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}})\ :=\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\ K_{\!1\!\times\!1}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\,K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\ \ \ \forall g\in G\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}\,\ \subseteq\ \mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,.

(55)

Note that, according to
Schur’s Lemma

[
75
]
, the requirement on
K_{\!1\!\times\!1}
to be an intertwiner prevents a mapping between fields that transform under non-isomorphic irreducible representations via
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolutions
.
This severe restriction is unavoidable with
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolution
kernels but will be resolved later when allowing for spatially extended kernels.

At this point we want to mention that we use the terms “gauge equivariant template function” and “gauge invariant template function” interchangeably.
This is justified by the observation that the invariance constraint in Eq. (
53
) can be written as an equivariance constraint

K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\,K_{\!1\!\times\!1}\ \ \forall g\in G
.
It is in general possible to view functions which are equivariant w.r.t. some group action in their domain and codomain as the invariants of the corresponding action on the function itself.
In our application, the equivariance viewpoint highlights that a transformation of the input field will lead to a corresponding transformation of the output field, which ensures that all involved quantities transform covariantly with each other.
On the other hand, the invariance viewpoint emphasizes that the template function can be shared in an arbitrary gauge.

4.1.2
Gauge equivariant bias summation

After applying a convolution operation, it is common to sum a (shared) bias vector to the individual feature vectors.
Together with the requirement of coordinate independence, the weight sharing will again lead to a linear constraint.
This constraint will only allow for biases to be summed to the invariant subspaces of the gauge action on the input feature field.

As before, we first consider the bias summation without requiring weight sharing.
We thus have biases
{b}_{p}
, depending on the position
p
on the manifold, which are summed to an input feature vector to produce an output feature vector

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)=f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)+{b}_{p}\,.

(56)

Relative to gauges
\psi_{p}^{A}
and
\psi_{p}^{B}
, the bias is represented by those coefficient vectors
{b}_{p}^{A}
and
{b}_{p}^{B}
in
\mathbb{R}^{c}
that satisfy
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)=f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)+{b}_{p}^{A}
and
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}(p)=f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{B}(p)+{b}_{p}^{B}
.
Since the summation of vectors does not allow to change their transformation laws, the group representations associated with the input and output feature necessarily agree, that is,

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}=:\rho\,.

(57)

Together with the requirement for coordinate independence, this implies that the diagram

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\ \ ,

(58)

which is the analog of that in Eq. (
51
), needs to commute.
Written out as an equation, this demands the relation

\rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)f^{A}_{p}+{b}_{p}^{B}\ =\ \rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\big(f^{A}_{p}+{b}_{p}^{A}\big)

to hold.
Since the linearity of
\rho(g)
allows to rewrite the right-hand side as

\rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)f^{A}_{p}+\rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big){b}_{p}^{A}
,
a subtraction of the input feature vector leads to

\displaystyle{b}_{p}^{B}\ =\ \rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,{b}_{p}^{A}\,.

(59)

The coefficient vectors which represent a coordinate independent bias relative to different gauges therefore need to transform exactly like the feature vectors to which they are summed.
As in the case of
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolutions
, the coordinate independence does
not
restrict the bias
{b}_{p}
in any way, but only requires different coordinatizations of the same bias to be consistent with each other.
An implementation could therefore pick an arbitrary gauge and freely parameterize the bias in that gauge by parameters in
\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}
.

The situation changes again when asking for spatial weight sharing.
Let
b\in\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}
be a template bias vector to be shared over the manifold.
Since the only way to do this without arbitrarily preferring any coordinatization is to share the bias vector in all gauges simultaneously, we have to require

\displaystyle{b}_{p}^{X}=b\quad\textup{for \emph{any} gauge}\ \ \big(U^{X},\psi^{X})\in{A}^{G}\ \ \textup{with}\ \ p\in U^{X}\,.

(60)

in analogy to Eq. (
52
).
The combination of the covariance constraint in Eq. (
59
) with this gauge independent weight sharing then leads to the invariance constraint

\displaystyle b\ =\ \rho(g)\,b\qquad\forall\ g\in G

(61)

on the bias vector template.
To complete the analogy to the case of
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolutions
, we show the adapted version of the commutative diagram in Eq. (
58
) with shared weights:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces+b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces+b}

(62)

To get an insight in the implications of the invariance constraint in Eq. (
61
), assume it to be satisfied for a given template vector
b
.
Due to the linearity of the constraint, any scaled vector
\alpha\!\cdot\!b
for
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
will then satisfy it as well, that is, any solution spans a
one-dimensional subspace of
\mathbb{R}^{c}
which is
invariant under the action of
\rho
.
Such an invariant subspace is denoted as a subrepresentation of
\rho
.
Since the subspaces in consideration are one-dimensional, they have themselves no proper subspace and are therefore trivial irreducible subrepresentations.
If follows that the vector space

\displaystyle{B}^{G}_{\rho}\ :=\ \big\{b\in\mathbb{R}^{c}\;\big|\;b=\rho(g)\mkern 2.0mub\ \ \ \forall g\in G\big\}

(63)

of gauge equivariant biases coincides with the (subspaces of) trivial subrepresentations of
\rho
.
The dimensionality of
{B}^{G}_{\rho}
– and therefore the number of learnable parameters – coincides with the multiplicity of trivial subrepresentations contained in
\rho
.
For compact groups
G
, Schur’s orthogonality relations imply that this dimensionality is given by
\dim\!\big({B}^{G}_{\rho}\big)=\int_{G}\operatorname{tr}\mkern-2.0mu\big(\rho(g)\big)dg
.
This statement covers the practically important cases of the orthogonal groups
G=\operatorname{O}(d)
and all of its subgroups.

Two simple examples of feature fields to which one might want to sum shared biases are scalar fields and tangent vector fields.
By definition, the coefficient field of a scalar field is invariant under gauge transformations, that is, it transforms according the trivial representation
{\rho(g)=1\ \ \forall g\in G}
.
One can therefore sum a (scalar) bias
b\in\mathbb{R}
to them.
In contrast, the coefficient field of a tangent vector field transforms according to the non-trivial, irreducible group representation
\rho(g)=g
.
Since this representation does not contain any trivial subrepresentation, it is impossible to sum a shared bias vector to tangent vector fields while maintaining coordinate independence.
As a third example, consider regular representations of compact groups, which describe for instance the feature fields of group convolutional networks.
By the Peter-Weyl theorem, it is known that regular representations contain exactly one trivial subrepresentation
[
84
,
75
]
.
The bias to be summed to regular feature fields is therefore seen to be described by a single parameter.

4.1.3
Gauge equivariant nonlinearities

Except from linear (convolution) operations and bias summations, the most basic operations used in any neural network are nonlinearities.
We will here consider the usual case of nonlinearities
\sigma_{p}
which act in a spatially localized way, that is, which compute output feature vectors as
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)=\sigma_{p}\big(f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(p)\big)
.
A shared nonlinearity will again be required to be gauge equivariant.
As the reasoning which leads to this conclusion is similar to that in the previous cases, we will only summarize it shortly.
Due to the generality of nonlinear maps it is impossible to derive linear solution spaces as in Eqs. (
55
) and (
63
), however, we will discuss some specific examples.

Similar to before, any coordinate free nonlinearity
\sigma_{p}
is relative to gauges
A
and
B
given by coordinate expressions
\sigma_{p}^{A}:\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}
and
\sigma_{p}^{B}:\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}
, which are by the demand for coordinate independence required to be related by
\sigma_{p}^{B}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\circ\sigma_{p}^{A}\circ\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}
.
A nonlinear template function
{s}:\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}
can only be shared in a coordinate independent way when sharing it with all gauges simultaneously.
This turns the covariance constraint in an invariance constraint
{s}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\circ{s}\circ\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\ \ \forall g\in G
on the template function, or, equivalently, in the corresponding equivariance constraint

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\circ{s}={s}\circ\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\qquad\forall\ g\in G\,.

(64)

Due to the nonlinearity of this constraint we are forced to investigate it on a case-by-case basis – we will therefore limit our discussion to some specific examples.
The arguably most simple case is that of nonlinearities which map between scalar fields, i.e. for which
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)=1
are for any
g\in G
invariant.
In this case the equivariance constraint in Eq. (
64
) becomes
{s}={s}
, which is trivially satisfied for
any
nonlinearity
{s}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}
.
A more interesting example is that of unitary representation
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
.
One possible nonlinearity for this case is given by the norm of feature vectors.
Since
\lVert\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\rVert=\lVert f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\rVert
is due to the unitarity of
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
invariant,
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
will be the trivial representation.
Taking the norm is thus seen to be a nonlinear, gauge equivariant operation that maps any unitary field to a scalar field.
A nonlinear map which preserves the field type, i.e. which satisfies
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
, can very similarly be defined as
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\mapsto\lVert f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)\rVert\cdot f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}(p)
.
Another option, which might play a role in learning physical interactions, and which was investigated in
[
122
,
120
,
2
,
12
]
, are tensor product nonlinearities.
Given two fields
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in,1}}^{A}(p)
and
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in,2}}^{A}(p)
, transforming according to

\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in},1}}}
and
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in},2}}}
,
respectively, such nonlinearities compute a tensor product feature
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}=f_{\textup{\;\!\!in,1}}^{A}(p)\otimes f_{\textup{\;\!\!in,2}}^{A}(p)
, which transforms equivariantly according to the tensor product representation

\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in},1}}}\otimes\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in},2}}}
.

All of these examples satisfy the gauge equivariance constraint in Eq. (
64
).
Which particular nonlinearity works well in practice is, however, still an open research question, which requires much more empirical investigation before it can be answered.
A first attempt in this direction has been made in
[
234
]
.

4.2
Kernel field transforms and
GM
-convolutions

The central operation of convolutional networks is the convolution operation, which linearly accumulates characteristic patterns of features from a local neighborhood around each point
p\in M
into a new feature vector
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)
.
A spatially extended convolution kernel determines thereby the specifics of this accumulation.
The principle of covariance requires coordinate independence, and therefore a specific transformation law of kernels under gauge transformations.
As in the previous examples, an additional demand for weight sharing results in a requirement on the template kernel to be gauge equivariant (
G
-steerable).

In accordance with the previous section, we clearly distinguish between the requirements for coordinate independence and weight sharing.
Section
4.2.2
therefore starts by discussing fields of kernels and their transformations laws without demanding the kernels at individual positions to be tied together.
Such unrestricted kernel fields give rise to
kernel field transforms
, which are integral transforms that can be seen as precursors of convolutions.
The actual
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, which are parameterized by a shared, necessarily gauge equivariant template kernel, are defined in Section
4.2.3
.
As a preparation, we will in the following Section
4.2.1
describe local representations of feature fields on the tangent spaces, where they will be matched with the convolution kernels.

4.2.1
A local observer’s view on feature fields

In contrast to Euclidean spaces or more general homogeneous spaces like the sphere, the local geometry of a general Riemannian manifold varies from point to point.
It is therefore not immediately clear how a convolution kernel should be defined on
M
and how it could be shared between different locations.
A common solution is to define the kernel as usual on a flat, Euclidean vector space
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, and to share it over the tangent spaces instead of the manifold itself;
see Sections
4.2.2
and
4.2.3
or prior work
[
150
,
173
,
220
,
39
,
38
,
238
,
48
,
246
]
.
Subsequently, the kernel can via the Riemannian exponential map be mapped down to the manifold.
It can be thought of as being applied by a local observer, who is measuring features in its surrounding relative to its local reference frame.
We will in this section shortly elaborate on how feature fields are perceived from the perspective of different local observers.
Mathematically, this is formalized as the pullback and parallel transport of the feature field to the tangent spaces; see Fig.
22
for a visualization.

In order to map between the tangent spaces and the manifold, we consider the
Riemannian exponential map
(corresponding to the Levi-Civita connection).
23
23

23

Even models which assume an
alternative (
G
-compatible) connection to transport features
utilize usually the canonical
Levi-Civita connection to compute geodesics
and exponential maps.

Assuming the manifold for simplicity to be geodesically complete
24
24

24

The assumption that
M
is
geodesically complete
means that the exponential maps
\exp_{p}
are for each
p\in M
defined on the whole tangent space
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
In cases where this assumption is violated one can resort to
zero padding
, which is commonly used in convolutional networks for finitely supported images.

,
the exponential map at a specific point
p\in M
is a map

\displaystyle\exp_{p}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to M\,.

(65)

It identifies vectors
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
with those points
\exp_{p}(v)\in M
that are reached when following the geodesic through
p
with an initial velocity of
v
for one unit of time.
While preserving radial distances, the exponential map does in general distort angels and fails to be injective.
For instance, if the manifold is a sphere, the exponential maps wrap their corresponding tangent space infinitely often around it.
It is, however, guaranteed that the exponential map is a local diffeomorphism if its domain is restricted to distances shorter than the distance to the cut locus (where injectivity fails).

Given the exponential maps, one can pull feature fields on the manifold back to the tangent spaces.
Specifically, let
f
be some feature field on
M
, then the
pullback

\exp_{p}^{*}f:=f\circ\exp_{p}
is defined as that map that assigns the feature vector
f(\exp_{p}(v))
from
\exp_{p}(v)
to
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
Note that, due to the missing injectivity of the exponential map, each tangent vector might be assigned to multiple tangent vectors
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
if
\exp_{p}(v_{1})=\exp_{p}(v_{2})
–  this is somewhat similar to gravitational lensing effects in physics.
For the case that the exponential map is injective, or when restricting it to its injectivity radius, the pullback corresponds to an expression of the feature fields in
geodesic normal coordinates

[
150
]
.

Recall that the purpose of pulling the feature vectors back to the tangent spaces is to enable that they can be accumulated by a convolution kernel.
Unfortunately, this is not immediately possible since the feature vectors at different locations live in different vector spaces and are expressed relative to different gauges.
25
25

25

A very similar circumstance motivates the definition of covariant derivatives, which also needs to combine geometric objects that live in different spaces.

It is therefore necessary to express all feature vectors
[\exp_{p}^{*}f](v)
in the same vector space and relative to the same gauge.
A natural idea, proposed by
Poulenard and Ovsjanikov 2018
, is to do this by
parallel transporting
the feature vectors along the geodesics that define the exponential map from
\exp_{p}(v)
to
v
.
26
26

26

The parallel transport along any other path would be equally valid.

We denote this pullback of
f
with additional transport as
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
to emphasizes its close relation to the usual pullback
\exp_{p}^{*}f
to
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
Fig.
22
gives a visual idea of this
transporter pullback
of feature fields to the tangent space and its representations
\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}
and
\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{B}
on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
relative to different coordinatizations.

Figure 22:
A feature field
f
on
M
and its local representation
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
via the
transporter pullback

\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}
.
Just like the usual pullback
\exp_{p}^{*}f
of
f
along the exponential map
\exp_{p}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to M
, the transporter pullback assigns feature vectors
f(\exp_{p}(v))
to tangent vectors
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
However, as we aim to accumulate the pulled back features by means of a convolution kernel, they need to be given in the same space and be expressed relative to the same gauge at
p
.
The transporter pullback therefore additionally applies the (
G
-compatible) parallel transporter along the geodesic from
\exp_{p}(v)
to
p
.
Via a gauge
\psi_{p}^{X}
, the transporter pullback of
f
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
can be expressed on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
as
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{X}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
– different choices of reference frames (observers) correspond hereby to different linear deformations of the feature field.
Kernel field transforms and
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions compute an output feature
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)
at
p
by matching a kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
with
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
(i.e. integrate their product over the tangent space; see Eq. (
76
)).

(Lizards and butterflies adapted under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

license

by courtesy of Twitter.)

We formalize
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
by defining it in terms of its coordinate expression relative to some choice of gauge.
To this end, let
\psi_{p}^{A}
be a gauge at
p
, relative to which the transported features will ultimately be expressed and let
\psi_{\exp_{p}(v)}^{\widetilde{A}}
be an arbitrary gauge at
\exp_{p}(v)
, which represents the feature vector at that location by a coefficient vector
f^{\widetilde{A}}(\exp_{p}(v))\in\mathbb{R}^{c}
.
Denote by

\displaystyle\rho\big(g^{A\widetilde{A}}_{p\leftarrow\exp_{p}\!v}\big)

(66)

the
G
-compatible parallel transporter of feature vector coefficients along the geodesic from
\exp_{p}(v)
to
p
.
Then we define the
transporter pullback
in coordinates as

\displaystyle\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}:\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c},\quad v^{A}

\displaystyle\mapsto\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}(v^{A})

\displaystyle\,:=\ \rho\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g^{A\widetilde{A}}_{p\,\leftarrow\,\exp_{p}(\psi_{p}^{A})^{\shortminus 1}(v^{A})}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\cdot f^{\widetilde{A}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\exp_{p}\big(\psi_{p}^{A}\big)^{\mkern-2.0mu-1}(v^{A})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\,,

(67)

where
v=\big(\psi_{p}^{A}\big)^{-1}(v^{A})\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
is the coordinate free tangent vector referred to by the coefficients
v^{A}
via
\psi_{p}^{A}
.
As claimed before, the choice of gauge
\psi_{\exp_{p}(v)}^{\widetilde{A}}
at
\exp_{p}(v)
is by the coordinate independence of all equations irrelevant and cancels out.
Specifically, one could have used any other gauge
\psi_{\exp_{p}(v)}^{\widetilde{B}}
at
\exp_{p}(v)
, implying gauge transformations

\rho\big(g^{A\widetilde{B}}_{p\,\leftarrow\,\exp_{p}(v)}\big)=\rho\big(g^{A\widetilde{A}}_{p\,\leftarrow\,\exp_{p}(v)}\big)\rho\big(g_{\exp_{p}(v)}^{\widetilde{B}\widetilde{A}}\big)^{-1}

of the transporter by Eq. (
35
) and

f^{\widetilde{B}}\big(\exp_{p}(v)\big)=\rho\big(g_{\exp_{p}(v)}^{\widetilde{B}\widetilde{A}}\big)f^{\widetilde{A}}\big(\exp_{p}(v)\big)

of the feature vector coefficients by Eq. (
28
), which annihilate when composing both expressions.

The transporter pullback
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{A}
depends, however, still on the gauge at
p
, and therefore transforms under gauge transformations
g_{p}^{BA}
at
p
.
As for any coordinatized function, its transformation law is determined by the gauge transformations on its domain
\mathbb{R}^{d}
and codomain
\mathbb{R}^{c}
.
It is therefore given by

\displaystyle\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{B}\ =\ \rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\circ\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}\circ\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\,,

(68)

which is summarized by the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g_{p}^{BA}\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\big[\mkern-1.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\big[\mkern-1.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{B}}

(69)

As visualized in Fig.
22
,
\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}
and
\big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{B}
should be thought of as the perspective of different local observers (reference frames) on the feature field.

In principle, one could consider alternative constructions for the pullback of feature fields from
M
to
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
Our definition of kernel field transforms and
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions in Sections
4.2.2
and
4.2.3
below is independent from this particular choice.

4.2.2
Coordinate independent kernels and kernel field transforms

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are coordinate independent operations which apply the same, shared kernel at each point of the manifold.
To clearly separate the assumptions being made, we first discuss more general
kernel field transforms
, which are coordinate independent operations but drop the requirement of weight sharing.
They are therefore similar to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions but apply a potentially different kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
to each point
p
of the manifold.
In order to respect the principle of covariance, the coordinate expressions of those kernels are required to transform in a principled manner, however, the kernels themselves are left unconstrained.

Coordinate independent kernels:

Since convolutions in deep learning map between fields of feature vectors of dimensionalities
\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textup{in}}}
and
\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textup{out}}}
, the convolution kernels are
{{c_{\textup{out}}}\mkern-3.0mu\times\mkern-1.5mu{c_{\textup{in}}}}
matrix-valued.
Discretized implementations of
d
-dimensional convolutions on Euclidean spaces typically represent such kernels as arrays of shape
(s_{1},\dots,s_{d},\;c_{\text{out}},c_{\text{in}}\mkern 1.0mu)
.
The first
d
axes represent hereby a spatial grid of
s_{1}\times\dots\times s_{d}
pixels, each of which is assigned a
{{c_{\textup{out}}}\mkern-3.0mu\times\mkern-1.5mu{c_{\textup{in}}}}
matrix, encoded in the last two axes.
27
27

27

The actual memory layout depends on the particular deep learning framework in consideration.

In the continuous, Euclidean setting, such kernels can be described as maps

\displaystyle K:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,,

(70)

which assign a
{{c_{\textup{out}}}\mkern-3.0mu\times\mkern-1.5mu{c_{\textup{in}}}}
matrix to each point of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
As mentioned in the previous Section
4.2.1
, we define
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions as matching the transporter pullback
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}

on the tangent space
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
with a kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
Since the tangent spaces are flat, it is natural to define this matching as in the usual, fully Euclidean setting.
We do therefore define the kernels
\mathcal{K}_{p}
via their coordinate expressions, which take the form in Eq. (
70
), that is,

\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,.

(71)

Fig.
23
shows a
given
coordinate free kernel on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
and its representations on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
relative to different reference frames.
28
28

28

We emphasize that we are here assuming a coordinate free kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
which is
given
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
and consider its coordinate expressions
\mathcal{K}_{p}^{X}
on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
relative to reference frames
X
.
Convolutional weight sharing will later on pose us with the question of how to
define
a coordinate free kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
given a template kernel
K
on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
Appendix
B
elaborates on these two concepts and their relation to the kernel’s
G
-steerability.

Figure 23:
A coordinate free kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
and its coordinate expressions
{\mathcal{K}_{p}^{X}\!:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
relative to gauges
\psi_{p}^{X}
(only one of the
{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
kernel channels is shown).
The gauge transformations that relate different coordinatizations of a kernel follow from the transformation laws of their domain
\mathbb{R}^{d}
and codomain
\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
.
They are therefore for any
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
given by

\mathcal{K}_{p}^{B}\big(g_{p}^{BA}{v}\big)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\>\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}({v})\>\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}
.
A kernel field
\mathcal{K}
on
M
is a smooth assignment of kernels over the tangent spaces (Def.
7.2
).

Note that we are here assuming the kernel on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
to be given and express it subsequently relative to different gauges on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
This is conceptually different from the situation depicted in
Figs.
1
,
4
,
16
and
69
,
where we assume a template kernel
K
to be given on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
and subsequently define
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
via convolutional weight sharing relative to some reference frame.
In order to preserve coordinate independence during the weight sharing process, the shared kernel needs to be
invariant
(or equivariant) under gauge transformations; see Section
4.2.3
and Appendix
B
.

The transformation law between the coordinate representations
\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}
and
\mathcal{K}_{p}^{B}
of a kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
follows as usual from the transformation laws of their domain and codomain.
On the domain
\mathbb{R}^{d}
the transformation law is given by
g_{p}^{BA}
, while the transformation law of
\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
is, as in Eq. (
50
), given by a simultaneous left multiplication with
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)
and right multiplication with
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}
.
The two coordinatizations of the kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
relate thus for any
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
by

\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{p}^{B}\big(g_{p}^{BA}{v}\big)\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot\mkern 1.0mu\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}({v})\mkern 1.0mu\cdot\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\,,

(72)

which is visualized by the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g_{p}^{BA}\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\;\scalebox{1.1}{$[\,\cdot\,]$}\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}_{p}^{B}}

(73)

As in the examples from Section
4.1
, the principle of covariance only requires a consistent transformation behavior between different kernel coordinatizations but does not lead to a constraint on the kernel itself.
One might therefore parameterize the kernels
\mathcal{K}_{p}
for any
p\in M
and an arbitrary gauge at
p
by some unrestricted, matrix-valued kernel.
We denote smooth fields of such kernels as kernel fields, which play a major role in our analysis of the isometry equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions in Section
8
.

Coordinate independent kernel field transforms:

Given a smooth kernel field
\mathcal{K}
, we can define
kernel field transforms
, which are similar to convolutions but differ in that they might apply a different kernel at each spatial position.
They compute a field of output feature vectors
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)
by
integrating the product of the corresponding kernel
\mathcal{K}_{p}
and transporter pullback
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
of
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
over
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
, that is,

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}(p)\ =\ \int_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}\mathcal{K}_{p}(v)\,\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}(v)\;dv\,.

(74)

To express this coordinate free definition in terms of coordinates, one has to replace all quantities by their coordinate expressions and to pull the integration via the chosen gauge from
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
As described in Appendix
C
, the appropriate (gauge invariant) Riemannian volume element is for a gauge
\psi_{p}^{A}
given by

\displaystyle\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\,\ dv^{A},

(75)

where the factor
\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}
, defined in Eq. (
599
), is the (positive) volume spanned by the reference frame
[e_{i}^{A}]_{i=1}^{d}
at
p
.
The coordinate expression of the kernel field transform thus reads

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\ =

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}(v^{A})\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}\mkern-1.0mu(v^{A})\ \sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ dv^{A}\,.

(76)

The coordinate independence of the kernel field transform is asserted by expressing it relative to an alternative gauge
\psi_{p}^{B}
and showing that the resulting output field transforms as expected, which is indeed the case:

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}(p)\ \overset{(1)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{K}_{p}^{B}(v^{B})\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{B}\mkern-2.0mu(v^{B})\,\ \sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|}\ dv^{B}

\displaystyle\overset{(2)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big[\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\!\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}v^{B}\big)\!\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\Big]\,\ \big[\mkern-1.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{B}\mkern-2.0mu(v^{B})\,\ \sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|}\ dv^{B}

\displaystyle\overset{(3)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}(v^{A})\,\ \Big[\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\big[\mkern-1.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{B}\mkern-2.0mu\big(g_{p}^{BA}v^{A}\big)\Big]\ \sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ dv^{A}

\displaystyle\overset{(4)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}(v^{A})\,\ \big[\mkern-1.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}\mkern-1.0mu(v^{A})\ \sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ dv^{A}

\displaystyle\overset{(5)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\,f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)

(77)

Here we used the definition of kernel field transforms and the transformation law of kernels (Eq. (
72
)) in the first two steps.
The third step follows by pulling
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
out of the integral and substituting
v^{B}
with
v^{A}=\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}v^{B}
, using that the volume element
\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|}\ dv^{B}=\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ dv^{A}
is by design gauge invariant.
The last two steps follow then by identifying the transformation law of the transporter pullback of the feature field in Eq. (
68
) and the definition of the kernel field transform in gauge
\psi_{p}^{A}
.
Note that the coordinate independence of the kernel field transform affirms the correctness of the kernel transformation law in Eq. (
72
).

A kernel field transform is only well defined if the integrals over the tangent spaces converge, which is more rigorously discussed in Section
7.2
and Appendix
G
.
Theorem
7.7
proves that a compact support of the kernels
\mathcal{K}_{p}
is sufficient to guarantee this well-definedness.
It further proves that kernel field transforms that are based on smooth kernel fields will map smooth input feature fields to smooth output feature fields.

4.2.3
GM
-convolutions and
G
-steerable kernels

The freedom of kernel field transforms to apply a different kernel at each location does not allow them to generalize learned inference over different locations and thus makes them data inefficient.
One does therefore typically consider convolutions, which can be seen as those specific kernel field transforms that are based on convolutional kernel fields, i.e. kernel fields that are parameterized by a single, shared template kernel.
As before, a coordinate independent weight sharing requires the template kernels to be gauge equivariant (
G
-steerable).
This gauge equivariance of the template kernels implies that patterns which appear in different,
G
-related geometric poses are guaranteed to evoke the same response up to a corresponding transformation of the feature vector via
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
.

Convolutional weight sharing:

Let
K:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
be a template kernel to be shared over all tangent spaces.
In order to not prefer any particular gauge – which would contradict our requirement for coordinate independence – we are forced to share the kernel with coordinatizations in all gauges simultaneously.
Naively, this seems to suggest to share the template kernel by setting
\mathcal{K}_{p}^{X}=K
for any point
p\in M
and any gauge
\psi_{p}^{X}
at
p
.
While such a definition of kernel sharing seems reasonable, it does not follow our principle of sharing local template functions in a strict sense:
instead of directly sharing the kernel, it is important to share the
whole
local operation – which is here the whole
integral transform in Eq. (
76
).
Since this operation is parameterized in terms of the kernel field
\mathcal{K}
, this leads indirectly to a sharing of the template kernel, however, with a slightly different result as the naive sharing considered above.

To find the correct definition of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutional kernel fields according to our principle of sharing local template functions, we first need to identify these local operations.
We do this by abstracting kernel field transforms (in coordinates) as a collection of local integral operators of the form

\displaystyle{I}_{\mathcal{K},p}^{A}:\ C^{\infty}\big(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{c}\big)\to\mathbb{R}^{c},\quad F\,\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{K}_{p}^{A}({v})\,F({v})\,\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ d{v}\,,

(78)

where
C^{\infty}\big(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{c}\big)
denotes the space of smooth maps from
\mathbb{R}^{d}
to
\mathbb{R}^{c}
.
In our application, these smooth maps are just the local feature field representations
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{A}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
as seen from the tangent spaces at
p
, which are by the kernel field transform mapped to an output feature vector
f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)={I}_{\mathcal{K},p}^{A}\big([\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{A}\big)
at
p
.
Given our template kernel
K:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
, we define a corresponding integral operator template

\displaystyle\mathfrak{I}_{K}:\ C^{\infty}\big(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{c}\big)\to\mathbb{R}^{c},\quad F\,\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\,F({v})\ d{v}\,,

(79)

which multiplies the local field representation
F
with the template kernel
K
and then integrates their product.
Note that
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
is as a template function necessarily agnostic to specific choices of gauges and does therefore not involve a frame volume factor.
A
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent convolutional weight sharing scheme is imposed by demanding that this template functional agrees with all the individual integral operators at any point and in any gauge, that is,

\displaystyle\mkern 28.0mu{I}_{\mathcal{K},p}^{X}=\mathfrak{I}_{K}\quad\textup{for \emph{any} gauge}\ \ \big(U^{X},\psi^{X})\in{A}^{G}\ \ \textup{with}\ \ p\in U^{X}\,,

(80)

where
{A}^{G}
is the (maximal)
G
-atlas corresponding to the considered
G
-structure; see Eq. (
25
).
This is equivalent to directly sharing the local template kernel according to

\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{p}^{X}=\frac{K}{\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{X}|}\,}\quad\textup{for \emph{any} gauge}\ \ \big(U^{X},\psi^{X})\in{A}^{G}\ \ \textup{with}\ \ p\in U^{X}\,,

(81)

where the normalization factor reduces the “kernel density” by the reference frame volume
\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{X}|}
.
As discussed below, this normalization is important for the equivariance under non-volume-preserving symmetry groups

We denote kernel fields which are parameterized by a shared kernel
K
according to Eq. (
81
) as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-
convolutional kernel fields
.
The simultaneous requirement for weight sharing and coordinate independence leads to an equivariance constraint on the template kernels.
To derive this constraint, insert the kernel sharing in Eq. (
81
) into the kernel transformation law in Eq. (
72
), which results in

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|\,}}\ K\big(g_{p}^{BA}{v}\big)\ =\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|\,}}\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)\cdot\mkern 1.0muK({v})\mkern 1.0mu\cdot\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)^{-1}\,.

(82)

Since the volumes of different reference frames are related by

\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}=\big|\mkern-2.0mu\det(g_{p}^{BA})\big|\,\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|}

and since the transformation law needs to hold for arbitrary
G
-related gauges, this implies the
G
-steerability
constraint
29
29

29

In contrast to prior work
[
235
,
234
,
38
,
111
,
48
]
, this constraint contains the factor
|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|
.
It did not appear in these works since they all considered (subgroups of) orthonormal structure groups
\operatorname{O}(d)
, for which the determinant factor vanishes.

\displaystyle K(g\mkern 1.5mu{v})\ =\ \frac{1}{|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\cdot K({v})\cdot\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\qquad\forall\ \ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \ g\in G\,.

(83)

on template kernels.
As proven by
Lang and Weiler 2020
, this constraint requires template kernels to be
representation operators

[

(generalizations of e.g. spherical tensor operators in quantum mechanics).
Diagrammatically, a

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \scalebox{.96}{$\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|}$}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\;\scalebox{1.1}{$[\,\cdot\,]$}\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}

(84)

for any
g\in G
.
Note that the inverse determinant factor
|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|
in the kernel’s transformation law makes it transform like a
matrix-valued
-1
-density
; see Table
2
for more details.
Intuitively,
G
-steerable kernels are exactly those kernels that can be shared relative to arbitrary
G
-related reference frames without that the particular choice of gauge would influence the result.
30

The

{K({v})=|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}1}\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.5muK(g^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}1}{v})\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.5mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}1}}

\mkern 8.0mu\forall\ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ g\in G
,
which emphasizes that
G
-steerable kernels are the
invariants
under the gauge action on the right-hand-side.
Being invariant under gauge transformations, a
G
-steerable kernel leads to the same coordinate free kernel

at

when being shared relative to any reference frame in
G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM

The ambiguity of kernel alignments – which motivated this work in the first place – is thus resolved by additional weight sharing over all the equivalent reference frames (all gauges) in the considered

Before coming to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, we comment on the space of
G
-steerable kernels.
Note that the set

\displaystyle{K}\ :=\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}K\!:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}\,.

(85)

of general, i.e. not necessarily equivariant kernels forms a vector space when being equipped with the standard summation and scalar multiplication on
\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
.
Since the
G
-steerability constraint in Eq. (
83
) is linear, it restricts the kernel space to a
linear subspace

\displaystyle{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}\,:=\ \Big\{K\!:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,\Big|\,K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=\frac{1}{|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|}\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\mkern-1.5mu\cdot\mkern-1.5muK({v})\mkern-1.5mu\cdot\mkern-1.5mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\ \ \ \forall\,\ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,\ g\in G\Big\}\,.

(86)

It is therefore possible to solve for a basis of
G
-steerable kernels, in terms of which the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution can be parameterized.
While this space is in theory usually infinite-dimensional, it is in practice often being discretized, such that one ends up with a finite basis
\{K_{1},\dots,K_{N}\}
of
G
-steerable kernels.
A set
\{w_{1},\dots,w_{N}\}
of real-valued weights
w_{i}\in\mathbb{R}
, which are optimized during the training process, then parameterize the convolution with
K=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}K_{i}
.
Note that the reduced dimensionality of the (sub)space of
G
-steerable kernels implies an improved parameter efficiency in comparison to conventional convolutions.

Section
5.3.3
discusses exemplary analytical solutions of reflection equivariant kernels spaces for different group representations of the reflection group
{R}
.
The resulting kernels, which are characterized by different types of reflectional symmetries, are visualized in Table
3
.

Further examples can be found in the literature on steerable CNNs:
an analytical solution of the kernel space constraint for the special orthogonal structure group
\operatorname{SO}(3)
in three dimensions and its irreducible representations was presented by
Weiler et al. 2018a
.

Weiler and Cesa 2019
generalized this approach to cover arbitrary group representations and solved the kernel space constraint for any representation of
\operatorname{O}(2)
and all of its subgroups
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)

– an implementation is available at
https://quva-lab.github.io/e2cnn/api/e2cnn.kernels.html
.
For finite structure groups the constraint might alternatively be solved numerically as explained by
Cohen and Welling 2017
.
A more general solution strategy, applying to arbitrary compact structure groups
G
(and thus all above mentioned cases), was proposed by
Lang and Weiler 2020
.
This solution generalizes the classical
Wigner-Eckart
theorem
[
1
,
104
,
239
,
240
]
to a Wigner-Eckart theorem for
G
-steerable kernels, which expresses the kernels in terms of harmonic basis functions, Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and endomorphisms of the representations (generalized reduced matrix elements).
We refer to
[
128
]
for a more detailed overview on prior and related work on steerable kernels.

GM
-coordinate independent convolutions:

Given a
G
-steerable template kernel
K\in{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
, the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution
K\star
with this kernel is defined as the kernel field transform with the corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutional kernel field, satisfying
\mathcal{K}_{p}^{X}=K/\sqrt{|\eta^{X}|}
for any point
p\in M
and any gauge
\psi_{p}^{X}
.
By inserting the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutional kernel field into Eq. (
76
), i.e. the kernel field transform, the coordinate expression of the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution boils down to

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\ =\ \big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}(p)\ :=

\displaystyle\,\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\!K({v})\,\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{\mkern-2.0muA}\mkern-1.0mu({v})\;d{v}\ \ =\,\ \mathfrak{I}_{K}\big([\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}]^{A}\big)\,.

(87)

It is thus simply given by matching the transporter pullback
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}]^{A}
of the feature field in an
arbitrarily chosen gauge

\psi_{p}^{A}
with the
gauge independent
convolution kernel
K
.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent convolutions are therefore easily implemented by
1) choosing arbitrary reference frames,
2) pulling (and transporting) the feature fields back to the tangent space coordinatizations and
3) contracting them there with a (trainable)
G
-steerable kernel.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions exhibit multiple related symmetry properties:

coordinate independence:

As specific instances of kernel field transforms,
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are (passively) coordinate independent, i.e. Eq. (
4.2.2
) applies to them.

global isometry equivariance:

They are equivariant under the
active
,
global
action of
G
-structure preserving isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
on feature fields.
Sections
4.3
and specifically
8
discuss this property in detail.

local
G
-equivariance:

The integral operator template
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
is by the
G
-steerability of
K
itself
G
-equivariant.
Any
G
-transformation of a local feature field representation on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
will therefore result in a corresponding transformation of the resulting feature vector; see Fig.
24
.
Independent
G
-transformations of patterns that are centered at different points
p_{i}\in M
will therefore lead to independent output feature transformations at these points (this holds
only
at these points and requires compactly supported kernels whose entire
field of view
transforms according to the
G
-transformation).

Figure 24:
Local
G
-equivariance of the shared integral operator template
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
underlying a
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution
K\star
.
An active
G
-transformation
\textphnc{b}_{\mkern-5.0mu\textup{in}}(g)
of a local field representation on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
moves feature vectors from
g^{-1}{v}
to
{v}
and transforms them additionally via
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)
.
While the former moves features spatially, the latter transforms their numerical coefficients (visualized as rotation and scaling of the individual (tangent) vectors in the figure).
The application of
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
to both inputs results in different output feature vectors.
However, by the
G
-equivariance of
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
, the responses are guaranteed to be related by
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)
; see Eq. (
4.2.3
).
An active
G
-transformation of an input field therefore results in a corresponding active
G
-transformation of the output feature vector.
Note that the
G
-equivariance of
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
is a direct consequence of the
G
-steerability of
K
.

To make the last point precise, we define active

-transformations of local feature field representations in

as

.
The claimed
G
-equivariance of
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
is easily seen by applying it to a transformed input, followed by a substitution and making use of the

-steerability of
