:

\displaystyle\qquad\mathfrak{I}_{K}\big(\textphnc{b}_{\mkern-5.0mu\textup{in}}(g)F\big)\ =

\displaystyle\ \mathfrak{I}_{K}\big(\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\circ F\circ g^{-1}\big)\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{def. of $\textphnc{b}_{\mkern-5.0mu\textup{in}}$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:local_field_G_trafo} }\big)

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\,F\big(g^{-1}{v})\ d{v}\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{def. of $\mathfrak{I}_{K}$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:local_integral_operator_template} }\big)

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K(g\mkern 1.0mu\tilde{{v}})\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\,F\big(\tilde{{v}})\;|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|\ d\tilde{{v}}\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{substitution of $\tilde{{v}}=g^{-1}{v}$ }\big)

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\,K(\tilde{{v}})\;F\big(\tilde{{v}})\ d\tilde{{v}}\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{$G$-steerability of $K$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:kernel_constraint} }\big)

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\;\mathfrak{I}_{K}(F)\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{def. of $\mathfrak{I}_{K}$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:local_integral_operator_template} }\big)

(89)

An active transformation of a local feature field representation
F
on some tangent space coordinatization by
\textphnc{b}_{\mkern-5.0mu\textup{in}}(g)
is therefore guaranteed to lead to a transformation of the resulting output feature vector by
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)
.
In other words, features which appear in different
G
-related geometric poses will evoke the same response up to a transformation via
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
.
In terms of a commutative diagram, this is concisely summarized as:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{I}_{K}\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textphnc{b}_{\mkern-5.0mu\textup{in}}(g)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \mathfrak{I}_{K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)}

(90)

Fig.
24
gives a visual interpretation of this equivariance property of
\mathfrak{I}_{K}
.

Note that the equivariance under local
G
-transformations in Eq. (
4.2.3
) requires the
G
-steerability constraint exactly as it is in Eq. (
83
), that is, in particular,
with
the determinant factor
|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|^{-1}
which makes the kernel transform like a
-1
-density.
This factor is traced back to our definition of convolutional weight sharing in Eq. (
81
)
with
the normalization by the reference frame volumes
\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{X}|}
.
The naive weight sharing mentioned in the beginning of this section would therefore not have lead to the desired transformation behavior.
In other words: both the naive and the normalized version of the kernel sharing are coordinate independent and behave therefore both consistently under passive gauge transformations – in particular such which change the frame volume.
However, in the case of the naive kernel sharing, this is taken care of by the invariance of the Riemannian volume element
\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{A}|}\ dv^{A}=\sqrt{|\eta_{p}^{B}|}\ dv^{B}
.
By
canceling
this factor in the normalized weight sharing, the consistency of the transformation behavior is not guaranteed by the integration measure itself anymore – which requires the
G
-steerable kernels themselves to explain volume changes via the determinant factor.
Only the latter generalizes to active transformations, where only the feature field is transformed, while the integration measure stays invariant.

As our definition of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions allows for arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, G-structures and field types, it is quite general and covers a wide range of related work.
We substantiate this claim in Part
8.3.2
, where we explain many CNNs on Euclidean affine spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
, the sphere
S^{2}
and general manifolds or meshes as specific instantiations of Eq. (
87
).
For an overview and a classification of these models, we refer to Table
.

4.3
Isometry equivariance

Figure 25:
A network layer is said to be equivariant under isometries when it commutes with their action on feature fields.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are by design equivariant w.r.t. those isometries
\phi\in\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
that are symmetries of the
G
-structure.
In equations, the convolution
K\star
is equivariant under the action of an isometry
\phi
when it satisfies the relation

{K\star\big(\phi\rhd\!f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big)=\phi\rhd\!\big(K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big)}

for any choice of input field
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
.
This relation is visualized by the commutative diagram in Eq. (
92
), a graphical interpretation of which is shown in this figure.

That
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant relies on the facts that
1) kernels are shared over the whole manifold,
2) isometries preserve the transporter pullback of feature fields and
3) that
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
induces
G
-valued gauge transformations, which are accounted for by the kernel’s
G
-steerability.

(Lizards adapted under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

license

by courtesy of Twitter.)

Given that a manifold exhibits symmetries it is usually desirable that neural networks respect these symmetries, i.e. are equivariant under their action on feature fields.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are by design guaranteed to be
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant, which means that they commute with the action of isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
on feature fields, as visualized in Fig.
25
.
32
32

32

Recall that an action on
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent feature fields can only be defined for the
G
-structure preserving isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
.
It is therefore not even possible to define a notion of isometry equivariance for isometries that are not symmetries the
G
-structure.
Note that this is without loss of generality since one can always choose a structure group
G=\operatorname{O}(d)
, for which
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\Isom(\mkern-1.5muM\mkern-0.5mu)
coincides with the full isometry group.

.
Expressed in equations, the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution
K\star
is equivariant when it satisfies the relation

\displaystyle K\star\big(\phi\rhd\!f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big)\ =\ \phi\rhd\!\big(K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big)\qquad\forall\ \ \phi\in\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}

(91)

for any possible input field
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
, that is, when the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd}

(92)

As a first step towards proving the isometry equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, recall that they are pointwise defined as the contraction of a kernel
K
with the transporter pullback
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}]^{A}
of the input field
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
.
Since isometries preserve the Riemannian geometry of
M
by definition, they preserve in particular the Riemannian exponential map and Levi-Civita transporters; see Section
8.1.4
and Fig.
42
.
33
33

33

More generally, whenever an alternative
G
-compatible connection is chosen to transport feature vectors, we assume this connection to be invariant under the action of
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
; see Section
8.1.4
.
This assumption is satisfied for all models that are covered in the literature review in Part
8.3.2
.

This implies that the transporter pullback of the pushforward field
\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
at
\phi(p)
will only differ from the transporter pullback of the original field
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}
at
p
by the isometry induced gauge transformation, that is,

\displaystyle\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{\phi(p)}(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big]^{A}\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\big)\circ\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{\widetilde{A}}\circ g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)^{-1}\,;

(93)

cf. Eq. (
68
) and, for the coordinate free formulation, Theorem
8.4
.

Given this identity, the isometry equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions
is proven by the following simple calculation, which crucially leverages the
G
-steerability of the template kernel
K
to explain away the isometry induced gauge action:

\displaystyle\big[K\star(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big]^{A}(\phi(p))\ \overset{(1)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{\phi(p)}(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big]^{A}({v})\ d{v}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(2)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ \Big[\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{\widetilde{A}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)^{-1}{v}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\Big]\ d{v}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(3)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big[K\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\,\tilde{{v}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\Big]\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{\widetilde{A}}(\tilde{{v}})\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\mkern-3.0mu\det g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\;d\tilde{{v}}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(4)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big[\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}K\big(\tilde{{v}}\big)\Big]\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{\widetilde{A}}(\tilde{{v}})\ d\tilde{{v}}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(5)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\big)\cdot f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{\widetilde{A}}(p)

\displaystyle\ \overset{(6)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \big[\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}\big]^{A}(\phi(p))

\displaystyle\ \overset{(7)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \big[\phi\rhd\big(K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big)\big]^{A}(\phi(p))

(94)

The first step follows hereby from the definition of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions in Eq. (
87
) while the second step inserted the induced gauge transformation according to Eq. (
93
).
A substitution from
{v}
to
\tilde{{v}}=g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)^{-1}\mkern 1.0mu{v}
justifies step three.
In the fourth step the
G
-steerability of the template kernel, i.e. Eq. (
83
), is applied (recall Eq. (
44
), which states that the
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-induced gauge transformations are
G
-valued).
What follows is that the resulting output feature vector is transformed by the induced gauge transformation.
After identifying this as the coordinate expression of the pushforward of the output field in Eq. (
46
), the statement follows.
As all steps are valid for arbitrary isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
, we see that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are automatically equivariant w.r.t. any
G
-structure preserving isometry
.
They are
not
necessarily equivariant w.r.t. general isometries in
\Isom(\mkern-1.5muM\mkern-0.5mu)
, which might disrespect the
G
-structure, however, full isometry equivariance is guaranteed for orthonormal structure groups
G=\operatorname{O}(d)
(or supergroups of it).

Invariant kernel fields:

A more in depth analysis of the isometry equivariance of general kernel field transforms can be found in Sections
8.2
and
8.3
.
The central result of this investigation is Theorem
8.8
, which states that
the isometry equivariance of a kernel field transform implies the isometry invariance of its kernel field
and vice versa.
Fig
43
visualizes such an invariant kernel field, which is required to share weights over the orbits of the isometry action.
The required invariance of the kernel field is intuitively plausible since isometry equivariance certainly requires the inference of the network to be the constant on each orbit.
This abstract results implies the isometry equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions by observing that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutional kernel fields – which are determined by a single, shared template kernel – are invariant under isometries in
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
; see Theorem
8.9
and Fig.
9
.
The template kernel’s
G
-steerability accounts thereby for the invariance of kernels under the action of stabilizer subgroups of the isometry group.

Homogeneous spaces:

While the demand for isometry equivariance requires kernels to be shared over orbits of the isometry group, it does in general not require convolutional weight sharing over the whole manifold.
An important exception is the case of manifolds that are
homogeneous spaces
of their isometry group, like for instance
\mathbb{R}^{d}
or the sphere
S^{2}
.
By definition, the isometry action is on such spaces transitive, that is, there exists only one single orbit.
Consequently, there will only be one independent kernel, which is via the action of the isometry group being shared over the whole space.
Theorem
8.14
in Section
8.3
proves that
isometry equivariant kernel field transforms on homogeneous spaces are necessarily coordinate independent convolutions
.
This observation establishes a formal link between our theory and prior work on convolutional networks on homogeneous spaces
by
Kondor and Trivedi 2018
,
Cohen et al. 2019a
and
Bekkers 2020
,
who are defining convolutions via their equivariance w.r.t. global symmetries of the underlying space.

Diffeomorphism equivariance:

The reader might wonder whether it is possible to make our coordinate independent CNNs fully diffeomorphism equivariant.
As one can easily see, the pointwise operations from Section
4.1
, i.e.
{1\kern-2.65pt\times\kern-3.0pt1}
-convolutions
, biases and nonlinearities, are already diffeomorphism equivariant.
Specifically, let

\displaystyle\Diff_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\ :=\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\phi\in\Diff(M)\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\ \big[\phi_{*}(e_{i})\big]_{i=1}^{d}\in G\mkern-1.4muM\quad\forall\ [e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\in G\mkern-1.4muM\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}\,\ \leq\ \Diff(M)

(95)

be the subgroup of
G
-structure preserving diffeomorphisms, i.e. the analog to Eq. (
42
) without the requirement on
\phi
to be an isometry.
Similarly to Eq. (
44
) and Theorem
8.3
, the coordinate expressions (induced gauge transformations) of
G
-structure preserving diffeomorphisms are guaranteed to take values in
G
, that is,

\displaystyle\phi\in\Diff_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\in G\ \ \ \forall\ p\mkern-1.0mu\in\mkern-2.0muM\,.

(96)

The
G
-equivariance of the shared pointwise template functions will guarantee that they commute with these
\Diff_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-induced gauge transformations – and therefore with the active diffeomorphism action itself.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions with spatially extended kernels, on the other hand, are in general
not
equivariant w.r.t. diffeomorphisms.
The reason for this is that the transporter pullback
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
relies on exponential maps, which are inherently Riemannian constructions that do not commute with diffeomorphisms.
However, as the kernels are
G
-steerable,
\Diff_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariance should nonetheless hold in the limit of the kernel support going to zero.
Given that convolution kernels are in typical deep learning applications quite small, diffeomorphism equivariance should in practice hold approximately.

Affine equivariance:

Euclidean spaces constitute a special case since they allow for
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions that are equivariant under the action of
affine groups

\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
That this is the case relies on the fact that the exponential map commutes on Euclidean spaces not only with the action of isometries but more generally with affine transformations.
The affine group equivariance of Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions is proven in Section
9.3
.

5
Toy model: reflection equivariant Möbius convolutions

To make the theoretical considerations in the previous sections more tangible, we turn now to an example application.
While not being of immediate practical importance,
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on the Möbius strip are a suitable toy model since its geometry and the involved representation theory are particularly simple.
Due to its non-orientability, reference frames can only be (smoothly) preferred up to reflections.
As expected, coordinate independent CNNs, applying reflection equivariant template functions, outperform a naive, coordinate dependent implementation.
They are furthermore shown to be equivariant under the action of the Möbius strip’s isometry group.

The following Section
5.1
discusses the geometry of the flat Möbius strip.
Due to its twist, its structure group can not be reduced further than to the reflection group
G={R}
, such that one needs to consider a
{R}
-atlas of gauges as visualized in Fig.
26
.
The isometry group is given by rotations along the strip and induces
{R}
-valued gauge transformations.

{R}\mkern-1.8muM
-coordinate independent feature fields, some of which are introduced in Section
5.2
, necessarily have to transform according to some representation of the reflection group.
Section
5.3
discusses orientation independent convolutional network operations.
This clarifies in particular the concept of
G
-steerable kernels but also covers reflection equivariant biases and nonlinearities.
A numerical implementation of the proposed model family is discussed and evaluated in Section
5.4
.
The code is publicly available at
https://github.com/mauriceweiler/MobiusCNNs
.

5.1
Geometry of the Möbius strip

The manifold
M
under consideration is the flat Möbius strip with boundary as shown in Fig.
3
(right).
It can be thought of as being constructed by taking a rectangular subset
[0,X]\times[0,Y]
of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
and gluing two opposing ends together in a twisted way.
Such defined, the Möbius strip inherits the canonical metric of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, which endows it with a Riemannian structure.
The metric specifies in particular a Levi-Civita connection and therefore exponential maps and parallel transporters, which are further discussed below.

Figure 26:
The flat geometry of the Möbius strip allows for local subsets which can be isometrically identified with corresponding subsets of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
.
We fix an isometric atlas, consisting of two charts
x^{A}
and
x^{B}
on
U^{A}
(red) and
U^{B}
(green), which cover the whole strip.
Gauges
\psi_{p}^{X}=\hat{d}x_{p}^{X}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
for
p\in U^{A}
are induced as chart differentials.
Due to the twist of the Möbius strip, the transition functions
g_{p}^{BA}
will at one of the overlapping regions be trivial, while the other region will necessarily transition between gauges via flips
s
.
The chosen atlas of charts therefore induces an
{R}
-atlas of gauges and implies a corresponding
{R}
-structure
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
, consisting of two reflected frames at each point of
M
.
Each of the charts
x^{X}
induces a smooth local frame field, given by the coordinate bases

\Big[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}^{X}}\mkern-1.0mu\big|_{p}\Big]\raisebox{-2.0pt}{$\rule{0.0pt}{11.0pt}_{i=1}^{d}$}
.
The flip in the transition functions at one overlap shows in a reflection of frames.

(Lizards adapted under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

license

by courtesy of Twitter.)

A first question to answer when constructing a coordinate independent CNN is to which extent the choice of reference frames is ambiguous.
Given the Riemannian metric on the strip, we can restrict our attention to orthonormal frames.
One can furthermore single out one of the two directions
along
the strip to (smoothly) disambiguate the rotation of the reference frames by aligning their first axes with this direction.
This leaves us with an ambiguity of frame handedness, with the two orientations corresponding to the two possible directions of the second frame axis perpendicular to the strip.
Being a non-orientable manifold, the Möbius strip does not admit a globally smooth (or even continuous) choice of frame orientations.
To get an intuition about this statement, consider the attempt of constructing a smooth frame field by picking an arbitrary frame at a random position and to smoothly extend this choice over the whole strip.
After one revolution around the strip the constructed frames will unavoidably be reflected w.r.t. the initial frames, and therefore contradict the desired smoothness.
It is thus topologically
impossible
to define an
\{e\}
-structure, i.e. a globally smooth field of frames, on the Möbius strip.
We are thus left with an irreducible structure group

\displaystyle G\,=\,{R}\,\cong\,\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\,,

(97)

which models the reflection of frames.
The reflection group contains only two elements, the identity
e
and the reflection (Spiegelung)
s
, which are composed according to the following simple multiplication table:

e

s

e

e

s

s

s

e

The only nontrivial statement in this table is that two reflections annihilate, that is,
s^{2}=e
, or, equivalently,
s^{-1}=s
.
Given the irreducibility of the structure group
{R}
, we will in the following need to consider the corresponding
{R}
-structure
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
which consists of two frames of opposing handedness at each point on the Möbius strip.

To encode smooth
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
-coordinate independent feature fields on
M
, one needs to specify an
{R}
-atlas, consisting of
{R}
-related gauges that cover the whole strip.
We choose to do this by fixing an atlas of
charts

\displaystyle x^{X}:U^{X}\to V^{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}

(101)

which cover the strip, and subsequently induce the gauges from it.
Fig.
26
visualizes such an atlas, consisting of two charts
x^{A}
and
x^{B}
on
U^{A}
(red) and
U^{B}
(green) which map two overlapping halves of the strip isometrically to corresponding rectangular regions of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
.
As described in Appendix
A.3
, the charts induce gauges, which are given by the chart differentials, that is,

\displaystyle\psi_{p}^{X}\,:=\,\hat{d}x^{X}_{p}:\ T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\ \ \ \textup{for any}\,\ p\in U^{X}\,\ \text{and}\,\ X=A,B\,.

(102)

The transition functions coincide then with the Jacobians

g^{BA}=\frac{\partial x^{B}}{\partial x^{A}}
.
Due to the twist, the transition maps are at one of the two overlapping regions all trivial, that is,
g_{p}^{BA}=e
, and on the other end necessarily reflected, i.e.
g_{p}^{BA}=s
.
The induced atlas of gauges is therefore indeed identified as an
{R}
-atlas.
Being derived from coordinate charts, the smooth local frame fields corresponding to the gauges are just the usual coordinate bases, that is, the frames
\big[e_{i}^{X}\big]_{i=1}^{d}
at
p\in U^{X}
are given by

\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}^{X}}\mkern-1.0mu\big|_{p}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\raisebox{-2.0pt}{$\rule{0.0pt}{11.0pt}_{i=1}^{d}$}
.
Since the charts are isometric, the induced frame field is automatically orthonormal.
However, the two rectangular regions
V^{A}
and
V^{B}
in
\mathbb{R}^{2}
must not be rotated relative to each other in order to induce an
{R}
-atlas and a corresponding
{R}
-structure
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
.

We need to emphasize that the approach of inducing gauges via coordinate charts is not strictly necessary
– it is just a convenient option since the
flat
Möbius strip is locally identified with regions of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
in an
isometric
way.
This will later allow us to transfer regular sampling grids from
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, like for instance the pixel grid
\mathbb{Z}^{2}
, to regular sampling grids on the strip.
As this is not possible for manifolds that are not locally flat, for instance meshes in computer graphics, most implementations on general manifolds (or meshes) assign coordinates immediately to the tangent spaces; see Section
12
.

The canonical Levi-Civita connection on the Möbius strip defines a notion of parallel transport of tangent vectors.
Since the strip is locally isometric to the plane
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, this transport can on local patches be understood as flattening these patches out into a plane and moving the vectors as usual on
\mathbb{R}^{2}
.
If no single patch can cover a path
\gamma
, there will be an open covering such that the full transport is explained by a sequence of transporters over the local patches.
It is easy to see that the transport will relative to frames of the chosen
{R}
-structure take values
g_{\gamma}^{A\widetilde{A}}
in the reflection group
{R}
.
This means that the Levi-Civita connection is
{R}
-compatible with
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
.
It does therefore imply well defined transporters
\rho\big(g_{\gamma}^{A\widetilde{A}}\big)
of
{R}
-associated feature vectors.

The group
\Isom_{{R}\mkern-1.8muM}
of isometries that preserve the
{R}
-structure contains all rotations which shift the strip along itself.
Note that a rotation once around the strip, which we denote by an angle of
2\pi
, does
not
correspond to the identity but rather maps the strip in a reflected way on itself.
Only a rotation by
4\pi
, i.e. two full revolutions, map the strip back to itself.
34
34

34

The Möbius strip is therefore seen to have the cylinder as double cover.

The action of the isometry group on the manifold and on reference frames is visualized in Fig.
27
.
Relative to coordinates, the isometry action will induce
{R}
-valued gauge transformations.

Figure 27:
Visualization of the group of
{R}
-structure preserving isometries
\Isom_{{R}\mkern-1.8muM}
of the Möbius strip, which is isomorphic to
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
It consists of all rotations along the strip.
Due to the twist, a rotation by
2\pi
, i.e. once around the strip, does not yet map it back to itself but results in a reflection.
After a second revolution, that is, a total rotation of
4\pi
, the strip is mapped back to itself.
Induced gauge transformations take values in
{R}
.

(Lizards adapted under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

license

by courtesy of Twitter.)

5.2
Orientation independent feature fields

The principle of covariance requires the feature fields on the Möbius strip to be
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
-coordinate independent, that is, they need to be equivalently expressible relative to frames of either handedness.
They are therefore characterized by a choice of group representation
\rho:{R}\to\operatorname{GL}(c)
of the reflection group, which specifies the transformation of numerical feature vectors when switching between the two orientations.
We will in the following discuss a few possible choices of such field types.
The reader might want to check that the proposed representations are indeed group homomorphisms, satisfying
\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)\,\ \forall\,g,h\in{R}
, as demanded in Section
3.2
and footnote
15
.

The most basic example, which exists for any structure group, is the
trivial representation

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}:{R}\to\operatorname{GL}(1)\ ,\qquad\begin{aligned} e&\mapsto\big[\mkern 2.0mu1\mkern 2.0mu\big]\\[2.0pt]
s&\mapsto\big[\mkern 2.0mu1\mkern 2.0mu\big]\\
\end{aligned}\quad,

(103)

which assigns the
{1\!\times\!1}
identity matrix to both group elements.
It models scalar fields
f_{\textup{triv}}
, which consist of one-dimensional feature vectors whose coordinatizations
f^{A}_{\textup{triv}}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{1}
stay
invariant under frame reflections
.
A second one-dimensional representation is the
sign-flip representation

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}:{R}\to\operatorname{GL}(1)\ ,\qquad\begin{aligned} e&\mapsto\big[\mkern 2.0mu1\mkern 2.0mu\big]\\[2.0pt]
s&\mapsto\big[\!\shortminus\!1\big]\end{aligned}\quad.

(104)

It assigns the negative
{1\!\times\!1}
identity matrix to reflections, and therefore describes pseudoscalar fields, i.e. one-dimensional feature fields
f_{\textup{sign}}
, whose numerical coefficients
f^{A}_{\textup{sign}}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{1}

change their sign under reflections
,
that is,

{\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}(s)\cdot f^{A}_{\textup{sign}}(p)=-f^{A}_{\textup{sign}}(p)}
.
Since the trivial representation and the sign-flip representation are one-dimensional, they are both irreducible representations (irreps) of the reflection group.
In fact, they are the only two irreps of the reflection group.
35
35

35

The reflection group is isomorphic to the cyclic group
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
of order two.
It is well known that the irreps of cyclic groups of order
N
correspond to the
N
-th roots of unity, which are for
N=2
just
+1
(trivial) and
-1
(sign-flip).

Since
{R}
is a finite group, it has a finite-dimensional (two-dimensional)
regular representation

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}:{R}\to\operatorname{GL}(2)\ ,\qquad\begin{aligned} e&\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-4.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-4.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\\[2.0pt]
s&\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-4.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-4.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}\quad,

(105)

which represents the group elements by permutation matrices.
By definition, the regular representation models the permutation of the group elements in
{R}
when acting on themselves.
Compare this to the columns of the multiplication table in Eq. (
5.1
):
the middle column can be thought of as originating from the action of
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(e)
on the leftmost column, while the swapped group elements in the right column correspond to the permutation described by the action of
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)
on the left column.
The regular feature fields
f_{\textup{reg}}
of
{R}
are numerically represented by two-dimensional feature vectors
f^{A}_{\textup{reg}}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}
whose two
channels are swapped under reflections
, that is,

\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-2.0muf^{A}_{\textup{reg}}(p)\,=\,\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-4.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-4.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-4.0mu\cdot\mkern-4.0mu\begin{bmatrix}f^{A}_{\textup{reg},1}\\
f^{A}_{\textup{reg},2}\end{bmatrix}\!(p)\,=\,\begin{bmatrix}f^{A}_{\textup{reg},2}\\
f^{A}_{\textup{reg},1}\end{bmatrix}\!(p)
.

The regular representation is reducible, that is, it contains two proper invariant subspaces, which correspond in this case to the trivial and the sign-flip representation.
It can therefore equivalently be thought of as being constructed of the direct sum
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\oplus\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}
of those two irreps and a change of basis
Q
:

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(g)\ =\ Q\,\big(\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\!\oplus\mkern-1.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}\big)\mkern-2.0mu(g)\;Q^{\top}\quad\ \textup{where }\quad Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}

(106)

The validity of this statement is easily asserted by inserting the r.h.s. for both group elements:

\displaystyle Q\,\big(\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\!\oplus\mkern-1.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}\big)\mkern-2.0mu(e)\;Q^{\top}\ =\ \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-6.0mu\cdot\mkern-6.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-6.0mu\cdot\mkern-6.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt\phantom{\shortminus}1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt\shortminus 1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(e)

(107)

\displaystyle Q\,\big(\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\!\oplus\mkern-1.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}\big)\mkern-2.0mu(s)\;Q^{\top}\,=\,\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-6.0mu\cdot\mkern-6.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}0\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-6.0mu\cdot\mkern-6.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt\phantom{\shortminus}1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt\shortminus 1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\,=\,\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\mkern-6.0mu\cdot\mkern-6.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt\phantom{\shortminus}1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt\shortminus 1&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\,=\,\begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\,=\,\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)

(108)

More generally, any finite-dimensional representations of compact (including finite) groups is
completely reducible
into a direct sum of irreps
[
75
,
52
,
198
]
.
This suggests that any covariant feature vector, transforming under a compact structure group, can up to a change of basis be constructed from irrep features.
As argued in
[
234
]
, it is in this case indeed possible to reduce any
linear
network operation to equivalent operations between irrep fields, which simplifies the construction of the space of
G
-steerable kernels in Eq. (
86
) and of invariant biases in Eq. (
63
).
However, as we will see below, the specific choice of basis of equivalent field types has a quite significant impact on the model performance.
The reason for this is that
nonlinear
network operations are sensitive to the chosen basis, i.e. to a specific choice from equivalent field types.

5.3
Orientation independent convolutional networks

In order to construct orientation independent CNNs on the Möbius strip we need to instantiate the gauge equivariant layers from Section
4
for the reflection group
{R}
.
More specifically, each of the shared equivariant template functions defining the orientation independent layers needs to be instantiated for any choice of the considered field types
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}
,
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}
and
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}
.
The following Section
5.3.1
starts by solving for the spaces
{B}^{R}_{\rho}
of gauge invariant bias templates from Eq. (
63
)
Some admissible choices of gauge equivariant nonlinearities for the different field types are proposed in Section
5.3.2
.
Section
5.3.3
will then derive the spaces
{K}^{{R}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
of
{R}
-steerable kernels (Eq. (
86
)) for each possible pair of input and output irreps.
While this section will mainly consist of theoretical derivations, the following Section
5.4
will cover more practical implementation details.

5.3.1
Orientation independent bias summation

The space of biases templates that can be summed to a field of type
\rho
without interfering with the coordinate independence assumption was in Section
4.1.2
shown to be given by

\displaystyle{B}^{{R}}_{\rho}\ :=\ \big\{b\in\mathbb{R}^{c}\;\big|\;b=\rho(g)\mkern 2.0mub\ \ \ \forall g\in{R}\big\}\,.

(109)

For the case of the reflection group, there are only two group elements and thus two constraints.
The constraint for the identity element
g=e
is trivially satisfied since
\rho(e)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{c}}
is by definition always the identity on
\mathbb{R}^{c}
.
In the following it is therefore sufficient to restrict attention to the constraint
b=\rho(s)\mkern 2.0mub
coming from the reflection
g=s
.

We start with the case of scalar fields, i.e. the trivial representation.
The reflection constraint then reads
b=\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}(s)\mkern 2.0mub=b
, which is always satisfied.
It follows that the space of bias templates

\displaystyle{B}^{{R}}_{\scalebox{.8}{$\rho_{{\textup{triv}}}$}}=\mathbb{R}

(110)

remains unconstrained such that arbitrary real-valued biases can be summed to scalar fields.
For the sign-flip representation the reflection constraint becomes
b=\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}(s)\,b=-b
and is therefore only satisfied for biases which are zero:

\displaystyle{B}^{{R}}_{\scalebox{.8}{$\rho_{{\textup{sign}}}$}}=\{0\}

(111)

It is thus impossible to sum biases to sign-flip fields while maintaining coordinate independence.
Our third exemplary field type is the two-dimensional regular representation.
The corresponding reflectional constraint on
b\in\mathbb{R}^{2}
reads

\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}b_{1}\\
b_{2}\end{bmatrix}\ =\ b\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)\mkern 2.0mub\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\!\cdot\!\begin{bmatrix}b_{1}\\
b_{2}\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}b_{2}\\
b_{1}\end{bmatrix}

(112)

and leads to the one-dimensional solution space

\displaystyle{B}^{{R}}_{\scalebox{.8}{$\rho_{{\textup{reg}}}$}}=\big\{b\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,\big|\,b_{1}=b_{2}\big\}=\bigg\{\begin{bmatrix}\beta\\
\beta\end{bmatrix}\,\bigg|\,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\bigg\}\ .

(113)

The coordinate independence of this constraint is intuitively clear:
since the regular representation swaps the two channels which make up the field, the bias summation is only then coordinate independent when the values summed to both channels are equal, such that their order does not matter.

As already claimed in Section
4.1.2
, the solution space
{B}^{{R}}_{\rho}
for a representation
\rho
coincides exactly with its trivial subrepresentations.
This is certainly true for the trivial representation, to which one can sum any bias, and the sign-flip representation, which has itself no trivial subrepresentation and therefore does not admit biases at all.
A more interesting example is the regular representation, which was in Eq.
106
shown to decompose into a direct sum of the trivial and the sign-flip representation.
The one-dimensional solution space in Eq.
113
corresponds exactly to the single trivial subrepresentation contained in
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}
.
To check the validity of this statement, note that the admissible biases for the direct sum representation
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\oplus\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}
are of the form
(\beta,\mkern 1.0mu0\mkern 1.0mu)^{\top}
, where
\beta\in\mathbb{R}
.
This results can via the change of basis
Q
be translated back to the regular representation, which indeed recovers our solution in Eq. (
113
):

\displaystyle Q\cdot\mkern-2.0mu\begin{bmatrix}\beta\\
0\end{bmatrix}\ \propto\ \begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\shortminus 1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu\phantom{\shortminus}1\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\!\cdot\!\begin{bmatrix}\beta\\
0\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\beta\\
\beta\end{bmatrix}

(114)

5.3.2
Orientation independent nonlinearities

To construct a deep network, we need to come up with equivariant nonlinearities for each of the field types.
As already discussed in Section
4.1.3
, scalar fields can due to their invariance under gauge transformations be acted on by any nonlinearity
{s}_{\textup{triv}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}
.
Usual choices are the pointwise ReLU or ELU nonlinearities.
For the sign-flip fields one might take the absolute value
\lVert f^{A}_{\textup{sign}}(p)\rVert
of feature vectors, which maps the sign-flip field to a scalar field.
In our implementation below we instead use nonlinearities of the form

\displaystyle{s}_{\textup{sign}}:{f}\ \mapsto\ \operatorname{ReLU}\!\big(\lVert{f}\rVert-b\big)\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\!\frac{{f}}{\lVert{f}\rVert},

(115)

where
b\in\mathbb{R}^{+}
is a learnable bias parameter.
This choice is easily seen to map sign-flip fields to sign-flip fields since the first multiplicand is acting on the gauge invariant norm of feature vectors while the second multiplicand is preserving the feature vector’s sign.
As a permutation representation, the regular representation allows for any pointwise nonlinearity, for instance ReLUs, to act on the individual field channels without changing the field type:

\displaystyle\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)\circ{s}_{\textup{reg}}\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}\\
{f}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-7.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-7.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ReLU}({f}_{1})\\
\operatorname{ReLU}({f}_{2})\end{bmatrix}\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ReLU}({f}_{2})\\
\operatorname{ReLU}({f}_{1})\end{bmatrix}\ =\ {s}_{\textup{reg}}\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{2}\\
{f}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\ =\ {s}_{\textup{reg}}\circ\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{reg}}}(s)\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}\\
{f}_{2}\end{bmatrix}

(116)

While the regular representation is linearly equivalent to
\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{triv}}}\oplus\rho_{\overset{}{\textup{sign}}}
, we can not apply independent pointwise nonlinearities on the two channels in the irrep basis.
This substantiates the claim that nonlinearities make the networks sensitive to the particular choice of basis of the representation.

5.3.3
Orientation independent convolutions

The last operations that we instantiate here are reflection equivariant convolutions.
This requires us on the one hand to explain the exponential map and parallel transport on the strip, and on the other hand to solve for the
{R}
-steerable kernel spaces.
Due to the flat geometry of
M
and the use of isometric charts, the former is almost trivial:
features are transported similarly as on
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, with the only difference that the feature vectors might experience a reflection by
\rho(s)
.
Our implementation of this part is visualized in Fig.
5.4.1
, which is further explained in the following Section
5.4.1
.
The current section focuses exclusively on the analytical solution of the kernel spaces.

For the Möbius strip with
{R}
-structure, the space of
{R}
-steerable kernels from Eq. (
86
) is given by

\displaystyle{K}^{{R}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}:=\ \Big\{K\!:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,\Big|\,K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\mkern-2.0muK({v})\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\mkern-2.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\quad\forall\ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\,\ g\in{R}\Big\}\,,

(117)

where we dropped the determinant factor
|\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|=1
and removed all inverses since
{g^{-1}\!=\!g\ \ \ \forall\mkern 4.0mug\in{R}}
.
As in the case of equivariant biases, the constraint coming from the identity element is trivially satisfied, such that only the reflectional constraint remains.
Reflection equivariant kernels are therefore characterized by the single constraint

\displaystyle K(s.{v})\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(s)\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.0muK({v})\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(s)\qquad\forall\>{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,,

(118)

which requires that the reflected kernel
K(s.{v})
equals the non-reflected kernel
K({v})
after being acted on by the input and output field representation.
We will in the following solve this constraint for all nine pairs of field types.
The resulting kernels, all of which are in one or another sense symmetric under reflections, are visualized in Table
3
.

\parbox[c][31.004pt][c]{28.1853pt}{\includegraphics[height]{figures/kernels/K_crisp_3f.png}}\mkern 4.0mu,&\mkern-16.0mu\parbox[c][31.004pt][c]{28.1853pt}{\includegraphics[height]{figures/kernels/K_crisp_1f.png}}\end{pmatrix}

Table 3:
Visualization of reflection-steerable kernels in
{K}^{{R}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
for all considered pairs of input and output field types
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
and
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
.
In general, these kernels need to satisfy the
{R}\mkern-1.2mu
-steerability kernel constraint
K(s.{v})\ =\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(s)\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.0muK({v})\mkern-1.0mu\cdot\mkern-1.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(s)
where
K:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
.
Each entry of the table states the specific constraint for the corresponding input and output representations and visualizes one exemplary steerable kernel.
Note that the constraint binds the reflected kernel
K(s.{v})
to a linear transformation of the unreflected kernel
K({v})
by the input and output representation.
It results therefore in reflectional symmetries of the kernels.

scalar
\bm{\to}
regular:

In order to map from a scalar field to a regular feature field one needs to apply kernels of the form

K=\begin{bmatrix}K_{\mkern-1.0mu1\mkern-1.0mu1}\\
K_{\mkern-1.0mu2\mkern-1.0mu1}\end{bmatrix}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}
,
which map from one input channel to two output channels.
The demanded permutation of the output channels is guaranteed if the kernel satisfies

\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}K_{\mkern-1.0mu1\mkern-1.0mu1}\\
K_{\mkern-1.0mu2\mkern-1.0mu1}\end{bmatrix}\mkern-4.0mu(s.{v})\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}\hskip 1.5pt0&\mkern-4.0mu1\hskip 1.5pt\\
\hskip 1.5pt1&\mkern-4.0mu0\hskip 1.5pt\end{bmatrix}\!\cdot\!\begin{bmatrix}K_{\mkern-1.0mu1\mkern-1.0mu1}\\
K_{\mkern-1.0mu2\mkern-1.0mu1}\end{bmatrix}\mkern-4.0mu({v})\cdot\!\big[\mkern 2.0mu1\mkern 2.0mu\big]\ =\ \begin{bmatrix}K_{\mkern-1.0mu2\mkern-1.0mu1}\\
K_{\mkern-1.0mu1\mkern-1.0mu1}\end{bmatrix}\mkern-4.0mu({v})\qquad\forall\ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,.

(121)

This constraint requires that the two channels contain kernels which are
reflected copies
of each other, that is,

K_{\mkern-1.0mu1\mkern-1.0mu1}(s.{v})=K_{\mkern-1.0mu2\mkern-1.0mu1}({v})
for all
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}

(this already covers the second line of the constraint in Eq. (
121
)).
This case is visualized in the bottom left entry of Table
3
.
