Relation to
GM
-convolutions:

The difference between
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions and general
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant kernel field transforms via
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-invariant kernel fields is that the former share
G
-steerable kernels over the whole manifold while the latter are only required to share
\operatorname{Stab}_{p}
-steerable kernels over orbits
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\!.p\in\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}\mkern-6.0mu\backslash\mkern-1.0muM
.
The requirement to share weights over the whole manifold is not strictly necessary but is – supported by Occam’s razor – likely to be a good inductive bias in practice.
It can be viewed as an analog to the assumption that the same physical laws apply throughout the whole universe.

Assume now that
M
is a
homogeneous space
with respect to the action of some isometry group
\mathcal{I}\leq\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
, that is, for any two points
p,q\in M
there is at least one isometry
\phi\in\mathcal{I}
that connects both points, i.e.
q=\phi(p)
.
In this case there is only one single orbit
\mathcal{I}.p
, which is just
M
itself, and the stabilizers
\operatorname{Stab}_{p}
of all points
p\in M
coincide up to isomorphism.
The quotient space
\mathcal{I}\backslash\mkern-1.5muM
is a singleton which is represented by a single representative point
r=r_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\mkern-3.0muM$}}}(\mathcal{I}\backslash\mkern-1.5muM)
in
M
.
By Theorem
8.13
, the space of
\mathcal{I}
-invariant kernel fields is equivalently expressed by a kernel field on orbit representatives.
Since we have only a single representative point
r
for homogeneous spaces, the full isometry invariant kernel field is in this case equivalent to a single kernel on
T_{\mkern-2.0mur}\mkern-1.0muM
.
This representative kernel is required to satisfy the stabilizer subgroup constraint in Eq. (
359
).
Via the lifting isomorphism
\widehat{\Lambda}
in Eq. (
361
), the representative kernel is shared over the whole manifold.

This sounds very similar to the definition of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, which share a single,
G
-steerability constrained kernel over the whole manifold.
Theorem
8.14
below asserts that there is indeed an equivalence between convolutions and equivariant kernel field transforms on homogeneous spaces.
The coordinate free
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
-steerability from the stabilizer constraint thereby translates (non-canonically) to the
H
-steerability of template kernels, where
H\cong\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
with
H\leq G
is an isomorphic representation of
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
relative to some coordinatization.
One can view the isometry (sub)group
\mathcal{I}\leq\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
as a principal
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
-bundle over
M
, whose (non-canonical) embedding into
G\mkern-1.4muM
gives rise to a
H
-(sub)structure
H\mkern-2.5muM
of
G\mkern-1.4muM
.
The sharing of a
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
-steerable kernel via the lifting isomorphism, which operates per action of
\mathcal{I}
,
then corresponds exactly to the sharing of an
H
-steerable kernel over
H\mkern-2.5muM
.
This implies that
\mathcal{I}
-equivariant kernel fields transforms on homogeneous spaces do indeed correspond to some
H\mkern-2.5muM
-convolution.

Theorem 8.14
(Equivariance on homogeneous
M
implies convolution).

Let
M
be a manifold equipped with a
G
-structure
G\mkern-1.4muM
.
Assume that there is an isometry group
\mathcal{I}\leq\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
which acts transitively on
M
, making it a
homogeneous space
.
Let
r\in M
be an arbitrary representative point of
M
and
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}\leq\mathcal{I}
its stabilizer.
Then

1)

There exists a
H
-(sub)structure
H\mkern-2.5muM\subseteq G\mkern-1.4muM
on
M
with:

–

H\cong\operatorname{Stab}_{r}\leq\mathcal{I}
is a subgroup of
G\cap\operatorname{O}(d)

–

H\mkern-2.5muM
is an embedding of
\mathcal{I}
(as principal
\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
-bundle
\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{I}/\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
) into
G\mkern-1.4muM
, which is preserved by
\mathcal{I}
, that is,
\Isom_{H\mkern-2.5muM}=\mathcal{I}

2)

Any
\mathcal{I}
-equivariant kernel field transform shares a single
H
-steerable kernel over the whole space
M
and is equivalent to a
H\mkern-2.5muM
-convolution with that kernel.

The specific choice of
H
-structure depends on the chosen isomorphism
H\cong\operatorname{Stab}_{r}
but is irrelevant since
\mathcal{I}
-equivariant kernel field transforms can be equivalently expressed in any such choice.

Proof
:

The proof is found in Appendix
E.2
.

\Box

Our definition of isometry equivariant kernel field transforms is on homogeneous spaces essentially equivalent to the
steerable convolutions on homogeneous spaces
as proposed by
Cohen et al. 2018b
[
37
]
.
The proven equivalence between isometry equivariant kernel field transforms and
H\mkern-2.5muM
-convolutions on homogeneous spaces therefore asserts that
H\mkern-2.5muM
-convolutions and steerable convolutions are essentially similar in this case.
However, while steerable convolutions are only defined on homogeneous spaces,
H\mkern-2.5muM
-convolutions generalize to general Riemannian manifolds.
More details on convolutions on homogeneous spaces are discussed in the related work Appendix
D
.

\@part

A literature review on coordinate independent CNNs

The formulation of coordinate independent CNNs in terms of associated
G
-bundles over Riemannian manifolds is quite general and covers a wide range of possible model instantiations.
To substantiate this claim, we review a large body of convolutional models from the literature and explain them from the unifying viewpoint of coordinate independent CNNs.
Most of the papers in the literature do not explicitly formulate their models in terms of
G
-structures and associated
G
-bundles.
The
implicitly assumed

G
-structures and group representations are therefore
deduced
from the models’ weight sharing patterns, kernel symmetries and equivariance properties; see for instance Fig.
52
.
Table
summarizes the resulting taxonomy of coordinate independent CNNs.
The following sections discuss the covered models and their properties in detail.

Section
9
covers
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
(affine group) equivariant convolutions on Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
They rely on
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-invariant
G
-structures as shown in Fig.
48
.
The models in Section
10
operate on punctured Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}\backslash\{0\}
; see Figs.
49
,
51
or
52
.
They are equivariant w.r.t. rotations around the chosen origin
\{0\}
but are not translation equivariant.
Spherical and icosahedral CNNs are discussed in Section
11
.
Most of these models assume the
G
-structures that are visualized in Figs.
55(a)
and
55(b)
and are therefore
\operatorname{SO}(3)
or
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-equivariant, respectively.
Section
12
reviews
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on general surfaces, which are mostly discretized as meshes.

The next few pages discuss various design choices of coordinate independent CNNs and give a first overview of the models in Table
.

Design choices and overview

A coordinate independent CNN is
in theory
fully specified by

1)

a choice of
Riemannian manifold

(M,\eta)

2)

its
G
-structure

G\mkern-1.4muM
,

3)

a
G
-compatible connection
which specifies feature transporters
\mathcal{P}_{\mkern-4.0mu\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A}$}\mkern 0.0mu,\gamma}}
,

4)

the
field types
or
G
-representations
\rho
of each feature space, and

5)

a choice of
G
-equivariant
nonlinearities
.

The
geodesics, exponential
and
logarithmic maps
follow from the canonical Levi-Civita connection on
M
.
82
82

82

It might seem strange to compute geodesics and feature transporters based on potentially different connections.
When the transporter connection differs from Levi-Civita, this is usually due to the Levi-Civita connection not being
G
-compatible with the chosen
G
-structure when
G<\operatorname{O}(d)
.
Some examples are given in the paragraph on
G
-compatible connections below.

The
isometry group

\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
w.r.t. which the network is equivariant follows from the metric and the
G
-structure.
All
kernel spaces

{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
are determined by the group representations of the feature spaces between which they map.

Weight sharing
is performed by placing a
G
-steerable template kernel relative to an arbitrary
G
-frame in
G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM
for each point
p\in M
.

In practice, the user is faced with additional design questions, for instance concerning the discretization of the geometry, the encoding of feature fields, numerical algorithms for computing geodesics and transporters, etc.
This section gives a high level overview of all relevant design choices.
More specific details are found in the following Sections
9
,
10
,
11
and
12
.

Discretizations of manifolds and feature fields:

The implementations differ in their representation of the manifolds and sampling of the feature fields.

Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
admit regular pixels grids, for instance
\mathbb{Z}^{d}
or the hexagonal grid
[
93
]
.
More generally, locally regular grids are suitable for locally flat manifolds like the Möbius strip and the icosahedron; see Figs.
5.4.1
and
61
.
Feature fields on Euclidean spaces may furthermore be sampled on a non-regular point cloud.
This is for instance useful when processing atomic environments, where the atom positions serve as sampling locations
[
224
]
.

An important difference between the two approaches is that regular pixel grids are not equivariant w.r.t. continuous translations in
\mathcal{T}_{d}=(\mathbb{R}^{d},+)
, but only w.r.t. the subgroup of discrete translations which preserves the grid, for instance
(\mathbb{Z}^{d},+)
.
CNNs on regular grids are furthermore usually applying spatial pooling operations which reduce the models’ equivariance even further.
Specifically, given that the pooling operation has a stride of
n
pixels, it is equivariant w.r.t. translations in
(n\mathbb{Z}^{d},+)
.
After
L
pooling layers in a convolutional network, this implies that the model as a whole is only equivariant w.r.t. translations in
(n^{L}\mathbb{Z}^{d},+)

– this issue was empirically investigated in
[
4
]
.

Zhang 2019
propose to remedy this issue by replacing stride
n
pooling layers with stride 1 pooling layers (with the same pooling window size), a low-pass filtering, and an
n
-pixel subsampling.
The additional low-pass filtering between the pooling and subsampling operations prevents aliasing effects, which is shown to make the networks sufficiently more stable under translations which are not elements of
(n\mathbb{Z}^{d},+)
.

Curved spaces like the 2-sphere
S^{2}
do in general not admit regular sampling grids.
A seemingly obvious discretization is in terms of a regular sampling grid in spherical coordinates (Eq. (
429
) and Fig.
57
), however, as these coordinates are non-isometric, they oversample the signal towards the poles
[
254
,
222
]
.
Approximately uniform sampling grids on
S^{2}
are the “generalized spiral set”
[
39
]
or the icospherical grid
[
105
,
111
]
.
Alternatively, feature fields may be discretized in the spectral domain.
For the sphere, this is done via an expansion in terms of spherical harmonics for scalar fields, spin-weighted spherical harmonics for irrep fields or Wigner D-matrices for general feature fields
[
61
,
64
,
35
,
122
]
.

General surfaces are most commonly represented by triangle meshes; see Section
12.1.2
.
Feature fields can then be sampled on the mesh vertices, edges or faces
[
46
]
.
A higher resolution of the feature fields can be achieved by encoding them via texture maps
[
133
,
98
]
.
Alternatively, surfaces may be represented as point clouds
[
221
,
107
]
.

G
-structures
GM
and structure groups
G
:

The specific choice of
G
-structure to be respected by the network depends on the learning task and the topology of
M
(if continuity or smoothness of the convolution is demanded).
In general,
M
comes equipped with an
\operatorname{O}(d)
-structure, i.e. a bundle of orthonormal reference frames with respect to the given Riemannian metric.
A
lift
to structure groups
G
with
{\operatorname{O}(d)<G\leq\operatorname{GL}(d)}
is uniquely determined by
G
-valued gauge transformations of orthonormal frames.

Reductions
of the structure group to
G<\operatorname{O}(d)
are, in contrast, not necessarily unique, and encode additional geometric information.
For instance, a reduction to
G=\operatorname{SO}(d)
requires an orientation on the manifold.
83
83

83

For a single, connected manifold, this choice is arbitrary as long as the kernel initialization is symmetric w.r.t. both orientations.
In this case the network will simply learn reflected kernels for different orientations.
When considering a dataset consisting of multiple manifolds, their relative orientation is relevant for a correct generalization.

The following sections discuss further (mostly implicitly made) choices of
G
-structures found in the literature; see for instance
Figs.
48
,

49
,

50
,

51
,

52

55
,
or
60
.
They are either determined by a demand for the equivariance under the isometry group
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
, canonically given on the manifold or, specifically for
\{e\}
-structures, algorithmically fixed via some heuristic.
Recall that
\{e\}
-structures are on non-parallelizable manifolds (by definition) necessarily discontinuous.

The most commonly encountered structure groups in the literature are the following:

trivial
group
\{e\}
, corresponding to non-coordinate independent CNNs with unconstrained kernels

reflection
group
{R}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}
, flipping the first frame axis

special orthogonal
groups
\operatorname{SO}(d)

(continuous rotations)

orthogonal
groups
\operatorname{O}(d)

(continuous rotations and reflections)

scaling
group
{S}\cong(\mathbb{R}^{+},*)
,

Since the last three groups are continuous Lie groups, they are in numerical implementations sometimes approximated by finite subgroups.
For instance,
\operatorname{SO}(2)
and
\operatorname{O}(2)
are often modeled by
cyclic
groups
\operatorname{C}_{\!N}
or
dihedral
groups
\operatorname{D}_{\!N}
, while three-dimensional rotations and reflections in
\operatorname{O}(3)
can be approximated by
polyhedral
groups (symmetry groups of Platonic solids, e.g. the icosahedron).
To reduce the complexity of the classification of models in Table
we chose to not distinguish between the continuous symmetries and their approximations by finite subgroups.
We will, however, state such approximations in our detailed discussion of the models in the following sections.

G
-compatible connections:

All of the models consider either the canonical
Levi-Civita
connection on
M
or the unique
trivial connection
which is induced by an
\{e\}
-structure.
The choice of connection becomes irrelevant (thus unspecified) for networks which operate solely on
scalar fields
, whose transport is always trivial.

More specifically, all Euclidean CNNs from Section
9
use Levi-Civita transporters, which transport vectors such that they remain parallel in the usual sense on Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
; see Fig.
20(a)
.
This is possible since the Levi-Civita connection is
G
-compatible with the models’
G
-structures (defined in Eq. (
373
) and visualized in Fig.
48
).
84
84

84

In contrast, the Euclidean
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
40(b)
would be incompatible with the Levi-Civita connection on
\mathbb{E}_{2}
.

The models on the punctured Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}\backslash\{0\}
from Section
10
are either based on
\{e\}
-structures and/or consider scalar fields.
They utilize therefore trivial connections which differ from the canonical Levi-Civita connection on
\mathbb{E}_{d}\backslash\{0\}
.

All spherical CNNs that rely on the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure in Fig.
55(a)
(reviewed in Section
11.2
) transport features according to the Levi-Civita connection on
S^{2}
(Fig.
20(b)
).
Those which operate on the
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
55(b)
(reviewed in Section
11.3
) are again considering a trivial connection since the spherical Levi-Civita connection is incompatible with this
\{e\}
-structure.
The icosahedral CNN with
\operatorname{C}_{6}
-structure, Fig.
60(c)
, transports features according to the
\operatorname{C}_{6}
-compatible icosahedral Levi-Civita connection.
85
85

85

Discrete Levi-Civita connections on meshes are discussed in Section
12.1.2
and
[
41
,
43
]
.

All CNNs on general surfaces that are listed in rows (37-39) of Table

assume oriented surfaces that are equipped with an
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure.
They transport features with the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-compatible Levi-Civita connection of the surfaces.
The other surface CNNs are based on
\{e\}
-structures and/or operate on scalar fields – their feature transport is therefore trivial.

Our Möbius strip convolutions transport features via the Levi-Civita connection, which is compatible with the assumed
{R}
-structure.

Recall that the Levi-Civita connection is uniquely determined by the metric, and is therefore generally isometry invariant; cf. footnote
74
in Section
8.1.4
.
As trivial
\{e\}
-compatible connections are uniquely specified by the
\{e\}
-structure they share its symmetries, that is, they are invariant under the action of
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}
.
This implies by Theorem
8.9
that the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, which are based on these connections, are
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant.

Transporter pullbacks and alternative projections to
\bm{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}
:

The transporter pullback
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
, defined in Def.
7.5
and Eq. (
4.2.1
), represents a feature field
f
in a geodesic parametrization on the tangent space
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
The transportation part of the operation is determined by the
G
-compatible connection.
Geodesics – and therefore exponential maps
\exp_{p}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to M
– have closed form expressions on Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
and the sphere
S^{2}
.
Specifically, the exponential maps on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
reduce in Cartesian coordinates to the vector summation in Eq. (
402
), such that Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions reduce to conventional convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
; see Theorem
9.7
.
Geodesics on
S^{2}
are well known to be given by the great circles of the sphere.
If the sphere is viewed as being embedded in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
, the exponential map is explicitly given by Eq. (
432
).
The geodesics on general surface meshes are not described by closed form solutions but are computed numerically; see Section
12.1.2
.
In contrast to the smooth setting, one needs to distinguishes between “shortest” and “straightest” geodesics on meshes
[
172
]
.

The pullback of feature fields into geodesic normal coordinates is not the only way of representing feature fields on the tangent spaces.
In the literature on spherical CNNs it is rather common to use gnomonic projections, which are visualized in Fig.
56
.
Theorem
11.3
shows that this projection can be viewed as a special case of our more general geodesic parameterization after applying a radial warp to the kernels.
The corresponding models are therefore exactly identified as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
Surfaces which are embedded in an ambient space like
\mathbb{R}^{3}
might furthermore rely on various projections in the embedding space; see for instance the last three models that are discussed in Section
12.3
.
Note that these approaches are truly different from ours, i.e. these three models are not exactly
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.

G
-representations and nonlinearities:

Almost all models consider either of the trivial representation, irreducible representations or regular representations as field types.
Exceptions are quotient representations, more general induced representations, tensor product representations and, specifically for
G=\operatorname{SO}(3)
, the quaternion representation.
Infinite-dimensional representations, in particular regular and quotient representations of Lie groups, are in implementations discretized.
This can either happen via Monte Carlo sampling or by falling back to the corresponding representations of finite subgroups as discussed above.

The nonlinearities are required to be equivariant w.r.t. the action of the chosen
G
-representations.
Since scalar fields are
G
-invariant, they are acted on by usual nonlinearities like ReLU.
Feature fields that transform according to permutation representations, most importantly regular representations, are acted on channel-wise.
All other field types require custom-tailored nonlinearities – we refer to
[
234
]
for a discussion of specific choices.

G
-steerable kernel spaces:

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions map input fields of type
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
to output fields of type
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
by convolving them with
G
-steerable kernels
K\in{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
.
Since the space
{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
of
G
-steerable kernels, Def.
7.3
, is a vector space, it is usually parameterized in terms of a basis
\{K_{1},\,\dots,\,K_{N}\}
of
{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
.

Before
computing the convolution, the learned kernel
K=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}K_{i}
is expanded in this basis, where
\{w_{1},\dots,w_{N}\}
are real-valued weights to be optimized.
Provably complete kernel spaces for the groups
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)
were implemented in
[
234
]
.
86
86

86

https://quva-lab.github.io/e2cnn/api/e2cnn.kernels.html

A generalization of the Wigner-Eckart theorem characterizes the kernel space bases for general compact structure groups
G

[
128
]
.

In practice, the majority of authors does not use a representation theoretic formulation of feature fields and steerable kernels, but formulate them based on intuition.
Specifically, most authors assume a given input field type and propose various convolution operations which are engineered such that the resulting output field transforms in an equivariant (or coordinate independent) manner.
87
87

87

This is opposed to our approach, which fixes the input and output fields and subsequently asks for the resulting constraint on convolution kernels.

While these approaches propose certain
G
-steerable kernels that map between
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
-fields and
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
-fields, these kernels do sometimes not span the complete space of possible kernels.
This applies for instance to the
MDGCNNs
and
PFCNNs
, which are discussed in Section
12.2
.

9
Euclidean coordinate independent CNNs

This section considers equivariant convolutions on Euclidean (affine) spaces
M=\mathbb{E}_{d}
, which are undoubtedly of greatest practical relevance.
Convolutional network on Euclidean spaces are applied for analyzing planar and volumetric images, audio signals, videos, physical events in (pseudo-Euclidean) Minkowski spacetime or planar environments in reinforcement learning.
The prototypical convolutional model architecture – both on Euclidean spaces and in general – is the conventional CNN on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
by
LeCun et al. 1990
.
Its success is to a large extent grounded in its translation equivariance, which allows it to generalize learned inference between different spatial locations.
Motivated by this observation, a lot of effort has been made to generalize the equivariance properties of CNNs to larger
global
symmetry groups of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
, for instance to the Euclidean isometries in Fig.
46
or more general affine transformations.

Interestingly, most of the
globally
equivariant models in the literature achieve their equivariance by applying some kind of
G
-steerable kernels.
This implies that these models are actually equivariant under
local
gauge transformations as well, despite not explicitly being designed for it.
The reason for this unintentional gauge equivariance is that the global equivariance of the models is usually designed for each layer individually, and therefore applies to the local receptive field of every neuron independently.
Here we explain globally equivariant Euclidean CNNs, listed in rows (1-26) of Table
, from the more general viewpoint of local gauge symmetries and discuss how their global equivariance is induced from their local gauge equivariance.
Theorem
8.9
asserts thereby that a
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution on
M=\mathbb{E}_{d}
is
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariant.
However, for the specific case of Euclidean spaces, one can make a stronger statement than mere isometry equivariance:
the convolution with a
G
-steerable kernel on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
implies the global equivariance of the model under the action of the affine group
\operatorname{Aff}(G):=\mathcal{T}_{d}\rtimes G
, as proven in Theorem
9.8
below.
The underlying reason for this result is that the geodesics and Levi-Civita transporters are on Euclidean spaces not only preserved by isometries, but are more generally preserved by any affine transformation.

Figure 46:
Visualization of the full isometry group
\Isom(\mathbb{E}_{d})=\operatorname{E}(d)
of Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
for
d=2
.
It contains subgroups of translations
\mathcal{T}_{d}\mkern-1.0mu=\!(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mkern-2.0mu+)
, rotations
\operatorname{SO}(d)
and reflections
{R}
.
Rotations and reflections form the orthogonal group
{\operatorname{O}(d)\!=\!\operatorname{SO}(d)\!\rtimes\!{R}}
while translations and rotations form the special Euclidean group
\operatorname{SE}(d)=\mathcal{T}_{d}\rtimes\operatorname{SO}(d)
.

Convolutions on Euclidean spaces are classically formulated
in coordinates

\mathbb{R}^{d}
of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
The advantage of formulating convolutions this way is that
\mathbb{R}^{d}
comes with all mathematical structure that is required for the definitions.
However,
\mathbb{R}^{d}
is equipped with an excess of structure, for instance a vector space structure (and thus an origin) or its canonical
\{e\}
-structure.
By designing the convolutions to be equivariant, the inference is then (partly) made independent from this structure:
for example, the translation equivariance of convolutions equalizes the particular choice of origin while
\operatorname{E}(d)
(isometry) equivariance equalizes the particular direction and orientation of the
\{e\}
-structure.
To clarify which mathematical structure is actually being assumed and required, we develop an alternative viewpoint:
we start out with the pure affine and metric structure of the Euclidean space
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
If a
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
assumes more geometric structure, this structure will subsequently be added by specifying an atlases of (affine) charts
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
, which induce gauges and
G
-structures.

To give an overview and a simple introduction, we review the classical formulation of
G
-steerable (affine equivariant) convolutions in coordinates
\mathbb{R}^{d}
in Section
9.1
.
The following Sections
9.2
and
9.3
define affine equivariant convolutions on Euclidean spaces in a coordinate free and coordinate independent setting.
Specifically, Section
9.2
discusses the affine geometry of Euclidean spaces.
Atlases of charts with transition functions in an affine group
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
(Fig.
47
) induce hereby the considered
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-invariant
G
-structures (Fig.
48
).
Section
9.3
considers
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on these
G
-structures and proves their global
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance.
The specific instantiations of such models found in the literature, i.e. rows (1-26) of Table
, are discussed in Section
9.4
.

The reader may choose to jump over the technical definitions in Sections
9.2
and
9.3
, which are not strictly necessary to understand the models in Section

Euclidean steerable CNNs:

\displaystyle F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}\,.

\displaystyle F_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}({x})\,:=\,[K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}]({x})\,:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}({x}+{v})\ d{v}\,,

(365)

{c_{\textup{in}}}

It can be shown that this operation is the most general linear and translation equivariant mapping between feature maps

For full generality, one would actually have to allow for kernels in the distributional sense (generalized functions).

The group

Their (canonical) action on

\displaystyle\operatorname{Aff}(G)\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad(tg,\,{x})\ \mapsto\ g\mkern 1.0mu{x}+t\,.

(368)

The action of an inverse group element

\displaystyle\big((tg)^{-1},\,{x}\big)\ \mapsto\ g^{-1}({x}-t)\,.

(369)

A feature field of type

\displaystyle(tg)\mkern 2.0mu\rhd_{\rho}F\ :=\ \big[\operatorname{Ind}_{G}^{\operatorname{Aff}(G)}\rho\big](tg)\,F\ :=\ \rho(g)\,F\,(tg)^{-1}\,,

\displaystyle\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\Big[$}}}}K*(tg\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}}\!F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}({x})\ =

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big((tg)^{-1}({x}+{v})\big)\ d{v}

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big(g^{-1}({x}+{v}-t)\big)\ d{v}

\displaystyle\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K(g\tilde{{v}})\;\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big(g^{-1}({x}-t)+\tilde{{v}}\big)\ |\mkern-2.0mu\det g\mkern 1.0mu|\ d\tilde{{v}}

\displaystyle\ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\,\big[K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]\big(g^{-1}({x}-t)\big)

\displaystyle\ tg\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}\big[K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]({x})\,,

Relation to Euclidean
GM
-convolutions:

How do these steerable convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
relate to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on Euclidean spaces
{M=\mathbb{E}_{d}}
?
The fact that steerable convolutions rely on
G
-steerable kernels suggests that they are not only globally
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariant but (more generally) locally
G
-equivariant.
To draw the connection between classical
G
-steerable CNNs on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
and our coordinate free
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, we need to identify the geometric structure that is implicitly being considered by the former.

In general,
\mathbb{R}^{d}
comes canonically equipped with an
\{e\}
-structure, visualized in Fig.
48(a)
.
93
93

93

Formally, the canonical
\{e\}
-structure of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
arises as follows:
the vector space
M=\mathbb{R}^{d}
comes itself with a canonical basis, given by the basis vectors
e_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
with elements
(e_{i})_{j}=\delta_{ij}
.
The canonical reference frames of tangent spaces
T_{p}\mathbb{R}^{d}
follow from this basis via the canonical isomorphisms

\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d},p}:T_{p}{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{R}^{d}
from Eq. (
542
).
Intuitively, the local frames of the tangent spaces
T_{p}\mathbb{R}^{d}
are “aligned” with the global frame of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
This is equivalent to introducing the identity map as global coordinate chart
x=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}:M=\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
and then defining the canonical
\{e\}
-structure as the field of induced coordinate bases
\big[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\big]_{i=1}^{d}
.

It furthermore comes with a Riemannian metric corresponding to the standard inner product of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
94
94

94

This standard metric
\eta
is defined as the pullback of the standard inner product

\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}

on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
via the canonical isomorphisms

\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d},p}:T_{p}{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{R}^{d}
from Eq. (
542
)
to the tangent spaces.
It is thus for any
v,w\in T_{p}\mathbb{R}^{d}
given by

{\eta_{p}(v,w):=\langle\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d},p}(v),\,\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d},p}(w)\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}}
.

The corresponding Levi-Civita connection gives rise to the parallel transporters in Fig.
20(a)
, which keep vectors parallel in the usual sense on Euclidean spaces.
When being expressed relative to the frames of the canonical
\{e\}
-structure, the parallel transporters become trivial and drop therefore out.
The exponential maps reduce to a mere summation (after applying some isomorphisms, see below).

While we are given an
\{e\}
-structure on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
,

-convolutions rely on less specific

\displaystyle G\mkern-1.4muM\ =\ \raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM\lhd G\ :=\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\,[e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\lhd g\;\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\;[e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\in\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM,\ g\in G\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}

(373)

of the canonical
\{e\}
-structure
\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM

Intuitively, these lifted

9.2
Affine geometry of Euclidean spaces
\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}_{\bm{d}}

Before discussing coordinate free convolutions on Euclidean spaces, we need to understand the underlying Euclidean geometry.
Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
are by definition
affine
spaces, that is, they come with an associated vector space of dimension
d
, which defines
translations
on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
In addition to being affine spaces, Euclidean spaces are endowed with an
Euclidean metric
(distance function).
This distance functions corresponds to a Riemannian metric
\eta
, i.e. an
\operatorname{O}(d)
-structure
\operatorname{O}\mkern-3.6muM
on the (Riemannian) manifold
M=\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
This metric has the property that its curvature vanishes everywhere, that is,
\mathbb{E}_{d}
is globally flat.

A standard example for Euclidean spaces are the
vector spaces

\mathbb{R}^{d}
, however, general Euclidean spaces consider less structure.
In particular, they do not come with a vector space structure and do thus not have a preferred origin.
Furthermore, they are in general not equipped with Cartesian coordinates.
We will therefore start with bare Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
and discuss how the relevant geometric structure is added to them.
One could in principle consider any
G
-structure, however, we are specifically interested in those
G
-structures that recover the classical steerable CNNs from the previous section, which explain all models in rows (1-26) of Table
.
Such
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-invariant
G
-structures are induced from
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlases, consisting of charts of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
whose transition functions take values in
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
(Eq. (
366
)); see Fig.
47
.
All statements made in coordinates
\mathbb{R}^{d}
can via charts be translated to a coordinate free setting, which we develop here.
More infos about the relation between coordinate charts and gauges can be found in Appendix
A
.

Figure 47:
Visualization of affine charts
x^{X}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
, which assign global coordinates to Euclidean spaces.
Both
\mathbb{E}_{d}
and
\mathbb{R}^{d}
are affine spaces, such that one can demand the charts to be affine maps, which preserve collinearity and ratios of distances.
We define an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas
{A}^{\operatorname{Aff}(G)}_{\mathbb{E}_{d}}
as consisting of charts that are related by transition functions
t^{BA}g^{BA}:=x^{B}\circ(x^{A})^{-1}
that are elements in
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
Charts in an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas differ at most in their choice of origin
(x^{X})^{-1}(0)
and a
G
-transformation.
A choice of an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas, consisting of charts
x^{X}
, induces a
G
-atlas
{A}^{G}
of gauges
\hat{d}x^{X}
.
The corresponding
G
-structure
G\mkern-1.4muM
, which is in Fig.
48
exemplified for different groups
G
, is invariant under the action of
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
Theorem
9.8
proves that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on such
G
-structures are
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariant.

license

by courtesy of Twitter.)

9.2.1
Affine charts and Aff(
G
)-atlases

A Euclidean space
\mathbb{E}_{d}
of dimension
d
is homeomorphic to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, and admits therefore global charts
95
95

95

The fact that
\mathbb{E}_{d}
and
\mathbb{R}^{d}
are globally homeomorphic (or even isometric) explains why most related work considers the vector spaces
\mathbb{R}^{d}
as models of Euclidean spaces.
Our approach in this section is a bit more careful as it introduces the minimal structure necessary to define
G\mkern-1.4muM
-coordinate independent convolutions on Euclidean spaces
M=\mathbb{E}_{d}
.

\displaystyle x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\,.

(374)

In the following we will always require these charts to be affine maps, i.e. isomorphisms of affine spaces, which preserve collinearity (i.e. they map straight lines to straight lines) and ratios of distances.
Since compositions of affine maps are affine maps, it follows that the chart transition functions

\displaystyle x^{B}\mkern-1.0mu\circ\mkern-1.0mu\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}:\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}

(375)

are affine transformations of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, i.e. elements in
\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{GL}(d))
.
The transition functions decompose therefore uniquely into a translation
t^{BA}\in\mathcal{T}_{d}
and an element
g^{BA}\in\operatorname{GL}(d)
:

\displaystyle t^{BA}g^{BA}\ :=\ x^{B}\mkern-1.0mu\circ\mkern-1.0mu\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}

(376)

The notation
g^{BA}
is hereby not accidental as these group elements agree with the gauge transformations that are induced by chart transitions, which is proven in Theorem
9.2
below.

Given a choice of affine group
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
, we define
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlases of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
as those atlases of global charts from
\mathbb{E}_{d}
to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, whose chart transition functions take values in
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
:

Definition 9.1
(
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas of Euclidean space).

Let
\mathfrak{X}
be an index set labeling charts and, for any
{X\mkern-2.0mu\in\mathfrak{X}}
, let
x^{X}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
be a global affine chart of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
The atlas

\displaystyle{A}^{\operatorname{Aff}(G)}_{\mathbb{E}_{d}}\ =\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{d},x^{X}\big)\;\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\ X\in\mathfrak{X}\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}

(377)

is said to be an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas if all of its chart transition functions take values in
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
, that is, if

\displaystyle x^{B}\mkern-3.0mu\circ\mkern-2.0mu\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\!\in\operatorname{Aff}(G)\quad\forall\ A,B\in\mathfrak{X}\,.

(378)

Fig.
47
visualizes affine charts and the
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-valued chart transition maps between them.

9.2.2
Induced
G
-atlases and
G
-structures

Any global coordinate chart
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
induces a global gauge, which is pointwise given by the chart gradients

\displaystyle\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}:=\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}:\ T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\,,

(379)

see Eq. (
A.3.1
) in Appendix
A.3
and Table
6
.
An atlas of charts corresponds therefore an atlas of gauges.
In particular, given that the charts form an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas, it is guaranteed that the gauge transformations are
G
-valued, that is, that the induced gauges form a
G
-atlas:

Theorem 9.2
(
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlases of charts induce
G
-atlases of gauges).

Let
{{A}^{\operatorname{Aff}(G)}_{\mathbb{E}_{d}}\!=\big\{(\mathbb{E}_{d},x^{X})\big|X\mkern-2.0mu\in\mkern-2.0mu\mathfrak{X}\big\}}
be an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas of
charts
.
The induced atlas of
gauges

\displaystyle{A}^{G}=\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{d},\hat{d}x^{X}\big)\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\,X\in\mathfrak{X}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}

(380)

is then guaranteed to be a
G
-atlas.
In particular, if the chart transition maps are given by
{x^{B}\circ(x^{A})^{-1}}=t^{BA}g^{BA}
, the transition maps between gauges are at any point
p\in\mathbb{E}_{d}
given by
{g_{p}^{BA}=g^{BA}\in G}
.

Proof
:

The transition functions between chart induced gauges coincide by Eq. (
A.3.2
) with the Jacobian of the chart transition maps, that is,

\displaystyle g_{p}^{BA}\,=\,\hat{d}x^{B}_{p}\circ\big(\hat{d}x^{A}_{p}\big)^{-1}\,=\,\frac{\partial x^{B}}{\partial x^{A}}\Big|_{x^{A}(p)}\,.

(381)

The last expression is the usual abuse of notation for Jacobians of chart transition maps, which was in Eq. (
559
) in components defined as

\displaystyle\frac{\partial x^{B}_{\mu}}{\partial x^{A}_{\nu}}\bigg|_{x^{A}(p)}\,:=\,\partial_{\nu}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}x^{B}_{\mu}\circ\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\Big|_{x^{A}(p)}\,.

(382)

Using that the chart transition maps are given by
x^{B}\circ\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}=t^{BA}g^{BA}
, this implies

\displaystyle\big(g_{p}^{BA}\big)_{\mu\nu}\ =\ \partial_{\nu}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}x^{B}_{\mu}\circ\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}({x})\big|_{x^{A}(p)}\ =\ \partial_{\nu}\big(g^{BA}{x}+t^{BA}\big)_{\mu}\big|_{x^{A}(p)}\ =\ g^{BA}_{\mu\nu}\,,

(383)

that is, that the induced gauge transformations
g_{p}^{BA}
are
G
-valued and agree with
g^{BA}
(which justifies the notation).
As this argument holds for any
p\in\mathbb{E}_{d}
and any charts
A,B\in\mathfrak{X}
, this implies that the induced atlas of gauges is a
G
-atlas.

\Box

The other three

.
According to Eq. (

\displaystyle G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM\ :=\ \big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\big)^{-1}(G)\,,

\big[\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{A}_{\mu}}\big|_{p}\big]_{\mu=1}^{d}=\big[\big(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}\big)^{-1}(\epsilon_{\mu})\big]_{\mu=1}^{d}

and all

As the maximal

Fig.

In the next section we prove that the corresponding

As it turns out,
G\mkern-1.4muM\xrightarrow{\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}}\mathbb{E}_{d}
is (non-canonically) isomorphic to
\operatorname{Aff}(G)\xrightarrow{{q}}\operatorname{Aff}(G)/G\cong\mathbb{R}^{d}
as a principal bundle, where

\displaystyle{q}:\ \operatorname{Aff}(G)\to\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \ tg\mapsto t

(385)

is the canonical quotient map of the affine group (after identifying cosets
tG
with translations
t
).
96
96

96

We implicitly employ a canonical isomorphism
\operatorname{Aff}(G)/G\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \ tG\mapsto t
, where
t
denotes a translation group element in
\mathcal{T}_{d}=(\mathbb{R}^{d},+)
on the l.h.s. and a vector in
\mathbb{R}^{d}
on the r.h.s.

Non-surprisingly, this principal bundle isomorphism depends on the choice of chart.

Theorem 9.3
(Principal bundle isomorphism between Aff(
G
) and
GM
).

Let
G\mkern-1.4muM
be an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas induced
G
-structure on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
Then
G\mkern-1.4muM
is isomorphic to
\operatorname{Aff}(G)\xrightarrow{{q}}\mathbb{R}^{d}
as a principal bundle, i.e. there are isomorphisms

\displaystyle\alpha^{A}:\operatorname{Aff}(G)\to G\mkern-1.4muM,\ \ tg\mapsto\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$(x^{A})^{-1}(t)$}}\big)^{-1}(g)

(386)

and

\displaystyle\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{E}_{d}

(387)

such that the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{Aff}(G)\times G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G\mkern-1.4muM\times G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{Aff}(G)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G\mkern-1.4muM}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{A}\times\mathrm{id}_{G}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\,\lhd}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{q}\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\,\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(x^{A})^{-1}}

(388)

The inverse of
\alpha^{A}
is hereby given by

\displaystyle\big(\alpha^{A}\big)^{-1}:G\mkern-1.4muM\to\operatorname{Aff}(G),\ \ [e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\mapsto tg\quad\textup{where}\ \ \begin{cases}t=x^{A}\circ\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}\big([e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\big)\\[4.30554pt]
g=\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}([e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d})$}}^{A}\big([e_{i}]_{i=1}^{d}\big)\end{cases}

(389)

Note that the isomorphisms are in one-to-one correspondence to the
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-compatible charts of the considered atlas.

Proof
:

To prove the statement, we need to show that
\alpha^{A}
and
(\alpha^{A})^{-1}
are indeed inverse to each other, that
\alpha^{A}
is a bundle map over
(x^{A})^{-1}
and that
\alpha^{A}
is right
G
-equivariant.
That
(\alpha^{A})^{-1}
is both a well defined left and right inverse of
\alpha^{A}
is easily checked by the reader.
That
\alpha^{A}
is a bundle map over
(x^{A})^{-1}
means that the bottom square of the diagram commutes.
This is seen by observing that

(x^{A})^{-1}\circ{q}(tg)=(x^{A})^{-1}(t)
and

\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}\circ\alpha^{A}(tg)=\pi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{ $\!G\!M$}}}\circ\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$(x^{A})^{-1}(t)$}}\big)^{-1}(g)=(x^{A})^{-1}(t)

agree for any
tg\in\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
The commutativity of the upper square in the diagram, i.e. the right
G
-equivariance of
\alpha^{A}
, follows from the fact that

\alpha^{A}(tg\cdot\tilde{g})=\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$(x^{A})^{-1}(t)$}}\big)^{-1}(g\tilde{g})=\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$(x^{A})^{-1}(t)$}}\big)^{-1}(g)\lhd\tilde{g}=\alpha^{A}(tg)\lhd\tilde{g}

holds for any
tg\in\operatorname{Aff}(G)
and any
\tilde{g}\in G
.
The second step made use of the fact that
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$G\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$(x^{A})^{-1}(t)$}}
is right
G
-equivariant (Eq. (
190
)), which implies the equivariance of its inverse.
Together, these properties show that
\alpha^{A}
is a principal bundle isomorphism.

\Box

9.2.3
Coordinate free affine transformations

As we want to prove the equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions under affine transformations in a coordinate free setting, we need to introduce groups of affine transformations of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
, instead of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
as above.
The charts will relate the coordinate free affine groups to the affine groups
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.

We start with the full group

\displaystyle\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})\ :=\ \big\{\phi:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{E}_{d}\,\big|\,\textup{$\phi$ is an affine transformation of $\mathbb{E}_{d}$}\big\}

(390)

of affine transformations of a Euclidean space
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
It is easy to prove that
\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})
is isomorphic to
\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{GL}(d))
, with isomorphisms given by
\phi\mapsto x^{A}\phi\,(x^{A})^{-1}
for an arbitrary choice of chart
x^{A}
.
This statement is proven in a more general setting in Theorem
9.6
below.

As in the case of isometries, we define subgroups
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\leq\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})
of
G
-structure preserving affine transformations:

Definition 9.4
(
G
-structure preserving affine transformations).

Let
G\mkern-1.4muM
be any
G
-structure on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
We define the corresponding subgroup of
G
-structure preserving affine transformations as

\displaystyle\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\ :=\ \big\{\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})\,\big|\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muF\mkern-2.0muM$}}}G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM=G_{\mkern-1.5mu\phi(p)}\mkern-1.5muM\ \ \ \forall p\in\mathbb{E}_{d}\big\}\,\ \leq\ \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})\,.

(391)

Compare this definition to that of
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
in Def.
8.1
.
As in the case of
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}
, the gauge transformations that are induced by affine transformations in
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
are guaranteed to be
G
-valued.
This statement is formalized by the following theorem, which is essentially analogous to Theorem
8.3
:

Theorem 9.5
(
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
in local trivializations).

Let
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{E}_{d})
be any isometry of
M=\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
Then the following three statements are equivalent:

1.

\phi
is
G
-structure preserving, that is,
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
.

2.

The affine transformation pullback
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{\widetilde{A}}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muF\mkern-2.0muM$}}}^{-1}
of any gauge
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{\widetilde{A}}
of the
G
-atlas of
F\mkern-1.5muM
that defines
G\mkern-1.4muM
is
G
-compatible with that
G
-atlas.

3.

The coordinate expression of
\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muF\mkern-2.0muM$}}}
relative to any gauges
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{\widetilde{A}}
and
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi(p)$}}^{A}
from the
G
-atlas of
F\mkern-1.5muM
takes values in the structure group, that is,

{g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p):=\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi(p)$}}^{A}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muF\mkern-2.0muM$}}}\,\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$F\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{\widetilde{A}}\big)^{-1}}=\hat{d}x^{A}_{\phi(p)}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muT\mkern-3.0muM$}}}\,\big(\hat{d}x^{\widetilde{A}}_{p}\big)^{-1}

is
G
-valued.

Proof
:

The proof is analogous to that of Theorem
8.3
.
More generally, the statement holds for arbitrary
G
-structure preserving
diffeomorphisms
.

\Box

Induced gauge transformations describe the transformation of the coordinate expressions of bundle elements, e.g. tangent or feature vector coefficients.
The action of the affine transformation
\phi
on the manifold
\mathbb{E}_{d}
itself can also be described in coordinates
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
This is achieved by a left and right multiplication of
\phi
with any (affine) chart, which we can w.l.o.g. take to be equal at the source and target location since we are only considering global charts.
The resulting coordinate expression
t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}
, defined by the following commutative diagram,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
t_{\phi}^{AA}\mkern 1.0mug_{\phi}^{AA}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{A}}

(392)

is guaranteed to take values in
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
if
\phi
preserves the
G
-structure.

Theorem 9.6
(
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
in global affine charts).

Let
G\mkern-1.4muM
be the
G
-structure induced by some
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas and let
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
be a chart of this atlas.
The coordinate expression of an element
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
relative to
x^{A}
is then given by

\displaystyle x^{A}\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\,=:\,t_{\phi}^{AA}\mkern 1.0mug_{\phi}^{AA}\ \in\,\operatorname{Aff}(G)\ ,

(393)

where

\displaystyle t_{\phi}^{AA}:=x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}(0)\ \in\ \mathcal{T}_{d}\qquad\textup{and}\qquad g_{\phi}^{AA}:=\hat{d}x^{A}_{\phi(p)}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muT\mkern-3.0muM$}}}\,\big(\hat{d}x^{A}_{p}\big)^{-1}\ \in\ G

(394)

The element
g_{\phi}^{AA}\in G
in the coordinate expression coincides hereby with the induced gauge transformation
g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)\in G
from Theorem
9.5
at
any
point
p\in\mathbb{E}_{d}
.

Furthermore, the coordinatization map

\displaystyle\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\to\operatorname{Aff}(G),\,\ \ \phi\mapsto x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,,

(395)

is a group isomorphism.

Proof
:

Since
x^{A}
and
\phi
are affine maps,
x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
is an affine transformation of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, i.e. an element of
\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{GL}(d))
(or some subgroup of it).
This implies that a first order Taylor expansion of the expression is
exact
.
The application of the coordinate expression to an arbitrary element
{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
can therefore be written in terms of the following Taylor expansion around the origin
0
of
\mathbb{R}^{d}
:

\displaystyle\big[x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\big]({x})\ =

\displaystyle\ \big[x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\big](0)\ +\ \frac{\partial}{\partial{x}^{\prime}}\big[x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\big]_{{x}^{\prime}=0}\cdot{x}

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ t_{\phi}^{AA}\ +\ g_{\phi}^{AA}\cdot{x}

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \big(t_{\phi}^{AA}\mkern 2.0mug_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\,{x}

(396)

Here we implicitly defined the translation
t_{\phi}^{AA}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
and the Jacobian
g_{\phi}^{AA}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}
and identified them with group elements, which is possible since all involved morphisms are invertible.

That the Jacobian
g_{\phi}^{AA}
agrees with the induced gauge transformation
g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)
at an arbitrary point
p\in M
is shown by rewriting it via Eq. (
543
) in terms of differentials:

\displaystyle g_{\phi}^{AA}\

\displaystyle=\ \frac{\partial}{\partial{x}^{\prime}}\big[x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\big]_{{x}^{\prime}=x^{A}(p)}

\displaystyle=\ \iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,d\big[x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A})^{-1}\big]_{x^{A}(p)}\,\big(\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big)^{-1}

\displaystyle=\ \iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,dx^{A}_{\phi(p)}\,d\phi_{p}\,\big(dx^{A}_{p})^{-1}\,\big(\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big)^{-1}

\displaystyle=\ \hat{d}x^{A}_{\phi(p)}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muT\mkern-3.0muM$}}}\,\big(\hat{d}x^{A}_{p})^{-1}

\displaystyle=\ g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)

(397)

In the penultimate step we identified the differential
d\phi
as an alternative notation for the pushforward
\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muT\mkern-3.0muM$}}}
and identified the chart gradients
\hat{d}x^{A}:=\iota_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,dx^{A}
as defined in Eq. (
A.3.1
).
The index
p
is dropped in the notation
g_{\phi}^{AA}=g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)
due to its arbitrariness.

That
t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}
is not only an element element of
\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{GL}(d))
but of its subgroup
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
is clear since Theorem
9.5
states that
g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)\in G
for any
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
.

To prove that the coordinatization map
C^{A}:\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\to\operatorname{Aff}(G),\,\ \phi\mapsto x^{A}\,\phi\,(x^{A})^{-1}
is indeed a group isomorphism, we need to show that it is
1) a group homomorphism,
2) injective and
3) surjective.
That
C^{A}
is a group homomorphism follows immediately from its definition since

\displaystyle C^{A}(\phi\,\tilde{\phi})\ =\ x^{A}\,\phi\,\tilde{\phi}\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\ =\ x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,x^{A}\,\tilde{\phi}\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\ =\ C^{A}(\phi)\,C^{A}(\tilde{\phi})

(398)

holds for any
\phi,\tilde{\phi}\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
.
The injectivity of
C^{A}
requires that, for any
\phi,\tilde{\phi}\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
, the equality
C^{A}(\phi)=C^{A}(\tilde{\phi})
implies
\phi=\tilde{\phi}
.
That this is the case is clear since
C^{A}(\phi)=C^{A}(\tilde{\phi})
is equivalent to

x^{A}\,\phi\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}=x^{A}\,\tilde{\phi}\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}
, which implies the equality of
\phi
and
\tilde{\phi}
since
x^{A}
is an isomorphism.
Lastly,
C^{A}
is surjective if and only if for any
tg\in\operatorname{Aff}(G)
there exists some
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
, such that
C^{A}(\phi)=tg
.
As an ansatz, let
\phi=\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,tg\,x^{A}
, such that
C^{A}(\phi)=tg
.
What remains to be shown is that this construction of
\phi
is indeed an element of
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
.
As one can easily check,
g_{\phi}^{AA}=g\in G
, such that
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
follows from Theorem
9.5
, with which surjectivity holds.
Overall, this proves that
C^{A}:\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\to\operatorname{Aff}(G)
is a group isomorphism if
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
is induced by an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas.

\Box

The isomorphism between
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
and
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
is not unique, as it depends on the particular chart considered.
Different choices are related by the inner automorphisms of
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
since

\displaystyle C^{B}(\phi)=x^{B}\,\phi\,(x^{B})^{-1}=x^{B}(x^{A})^{-1}x^{A}\,\phi\,(x^{A})^{-1}x^{A}(x^{B})^{-1}=(t^{BA}g^{BA})\,C^{A}(\phi)\,(t^{BA}g^{BA})^{-1}\,.

(399)

This concludes our analysis of the Euclidean geometry and
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-invariant
G
-structures that are required for the definition of coordinate free Euclidean convolutions in the next section.

9.3
Affine group equivariant CNNs on Euclidean spaces
\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}_{\bm{d}}

We now turn to investigate Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas induced
G
-structures.
When being expressed in a chart, these convolutions boil down to classical
G
-steerable convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, as we show next.
Their affine equivariance is in Theorem
9.8
proven in a coordinate free setting.

Recovering conventional convolutions on
\boldsymbol{\mathbb{R}^{d}}
:

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions rely crucially on the transporter pullback
\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf
of feature fields, which in turn depends on parallel transporters and the exponential map.
On Euclidean spaces, these operations take a particularly simple form, which we discuss first.

As stated before, Levi-Civita transporters move tangent vectors such over Euclidean spaces that they remain parallel in the usual sense on Euclidean spaces; see Fig.
20(a)
.
Let
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
be any global chart of an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas.
As the induced frame field is “parallel”, the transporters along
any
path
\gamma
become trivial when being expressed relative to the induced gauges
\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}
:

\displaystyle g_{\gamma}^{AA}\,

\displaystyle=\,e

\displaystyle\textup{for \emph{any} path}\ \gamma

(400)

This implies in particular that the feature vector transporters are in this gauge given by identity maps, i.e.

\displaystyle\rho\big(g_{\gamma}^{AA}\big)\,

\displaystyle=\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{c}}

\displaystyle\textup{for \emph{any} path}\ \gamma\,.

(401)

When expressing the exponential map in a chart, it reduces to a summation of the point and vector coordinate expressions:

\displaystyle x^{A}\big(\exp_{p}v\big)\ =\ x^{A}(p)+\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}(v)

(402)

We furthermore need to express feature fields in coordinates, that is, we pull them via the (global, inverse) chart from
\mathbb{E}_{d}
back to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
,

\displaystyle F^{A}\ :=\ f^{A}\circ\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,:\,\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}\,,

(403)

which is visualized by the following commutative diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
F^{A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{A}}

(404)

With these ingredients at hand, the transporter pullback, Eq. (
4.2.1
), of feature fields on Euclidean spaces can in coordinates be expressed as

\displaystyle\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf\big]^{A}({v})\ =

\displaystyle\,\ \rho\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}g^{AA}_{p\,\leftarrow\,\exp_{p}(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A})^{\shortminus 1}(v^{A})}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\,f^{A}\,\exp_{p}\!\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\!\big(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}\big)^{\mkern-2.0mu-1}({v})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\,\ f^{A}\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,x^{A}\exp_{p}\!\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\!\big(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}\big)^{\mkern-2.0mu-1}({v})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\,\ F^{A}\big(x^{A}(p)+{v}\big)\,.

(405)

The coordinate expression of the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution, Eq. (
87
), becomes therefore

\displaystyle f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}(p)\ =\ \big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}(p)\ =\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\,\big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}({v})\ d{v}\ =\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big(x^{A}(p)+{v}\big)\ d{v}\,.

(406)

This shows that
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on Euclidean spaces are conventional convolutions (correlations).

Theorem 9.7
(
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on Euclidean spaces recover convolutions on
\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{R}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{R}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{R}$\crcr}}}^{\boldmath{d}}
).

Let
G\mkern-1.4muM
be a
G
-structure induced by an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas of charts as defined in Section
9.2
.
When being expressed relative to any global chart
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
of this
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas, the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution takes the form of a conventional convolution (correlation)
*
:

\displaystyle F_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}({x})\ =\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\,F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big({x}+{v}\big)\ d{v}\ =\ \big[K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big]({x})

(407)

Proof
:

The statement follows by evaluating Eq. (
406
) at
p=\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}({x})
and identifying
F_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}=f_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}\circ\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}
on the l.h.s.

\Box

Before proceeding to our proof of the Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions’ equivariance in a
coordinate free
setting, we consider its
coordinate independence
– as we will see, both notions are closely related.
All that is required to demonstrate the coordinate independence is the transformation law of the feature field pullbacks to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
via charts.
The transformation law follows directly from transition functions and can from the commutativity of the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{E}_{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{d}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces t^{BA}g^{BA}\ }
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ \rho\big(g^{BA}\big)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{B}}

(408)

be read off to be given by

\displaystyle F^{B}\ =\ \rho\big(g^{BA}\big)\,F^{A}\,\big(t^{BA}g^{BA}\big)^{-1}\,.

(409)

Note that this transformation law is exactly the induced representation
F^{B}=t^{BA}g^{BA}\rhd_{\rho}F^{A}
as introduced in Eq. (
370
).
Leveraging the equivariance of the conventional convolution with
G
-steerable kernels from Eq. (
371
), this implies

\displaystyle K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{B}\ =\ K*\big(t^{BA}g^{BA}\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}}F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\ =\ t^{BA}g^{BA}\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}\big(K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\ =\ t^{BA}g^{BA}\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}F_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{A}\ =\ F_{\textup{\>\!\!out}}^{B}

(410)

The
active
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance
of classical
G
-steerable convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
from Section
9.1
is therefore seen to imply the
passive
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
coordinate independence
of Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions and vice versa.
The two are two sides of the same coin.
In addition, one can prove the
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance of the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution in the coordinate free setting, which we will do next.

Affine group equivariance

To prove the affine group equivariance of Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, we first define the transformation law of coordinate free feature fields
f\in\Gamma(\mathcal{A})
under affine transformations
\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
as

\displaystyle\phi\,\rhd f\ =\ \phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}\,f\>\phi^{-1}\,,

(411)

i.e. as for isometries in Def.
8.2
.
97
97

97

Since the feature vector bundle is defined as a
G
-bundle, i.e. associated to
G\mkern-1.4muM
, pushforwards can only be defined for the
G
-structure preserving affine transformations in
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
.

The (Levi-Civita) transporter pullback of an affine transformed feature field
\phi\rhd\!f
is relative to an affine chart
x^{A}
given by:

\displaystyle\ \ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}(\phi\rhd\!f)\big]^{A}({v})

\displaystyle\ \overset{(1)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}(\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}f\,\phi^{-1})\big]^{A}({v})

\displaystyle\ \overset{(2)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \underbrace{\rho\big(g^{AA}_{p\,\leftarrow\,\exp_{p}(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A})^{-1}({v})}\big)}_{=\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{c}}}\,\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\,(\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}f\,\phi^{-1})\,\exp_{p}\!\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\!\big(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}\big)^{-1}({v})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(3)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}\big)^{-1}\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\,f\>\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\,x^{A}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\,\phi^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\res
