\displaystyle\ \overset{(4)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}\,\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}\big)^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}\,f\,\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}x^{A}\,\phi^{-1}\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}x^{A}\exp_{p}\!\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\!\big(\hat{d}x_{p}^{A}\big)^{-1}({v})\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}

\displaystyle\ \overset{(5)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \rho\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\,F^{A}\,\big(t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)^{-1}\big(x^{A}(p)+{v}\big)

\displaystyle\ \overset{(6)}{=}

\displaystyle\ \ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\big(t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\rhd_{\rho}F^{A}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\,\big(x^{A}(p)+{v}\big)

(412)

It relates to the transporter pullback of the untransformed field via the induced representation (Eq. (
370
)), acting with the coordinate expression
t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}
of
\phi
(Eq. (
393
)).
The first two steps make use of Eq. (
411
) and the definition of the transporter pullback in coordinates, where
(\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}f\,\phi^{-1})^{A}:=\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}(\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}$ }}}f\,\phi^{-1})
.
To translate all morphisms into the corresponding coordinate expressions, step three inserts identities
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{c}}=\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}\big)^{-1}\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$\!\mathcal{A},$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi^{-1}\mkern-1.0mu(p)$}}^{A}
and
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}=\big(x^{A}\big)^{-1}x^{A}
, which are in step four rebracketed to clarify which combinations result in the coordinate expressions after step five.
Recall for step 5 that, by Theorem
9.6
,
g_{\phi}^{AA}(p)=g_{\phi}^{AA}
for any
p
in
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
As stated above, the last step identifies the resulting transformation law in coordinates as the action of the induced representation.

With this result we can prove the
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariance of Euclidean convolutions in the coordinate free setting.
This generalizes Theorem
8.9
, proving the isometry equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions for the specific case of Euclidean spaces.

Theorem 9.8
(Affine equivariance of Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions).

Let
G\mkern-1.4muM
be a
G
-structure that is induced by some
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas of the Euclidean space
{M=\mathbb{E}_{d}}
and assume feature vectors to be transported according to the Levi-Civita connection on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
The corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions is then guaranteed to be equivariant under the action of
G
-structure preserving affine transformations
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\cong\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
In equations, we have for arbitrary feature fields
f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\in\Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\textup{in}})
and
G
-steerable kernels
K\in{K}^{G}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
that

\displaystyle\big[K\star(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big]\ =\ \phi\rhd\big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]\qquad\forall\,\phi\in\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\,,

(413)

i.e. that the following diagram commutes for any
\phi
in
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\textup{in}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\textup{in}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\textup{out}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\textup{out}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K\star\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\,K\star}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\,\rhd}

(414)

Proof
:

Let
x^{A}:\mathbb{E}_{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}
be any global chart of the considered
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas and let
p\in\mathbb{E}_{d}
.
Our proof of the
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}
-equivariance is then performed by expressing the convolution relative to these coordinates and making use of the
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance of classical
G
-steerable convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
from Eq. (
371
):

\displaystyle\ \ \psi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.65}{$\!\!\mathcal{A}$}_{\textup{out}},p}}^{A}\,\big[K\star(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big](p)

(415)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ \big[\mkern-2.0mu\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}(\phi\rhd f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}})\big]^{A}({v})\,\ d{v}\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{$G\mkern-1.4muM$-convolution in coordinates, Eq.~\eqref{eq:gauge_conv_coord_expression} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\big(t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}}\!F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\,\big(x^{A}(p)+{v}\big)\,\ d{v}\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{transformed transporter pullback, Eq.~\eqref{eq:affine_transformed_transporter_pullback} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}K*\big(t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}}\!F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\big(x^{A}(p)\big)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{identified convolution $*$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}\big(K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}\big(x^{A}(p)\big)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{$\operatorname{Aff}(G)$-equivariance on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:Euclidean_conv_equiv_in_coords_Rd} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\big(K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big($}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big($}}}}}\big(t_{\phi}^{AA}g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)^{-1}x^{A}(p)\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{360448}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big)$}}}}}\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{induced representation $\rhd_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:induced_rep_affine} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\big(K*F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big)\big(x^{A}(\phi^{-1}(p))\big)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{coordinate expression of $\phi$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:AffGM_in_charts_eq} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ F_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}^{A}\big(x^{A}\big(\phi^{-1}(p)\big)+{v}\big)\,\ d{v}\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{expanded convolution $*$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K({v})\ \big[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{\phi^{-1}(p)}\mkern-2.0muf_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]^{A}({v})\,\ d{v}\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{Euclidean transporter pullback, Eq.~\eqref{eq:transporter_pullback_Euclidean} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\phi}^{AA}\big)\psi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.65}{$\!\!\mathcal{A}$}_{\textup{out}},\phi^{-1}(p)}}^{A}\big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]\,\phi^{-1}(p)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{$G\mkern-1.4muM$-convolution in coordinates, Eq.~\eqref{eq:gauge_conv_coord_expression} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \psi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.65}{$\!\!\mathcal{A}$}_{\textup{out}},p}}^{A}\,\phi_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0mu\mathcal{A}_{\textup{out}}$ }}}\big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]\phi^{-1}(p)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{pushforward in coordinates, Eq.~\eqref{cd:pushforward_A_coord} }\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ \ \psi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.65}{$\!\!\mathcal{A}$}_{\textup{out}},p}}^{A}\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big[$}}}}}\phi\rhd\big[K\star f_{\textup{\;\!\!in}}\big]\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big]$}}}}}(p)\quad

\displaystyle\big(\text{$\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}$ action on feature fields, Eq.~\eqref{eq:affine_action_sections} }\big)

The statement follows since
\psi_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.65}{$\!\!\mathcal{A}$}_{\textup{out}},p}}^{A}
is an isomorphism.

\Box

In summary, Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions with
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas induced
G
-structures have the following two properties:

\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-coordinate independence:

They are guaranteed to produce equivalent results in any chart of the
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas
{A}^{\operatorname{Aff}(G)}_{\mathbb{E}_{d}}
.
This property was shown in Eq. (
410
) and is in Fig.
47
visualized as the transformation
between charts
.

active
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance:

As proven in Theorem
9.8
they are equivariant under active transformations of feature fields by
\operatorname{Aff}_{\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-1.4muM}\cong\operatorname{Aff}(G)
.
In Fig.
47
, this would correspond to an transformation of the signal on
\mathbb{E}_{d}
, which would reflect in an active transformation on its representation relative to the
same chart
.

The proofs of both properties rely ultimately on the active
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance of classical
G
-steerable convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
in Eq. (
371
).

9.4
Euclidean CNNs in the literature

All of the models in rows (1-26) of Table
are
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariant
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
as discussed in the previous sections.
They differ in the dimensionality
d
of the Euclidean space, the structure group
G
and thus global symmetry group
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
, the group representations or field types
\rho
and choices of discretizations.
This section discusses the models briefly by grouping them by their field types into irrep models, regular representation models (corresponding to group convolutions) and variations of them, quotient representation models and others.
Conventional CNNs, which we review first, fall a bit out of this classification as their trivial structure group leads to feature fields and kernels without any symmetry constraints.

Row (1) lists Euclidean
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on translation invariant
\{e\}
-structures as visualized in Fig.
48(a)
.
Due to the triviality of the structure group
G=\{e\}
no (non-trivial) gauge transformations exist and the only possible choice of group representation is the trivial representation.
The
G
-steerability constraint becomes therefore trivial, such that the space of admissible convolution kernels remains unrestricted.
When being pulled back to
\mathbb{R}^{d}
via a chart, the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution becomes by Theorem
9.7
a conventional convolution (correlation).
Theorem
9.8
asserts its translational equivariance.
The models are therefore seen to correspond to the conventional convolutional networks by
LeCun et al. 1990
.

All of the other Euclidean models in rows (2-26) consider non-trivial structure groups.
They can be thought of as conventional convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
with the additional constraint on the kernels to be
G
-steerable, which guarantees their
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariance.

Irrep features:

The networks in rows (4, 9, 10, 17, 23) and (26) operate on feature fields that transform according to
irreducible representations
(irreps) of
G
.
For
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
, listed in row (4), this leads to so-called harmonic networks
[
244
,
234
]
.
This name is motivated by the fact that the kernel constraint allows in this case only for spectrally localized circular harmonics of frequency
m-n
when mapping between fields that transform according to irreps of order
n
in the input and order
m
in the output.
98
98

98

Only frequency
m-n
is allowed when considering
complex
irreps of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
For
real
irreps, the constraint allows for frequencies
|m-n|
and
m+n
.
More details can be found in Appendices F.5 of
[
234
]
and E.1 and E.2 of
[
128
]
.

The additional reflectional constraint for
G=\operatorname{O}(2)
, listed in row (10), adds parity selection rules that fix the phase of the circular harmonics, suppressing half of the degrees of freedom as compared to the
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
case
[
234
]
.
The models by
[
235
,
224
,
156
,
120
,
2
]
in row (17) consider irreps of
G=\operatorname{SO}(3)
and can therefore be seen as the analog to the models in row (4) in three dimensions.
The space of valid kernels to map between fields that transform according to irreps (Wigner D-matrices) of orders
n
and
m
is here spanned by all spherical harmonics of the
2(\min(m,n)+1)
orders
j
with
|m-n|\leq j\leq m+n
.
As proven in
[
128
]
, this generalizes to any compact structure group, with the admissible frequencies of the harmonics being determined by the corresponding Clebsch-Gordan coefficients labeled by
m,n
and
j
.
A variation of this approach is listed in row (23)
[
174
]
.
A convolution of an input scalar field with spherical harmonics yields irrep fields of the corresponding order.
However, instead of processing these irrep features further via convolutions, the authors compute their norm.
This results in scalar fields, which are in the next layer processed in the same manner.
The model from
[
205
]
in row (26) does not assume the standard Euclidean metric but the Minkowski metric.
Its structure group is the Lorentz group
G=\operatorname{SO}(d-1,1)
and the global symmetry group is the Poincaré group.
In addition to building the equivariant network, the authors propose an algorithm to compute the irreps of Lie groups from the structure constants of their Lie algebra.

A special case of irreps are
trivial representations
, which describe
G
-invariant feature vectors (scalars).
Due to their invariance, such features can not encode differences between any patterns in
G
-related poses.
The constraint on kernels that map between scalar fields becomes
K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=K({v})
for any
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
and any
g\in G
, enforcing kernels that are (in every channel individually) invariant under the action of
G
.
This is for reflections
G={R}
visualized in the upper left entry of Table
3
.
Interpreting the pixel grid of an image as a graph and applying a standard graph convolution to it corresponds to a trivially steerable convolution with
\operatorname{O}(2)
-invariant kernels since standard graph convolutions apply isotropic kernels
[
110
]
.

An advantage of irrep features from a practical viewpoint is their low dimensionality and thus memory consumption per feature field.
However, empirical results show that irrep field based steerable convolutions usually achieve a lower performance than other field types, for instance those based on regular representations.
This statement is reflected in our evaluation of Möbius convolutions in Section
5.4.2
and the benchmark of isometry equivariant Euclidean convolutions in
[
234
]
.

Regular features and group convolutions:

The probably most prominent class of group representations in equivariant deep learning are
regular representations
of the structure groups.
Regular representations operate on a suitable
99
99

99

For instance, for topological groups, the functions are typically required to be continuous.
For locally compact groups one usually considers the space
L^{2}(G)
of square integrable functions on
G
.

space of functions
\digamma:G\to\mathbb{R}
by translating them, that is,

\big[\rho_{\textup{reg}}(\tilde{g})\digamma\big](g)=\digamma\big(\tilde{g}^{-1}g\big)
.
100
100

100

Regular representations over a different field
\mathbb{K}
than the reals take values in this field, i.e.
\digamma:G\to\mathbb{K}
.

For finite groups this implies feature fields with the number of channels
c=|G|
given by the order of the group.
As non-finite groups imply non-finite regular representations, the corresponding features are in practice discretized, which is mostly done by considering a finite subgroup of the structure group.
Since regular feature fields
f\in\Gamma(\mathcal{A})
assign a function
f^{A}(p):G\to\mathbb{R}
to each point
p\in M
(when being expressed relative to any gauge
A
at
p
), they are equivalent to real-valued functions
\tilde{f}:G\mkern-1.4muM\to\mathbb{R}
on the
G
-structure
G\mkern-1.4muM
.
101
101

101

Theorem
H.1
in Appendix
H
proves this isomorphism

C^{\infty}(G\mkern-1.4muM)\ \cong\ \Gamma(\mathcal{A}_{\rho_{\textup{reg}}})

for the practically relevant case of
G
being a finite group.

For the case of
G\mkern-1.4muM
being induced by an
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-atlas, this is furthermore equivalent to real-valued functions
\accentset{\approx}{f}:\operatorname{Aff}(G)\to\mathbb{R}
on
\operatorname{Aff}(G)\cong G\mkern-1.4muM
(along the isomorphism in Eq. (
386
)).
Equivariant linear maps between functions on the group
\operatorname{Aff}(G)
are
group convolutions
(see Eq. (
D.1
) in Section
D
and Section 7.11 in
[
75
]
), which means that affine group convolution based CNNs are covered by our framework
[
33
,
121
,
7
]
.

\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-group convolutions are in Table
listed in rows (2,3,5,11,15,19,21,24) and (25).
As these models typically process gray-scale or scalar images, they apply an initial convolution from scalar fields to regular fields, followed by group convolutions, i.e. convolutions from regular to regular fields.
As regular representations are permutation representations, they typically apply pointwise nonlinearities like ReLUs to each of the field channels individually.
102
102

102

As the action of nonlinear maps depends on the chosen basis, this is what really distinguishes regular (or any other non-irreducible) feature fields from their decomposition into irrep fields; see footnote
16
and the discussion in Section
5.2
.

The reflection equivariant CNN on
\mathbb{E}_{2}
from
[
234
]
in
row (3)
applies
{R}
-steerable kernels, as derived in Section
5
and visualized in the bottom right entry of Table
3
.
As the reflection group is finite with order
|{R}|=2
, the regular feature fields have two channels, each of which is associated to one of the two frame orientations of the
{R}
-structure in Fig.
48(c)
.
The resulting model is globally
\mathcal{T}_{2}\rtimes{R}=\operatorname{Aff}({R})
equivariant.
To construct
\operatorname{SE}(2)=\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{SO}(2))
equivariant group convolutions one would in theory have to consider the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure in Fig.
48(b)
with feature fields transforming according to the regular representation of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
In practice, most of the models in
row (5)
of Table

approximate this via regular representations of the cyclic groups
\operatorname{C}_{\!N}\leq\operatorname{SO}(2)
, which are finite subgroups of discrete rotations by multiples of
2\pi/N
.
As the order of these groups is
|\!\operatorname{C}_{\!N}\!|=N
, the corresponding feature fields are
N
-dimensional.
While the model performance is initially significantly increasing with
N
, it is empirically found to saturate at approximately
8
to
12
sampled directions
[
236
,
234
,
7
]
.
For an intuition on the spaces of
\operatorname{C}_{\!N}
-steerable kernels we refer to the visualizations in
[
236
,
8
,
7
]
.
The
\operatorname{E}(2)=\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{O}(2))
equivariant group convolutions in
row (11)
are similarly approximated via dihedral subgroups
\operatorname{D}_{\!N}\leq\operatorname{O}(2)
, which consist of
N
rotations, each in two reflections.
The feature fields are in this case
|\!\operatorname{D}_{\!N}\!|=2N
-dimensional.
Simultaneous equivariance under translations and scaling is achieved by the
\mathcal{T}_{d}\rtimes{S}=\operatorname{Aff}({S})
group convolutions in
rows (2) and (15).
The scaling group is hereby commonly discretized.
As this would still lead to a (countably) infinite group order, the implementations introduce cutoffs, i.e. minimal and maximal scales as shown by the frames in Fig.
48(d)
.
Note that this leads to similar boundary effects as for conventional convolutions at the border of an image.
The models in
rows (19) and (21)
are equivariant w.r.t. translations, rotations and, for the latter, reflections on three-dimensional Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{3}
.
While
Finzi et al. 2020b
choose a Monte-Carlo discretization of the regular representation,
the models in
[
242
,
241
]
are based on different discrete subgroups of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
or
\operatorname{O}(3)
.
A current limitation of group convolution based rotation and reflection equivariant models in three dimensions is their high memory and compute requirement.
For instance, the symmetry group of the cube, which has still a quite coarse resolution of rotations by
\pi/2
, already consists of
48
group elements, implying
48
-dimensional feature fields in three-dimensional space.
On the other hand, the large number of symmetries reflects the greatly enhanced data efficiency of such models:
the authors of
[
241
]
report the same performance of an equivariant model in comparison to a non-equivariant (
\{e\}
-steerable) network despite training on a
10
times smaller dataset.
The models in
rows (24) and (25)
convolve on
\mathbb{E}_{3}
, however, they consider cyclic and dihedral structure groups
\operatorname{C}_{4}
and
\operatorname{D}_{4}
, i.e. planar rotations and reflections around the (thus defined)
z
-axis.
Their steerable kernels are therefore similar to those of the models from
rows (5) and (11)
but extend additionally in a new
z
-direction.

Regular to scalar and vector pooling:

A variation of group convolutional networks are the models in
rows (7,8,13,16) and (20),
which are labeled by regular
\xrightarrow{\textup{pool}}
trivial and regular
\xrightarrow{\textup{pool}}
vector.
After applying a convolution to regular feature fields, they perform a
\operatorname{max}
-
pooling
operation over channels, which results in scalar (trivial) fields
[
33
,
143
,
234
,
77
,
3
]
, or a
\operatorname{max}
-pooling together with an
\operatorname{argmax}
, from which vector fields can be computed
[
144
,
234
]
.
Subsequent convolutions map from the resulting scalar or vector fields back to regular feature fields.
As the pooling operations reduce the number of channels significantly from
|G|
to
1
or
d
, respectively, the models become more memory and compute efficient than conventional group convolutions.
On the downside the pooling is accompanied with a loss of information, which is empirically found to decrease the model performance
[
234
]
.

Quotient features:

Rows (6,12) and (22) list models whose feature fields transform according to
quotient representations
of the structure group, which are permutation representations that are similar to regular representations.
Given a subgroup
\widehat{G}
of
G
, the corresponding quotient representation acts on scalar functions
\digamma:G/\widehat{G}\to\mathbb{R}
on the quotient space
G/\widehat{G}
via translation, that is,

\big[\rho_{\textup{quot}}^{G/\widehat{G}}(\tilde{g})\mkern 2.0mu\digamma\big](g\mkern 1.0mu\widehat{G})=\digamma(\tilde{g}^{-1}g\mkern 2.0mu\widehat{G})
.
The dimensionality of the feature fields is therefore given by the index
{|G:\mkern-2.0mu\widehat{G}|}
of
\widehat{G}
in
G
, which is for finite groups equal to
|G|/|\widehat{G}|
.
Feature fields that transform under quotient representations can be seen as symmetry-constrained regular feature fields that are forced to take the same value on all group elements in the same coset
g\widehat{G}
of
\widehat{G}
in
G
.
A specific example are the representations in row (22), which are associated with the quotient
\operatorname{O}(3)/\operatorname{O}(2)\cong S^{2}
.
Instead of allowing for arbitrary convolution kernels, the kernel constraint leads here to kernels which are invariant under rotations around the
z
-axis; see the visualizations in
[
103
]
.
More details and a graphical intuition on quotient representation based feature fields can be found in Appendix C of
[
234
]
.
The theory proposed in
[
121
]
covers quotient fields from an alternative viewpoint of group convolutions on right quotient spaces.

Induced representations:

A generalization of regular and quotient representations are induced representations like the
induced
\operatorname{SO}(2)
irreps
in row (14)
of Table
.
Given any
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-irrep
\rho:\operatorname{SO}(2)\to\operatorname{GL}(n)
, the induced representation
\operatorname{Ind}_{\operatorname{SO}(2)}^{\operatorname{O}(2)}\rho:\operatorname{O}(2)\to\operatorname{GL}(c)
of
\operatorname{O}(2)
with
c=n\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\!{|\operatorname{O}(2):\operatorname{SO}(2)|}=2n

acts in the following way:
reflections permute two
n
-dimensional, orthogonal subspaces of
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
which correspond to the two cosets in
\operatorname{O}(2)/\operatorname{SO}(2)
while rotations act on the individual subspaces via
\rho
.
For
\rho
being the trivial representation of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
this recovers quotient representations as discussed above.
In comparison to
\operatorname{O}(2)
-irrep feature fields, the induced
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-irrep fields show a significantly improved performance.
A more detailed description and empirical evaluation of these field types can be found in
[
234
]
.

The last type of representation listed in Table
is the quaternion representation of three-dimensional rotations in row (18)
[
250
]
.
It makes use of the usual representation of rotations via quaternions, which relies the identification of unit quaternions with
\operatorname{SU}(2)
and the existence of a surjective group homomorphism from
\operatorname{SU}(2)
to
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.
Note that the quaternion representation is actually a projective representation of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.

While our theory is formulated on continuous Euclidean spaces, implementations sample feature fields on discrete subsets.
The most common discretization of
\mathbb{E}_{d}
is in terms of the pixel grid
\mathbb{Z}^{d}
.
An alternative are hexagonal planar grids on
\mathbb{E}_{2}
as investigated by
Hoogeboom et al. 2018
.
If such regular pixel grids are chosen, a basis of
G
-steerable kernels can be precomputed and sampled on this grid.
Data like events in spacetime
[
205
]
or molecules in
\mathbb{R}^{3}

[
224
,
120
,
2
,
156
]
are instead usually represented by irregular point clouds.
In this case the kernels need to be given analytically, which allows their online sampling during the forward pass.

Finally, we want to mention that there exist
globally

\operatorname{Aff}(G)
-equivariant models which are
not locally

G
-equivariant.
An example is TI-pooling (transformation-invariant pooling)
[
129
]
, which feeds a set of globally transformed feature fields through a conventional CNN and finally pools the resulting features over these transformations, which results in an invariant descriptor.

We start with the conceptually simplest models, which are globally rotation equivariant networks that rely on solely rotation invariant
\{e\}
-structures on
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}

[
67
,
30
]
.
These models assume the standard Euclidean metric on
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
, relative to which the frames are orthonormal.
Together, these two requirements imply
\{e\}
-structures as shown in Fig.
49
.

In addition to the considered
G
-structures, the networks depend on the specific implementation of the transporter pullback and thus on the geodesics and parallel transporters.
The geodesics are in both models assumed to be the standard geodesics on Euclidean spaces (i.e. straight lines), corresponding to the Levi-Civita connection of the Euclidean metric.
As
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
is not geodesically complete, zero-padding has to be used for exponential maps that would end at the origin.
Note that this does not have an impact on the final result as the lost geodesics are of measure zero.

The parallel transport of feature vectors, on the other hand, does
not
correspond to the Levi-Civita connection since the Levi-Civita connection is not compatible with the
\{e\}
-structures.
Instead, the models assume the unique
\{e\}
-compatible
trivial connections
which are implied by the respective
\{e\}
-structures.
104
104

104

An animation of the
\{e\}
-compatible transport corresponding to Fig.
49(a)
can be found on

Wikipedia
.

According to the trivial connections, the numerical coefficients of feature vectors do not transform when being transported, despite the frames being rotated relative to the usual notion of parallelism on Euclidean spaces.
In practice, this just means that the transporters
\rho(g^{A\widetilde{A}}_{\gamma})=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{c}}
can be ignored in the implementation – which is the reason that they are not being discussed in the original papers
[
67
,
30
]
.

As rotations leave the considered
\{e\}
-structures invariant and are at the same time isometries, we have

\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\operatorname{SO}(2)
for the model by
Finzi et al. 2020b
(Fig.
49(a)
) and

\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\operatorname{C}_{8}
for the model by
Chidester et al. 2019
(Fig.
49(b)
).
Theorem
8.9
asserts then that the corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}
-equivariant, which is in agreement with the statements made by the authors.

Figure 50:

\operatorname{O}(2)

.
The corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution is simultaneously equivariant w.r.t. global rotations and reflections in
\Isom_{{R}\mkern-1.8muM}=\operatorname{O}(2)
around the origin.

Before going on we want to mention that the
\operatorname{C}_{8}
-invariant
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
49(b)
is not continuous and does therefore not guarantee a continuous (or smooth) inference.
An advantage of this
\{e\}
-structure from an engineering viewpoint is that it is locally isometric to the canonical
\{e\}
-structure of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, which allows to run conventional Euclidean convolution routines on each octant.
The authors discuss the generalization to
\operatorname{C}_{\!N}
-invariant
\{e\}
-structures, which become in the limit
N\to\infty
equivalent to the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-invariant
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
49(a)
.

It is furthermore possible to make the models globally
\operatorname{O}(2)
-equivariant by using reflection steerable kernels instead of unconstrained kernels.
From a theoretic viewpoint this corresponds to the
\Isom_{{R}\mkern-1.8muM}=\operatorname{O}(2)
-invariant
{R}
-structure
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
on
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
shown in Fig.
50
.
Note that
{R}\mkern-1.8muM
is a
{R}
-bundle over
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
, whose restriction to circles of constant radius is as a principal bundle isomorphic to
\operatorname{O}(2)
, interpreted as
{R}
-bundle over the quotient space
\operatorname{O}(2)/{R}\cong S^{1}
.

Global rotation and scale equivariance on

via log-polar coordinates

are isometries relative to the induced metric.

Esteves et al. 2018b
implement such

\mathbb{R}^{2}
.

By making the rotation invariant

-convolutions become equivariant w.r.t. the direct product group

Such

, shown in Fig.

, which allow for a convenient implementation of the

\mathbb{R}^{2}

The translation equivariance of convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{2}
corresponds then to the
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance on
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
For clarity, we start by describing the model in terms of log-polar coordinates as proposed by
Esteves et al. 2018b
.
105
105

105

The idea to implement rotation invariant correlations via log-polar transforms appeared already in the 80’s
[
190
,
23
]
.

Subsequently, we investigate how this model and its properties are explained in our framework.

Log-polar coordinates of the punctured Euclidean vector space
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
are defined in terms of the smooth surjection

\displaystyle\chi:\,\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}\,,\ \ (\varphi,\xi)\mapsto\big(e^{\xi}\cos(\varphi),\,e^{\xi}\sin(\varphi)\big)\,,

(416)

which assigns points
p=\chi(\varphi,\xi)
in
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
to a given polar angle
\varphi\in\mathbb{R}
and log-radius
{\xi=\log\lVert p\rVert\in\mathbb{R}}
.
This map is
2\pi
-periodic in the angular coordinate (note the repetition of the blue stripe on the r.h.s. of Fig.
51
) and is therefore in particular non-injective.
A restriction to
[0,2\pi)\times\mathbb{R}
would be bijective and continuous, however, not homeomorphic – this will require us below to consider at least two charts to cover the punctured plane.
Cartesian coordinates identify
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
with
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
, and therefore allow to assign log-polar coordinates to the latter.
As different (right-handed) Cartesian coordinate systems that are centered in the origin of
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
differ only by rotations, the assignment of log-polar coordinates is ambiguous by a shift in the angular component.

Given a feature map
f:\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
(an
\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM
-associated feature field, as clarified below),
Esteves et al. 2018b
consider its pullback
\tilde{f}:=f\circ\chi\ :\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
via log-polar coordinates, defined by the commutativity of the following diagram:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{c}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi}
\tilde{f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

(417)

A rotation and scaling equivariant group convolution of the feature field
f
on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
is then defined by
1) pulling it via
\chi
back to coordinates
\mathbb{R}^{2}

2) applying a conventional Euclidean convolution there and
3) mapping the result back to
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
This procedure is well defined since
\chi
is smooth, such that smooth feature maps (feature fields)
f
result in smooth and periodic pullbacks
\tilde{f}
.
Since convolutions are position independent, their output feature map will still be periodic and smooth, and corresponds therefore uniquely to a smooth feature map on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
106
106

106

To see this, note that
\chi
is a quotient map (since its angular part is a quotient map
\mathbb{R}\to S^{1}\cong\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}
).
For continuous (instead of smooth) feature maps the statement follows from the universal property of quotient spaces; see e.g.

Wikipedia
.
As the smoothness of a function is defined as its continuous differentiability, the universal property can be applied recursively to show that the statement holds for smooth feature maps as well.

The rotation and scaling equivariance of the implied group convolution on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
follows from the translation equivariance of the coordinate function
\chi
.
107
107

107

That this is possible relies on the fact that there is a group homomorphism

\mathcal{T}_{2}\to\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S},\ (\Delta\varphi,\,\Delta\xi)\mapsto(R_{\Delta\varphi},\,e^{\Delta\xi})
,
defined by the group isomorphism
\exp:\mathcal{T}_{1}\to{S}
on the second factor and the group homomorphism (quotient map)
R:\mathcal{T}_{1}\to\operatorname{SO}(2)\cong\mathcal{T}_{1}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}
on the second factor, where
R_{\Delta\varphi}

denotes the rotation matrix by an angle of
\Delta\varphi
.

Let
(\varphi,\xi)
be any coordinates in
\mathbb{R}^{2}
and let
(\Delta\varphi,\Delta\xi)
be any translation in
\mathcal{T}_{2}
.
The point of
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
that corresponds to translated coordinates
{(\varphi\!+\!\Delta\varphi},\,{\xi\!+\!\Delta\xi)}
relates then to the point corresponding to non-translated coordinates
(\varphi,\xi)
via a scaling by the factor
e^{\Delta\xi}
and rotation by the angle
\Delta\varphi
:

\displaystyle\chi\big(\varphi+\Delta\varphi,\,\xi+\Delta\xi\big)\

\displaystyle=\ e^{\xi+\Delta\xi}\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\varphi+\Delta\varphi)\\
\sin(\varphi+\Delta\varphi)\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=\ e^{\Delta\xi}\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\Delta\varphi)\mkern-8.0mu&-\sin(\Delta\varphi)\\
\sin(\Delta\varphi)\mkern-8.0mu&\phantom{-}\cos(\Delta\varphi)\end{pmatrix}e^{\xi}\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\varphi)\\
\sin(\varphi)\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=\ e^{\Delta\xi}\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\Delta\varphi)\mkern-8.0mu&-\sin(\Delta\varphi)\\
\sin(\Delta\varphi)\mkern-8.0mu&\phantom{-}\cos(\Delta\varphi)\end{pmatrix}\chi(\varphi,\,\xi)

\displaystyle=:\ (\Delta\varphi,\,\Delta\xi)\,\rhd\,\chi(\varphi,\,\xi)

(418)

In terms of a diagram, this means that

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\Delta\varphi{,}\,\Delta\xi)+}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\,\chi}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\Delta\varphi{,}\,\Delta\xi)\rhd}

(419)

commutes for arbitrary translations.
Together with the translation equivariance of conventional convolutions on
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, this implies that rotated and scaled input feature maps on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
will lead to rotated and scaled output feature maps on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
, i.e. the
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance of the convolution on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
More details on this viewpoint are found in
[

]
and
[

]
.

We will now revisit this convolution operation and its properties from the viewpoint of coordinate free
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
To do so, we consider an atlas of charts that are consistent with the log-polar coordinates, and discuss the induced
\{e\}
-structure, gauges, Riemannian metric, geodesics and parallel transport that it implies.
The claimed
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance follows immediately from the
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}
-equivariance of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
For notational convenience, we will again identify
\mathbb{E}_{2}\backslash\{0\}
via some choice of Cartesian coordinates with
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.

As the restriction
\tilde{\chi}:[0,2\pi)\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
of the log-polar coordinates
\chi
to non-redundant angles is bijective and continuous, one might be tempted to take its inverse as a coordinate chart.
This is, however, not possible, since
\tilde{\chi}
is not a homeomorphism, as required for charts.
Instead, we consider an atlas consisting of two charts that are defined in terms of restrictions of
\chi
and that cover
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
One particular choice is to define chart codomains as open sets
V^{A}=(0,2\pi)\times\mathbb{R}
and
V^{B}=(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\times\mathbb{R}
for some
0<\epsilon<\pi
and, for
X=A,B
, define charts on
U^{X}=\chi(V^{X})
as
x^{X}:=\big(\chi\big|_{V^{X}}\big)^{-1}:U^{X}\to V^{X}
.
Intuitively, this atlas achieves the same as the naive attempt to define charts as the inverse
\tilde{\chi}
.
The important difference is, however, that the charts are diffeomorphic, which is necessary to assure the smoothness of all operations.

As usual, these charts induce local frame fields and bundle trivializations on
U^{A}
and
U^{B}
, respectively.
It is easy to see that the transition maps
g_{p}^{BA}=\frac{\partial x^{B}}{\partial x^{A}}|_{x^{A}(p)}
on
U^{A}\cap U^{B}
are trivial, which implies that the union of the frame fields defines a smooth
\{e\}
-structure
\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM
on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
These coordinate bases, which are in the literature often denoted as
\big[\frac{\partial}{\partial\varphi},\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\big]
, are shown in Fig.
51
(left).
Our calculation in Eq. (
10
) above implies that the induced
\{e\}
-structure is
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-invariant.

The charts induce furthermore a Riemannian metric, which differs from the usual Euclidean metric on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
.
It is defined as the pullback of the Euclidean metric
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}
in the charts’ codomains, and is therefore pointwise given by

\displaystyle\eta_{p}(v,w)\,:=\,\big\langle\hat{d}x^{X}_{p}(v)\,,\,\hat{d}x^{X}_{p}(w)\big\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\,,

(420)

where
v,w\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
and
X
denotes either chart with
p\in U^{X}
.
The chart induced
\{e\}
-structure consists by construction of
frames that are orthonormal w.r.t. this chart induced metric
, even though these
frames grow with the radius when measured relative to the standard Euclidean metric
.
The Levi-Civita connection of the induced metric differs from the usual Euclidean connection and implies therefore alternative geodesics and parallel transporters.
As the metric is pulled back via the charts, the geodesics correspond to straight lines in the charts’ codomains – an example are the coordinate lines on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
in Fig.
51
.
The parallel transport corresponds to the usual transport in the charts’ codomains as well, which implies that it keeps transported vectors in a fixed angle to the coordinate lines on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
; cf. footnote
104
.
Note that this is the same transport as already discussed above in the models corresponding to Figs.
49
, where it was
not
the transport corresponding to the Levi-Civita connection since these models assumed the standard metric on
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
instead of the chart induced metric.

The
\{e\}
-structure preserving isometries
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}\cong{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}

relative to the chart induced metric
are given by rotations and rescaling of the
\{e\}
-structure
relative to the usual Euclidean metric
.
Theorem
8.9
implies the
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance of the corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution – which recovers the statement made by
Esteves et al. 2018b
in our theory.
As stated above, the fact that the metric is induced via the charts means that all operations reduce to the usual Euclidean operations when being expressed in the chart.
The
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution is therefore best implemented via a conventional convolution on the chart, as proposed by
Esteves et al. 2018b
.

Note that the
{\operatorname{SO}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance of the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution is easily extended to
{\operatorname{O}(2)\!\times\!{S}}
-equivariance, which includes reflections.
This is implemented by performing a reflection equivariant convolution in the chart, which corresponds to the
{R}
-structure shown in Fig.
48(c)
.
On
\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}
, this implies a
{R}
-structure that looks similar to that in Fig.
50
above, with the difference that the
{R}
-structure is additionally invariant under a global rescaling.

Global rotation equivariance on
\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{E}$\crcr}}}_{\bm{3}}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\backslash$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\backslash$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\displaystyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\displaystyle\backslash$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\backslash$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\backslash$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\textstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\textstyle\backslash$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\backslash$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptstyle\backslash$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\backslash$\cr\vskip 0.08pt\cr\kern-0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\backslash$\cr\kern 0.14pt$\scriptscriptstyle\backslash$\crcr}}}\bm{\{0\}}

The ideas presented above can be generalized to the three-dimensional setting, i.e. to the punctured Euclidean space
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.
Globally rotation equivariant
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions correspond here to
G
-structures that are invariant under
\operatorname{SO}(3)
rotations around the origin.
While the radial dependency of such
G
-structures is left unconstrained, the demand for rotational invariance imposes a constraint on their form over spherical shells at fixed radii, which are the orbits of the action of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
on
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.
The fact that the sphere
S^{2}=\operatorname{SO}(3)/\operatorname{SO}(2)
is a homogeneous space of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
with stabilizer subgroups isomorphic to
\operatorname{SO}(2)
implies that the structure group of an
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-invariant
G
-structure can not be reduced further than
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
; see Fig.
55(a)
.
We are therefore essentially considering spherical CNNs with an additional radial dimension.
For a review on spherical CNNs we refer the reader forward to Section
11
.

Ramasinghe et al. 2019
identified this situation and designed
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant convolutions on
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.
Before coming to our classification as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution, listed in row (29) of Table
, we briefly review the authors’ formulation and implementation.
Their implementation is based on spherical CNNs with the addition that
1) kernels extend in the radial direction and
2) are shared over shells at different radii; see Fig.
52
(left).
As commonly done for spherical CNNs, the angular dependency of the kernels is encoded via their Fourier spectrum on
S^{2}
, that is, in terms of spherical harmonics expansion coefficients.
The sharing of these expansion coefficients implies that the shared kernels cover the same solid angle for all radii, implying that the
kernels dilate in angular direction linearly with the radius
.
108
108

108

The dilation is here measured relative to the standard Euclidean metric of
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.

In the discretized implementation, the spherical shells are located at equidistant radii – which implies that the
kernels do not dilate in radial direction
.
From these insights we infer the specific
G
-structure that the model assumes below.
The kernels themselves are constrained such that they are invariant under
\operatorname{SO}(2)
rotations around the radial axis through their center, which is often referred to as
zonal kernels
;
see Fig.
53
and
[
61
]
.
As proven in
[
61
]
and
[
178
]
, the convolution with such kernels is
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant.
That this is the case is intuitively clear since rotations of the spherical shells have
\operatorname{SO}(2)
as stabilizer subgroup, w.r.t. which the zonal kernels are invariant.
As we will argue below, the model is actually
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant, that is, additionally equivariant under reflections.

G
-structure that was implicitly assumed by

can be deduced from the weight sharing scheme.

as proposed in

.
The kernels are defined to cover the same solid angle, independent of the distance from the origin, such that their diameter grows linearly with this distance.
The kernels’ extent in radial direction is independent from the distance from the origin..

In our theory, kernels are shared relative to reference frames of the
G
-structure.
To recover the proposed weight sharing scheme,
G\mkern-1.4muM
needs to consist of frames whose axes in angular direction grow linearly with the radial distance from the origin, while the axes in radial directions need to keep their size fixed (both relative to the standard Euclidean metric).
Such frames imply an alternative Riemannian metric on
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.

Right:

As the resulting

-convolution should be
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant, the
G
-structure is required to be invariant under rotations around the origin.
This requires (at least) an
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure, whose restriction to one spherical shell is shown in the right part of the figure.
Compare this to the
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-invariant
\operatorname{SO}(2)

.

).

To recover this model from the viewpoint of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, we need to determine the corresponding
G
-structure on
