.
As stated above, the
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariance of the model requires the
G
-structure to be invariant under the action of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
but does not constrain their radial variation.
To infer this radial dependency of the
G
-structure, recall that we defined convolutional weight sharing at
p\in M
as aligning the template kernel
K:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
relative to some (arbitrary) frame in
G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM
of the tangent spaces
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
The kernel sharing considered by
Ramasinghe et al. 2019
lets us therefore draw conclusions about the implicitly considered
G
-structure.
The authors share kernels such that their area tangent to the spherical shells extends with growing distance from the origin (they cover the same solid angle at each radius) while their radial thickness remains constant.
Fig.
52
(left) shows this radial variation of the shared kernels while
Fig.
52
(middle) shows the corresponding scaling of exemplary reference frames.
Together with the required
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-invariance of the
G
-structure, this implies (at least) an
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure, whose restriction to one spherical shell is visualized in Fig.
52
(right).
109
109

109

The two-dimensional analog would look similar to the
G
-structure in Fig.
51
but with all frame vectors in radial direction having unit norm (relative to the Euclidean metric).

The considered metric follows from this
G
-structure, since its frames define the relevant notion of orthonormality.
Note that this metric differs from the usual Euclidean metric.

By construction, we have rotations
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
as
G
-structure preserving isometries.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions defined by this
G
-structure, which may differ in their input and output field type, will therefore (by Theorem
8.9
) be rotation equivariant.
The specific
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution assumed by
Ramasinghe et al. 2019
, i.e. the assumed field types, can be deduced from the fact that the authors assume zonal kernels:
such kernels arise naturally when considering
scalar fields
, i.e. trivial field representations, since the kernel constraint, Eq. (
83
), becomes in this case

\displaystyle K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=K({v})\quad\ \forall\ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\ g\in\operatorname{SO}(2)\,,

(421)

enforcing isotropic (zonal) kernels.
110
110

110

Kernels which map between “scalar fields”, i.e. fields that transform according to the trivial representation of
G
, are always
G
-invariant.
For
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
, this implies isotropic (zonal) kernels, while
G={R}
implies the reflection invariant kernels in the upper left entry of Table
3
.

As a variation of the model, one could consider the
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structure that follows from the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure by adding reflected reference frames (reflecting over an arbitrary axis within the planes tangent to the spherical shells, keeping the radial frame vectors still pointing outwards).
111
111

111

This
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structure is the counterpart of the
\operatorname{O}(1)={R}
-structure in Fig.
50
for
d=3
instead of
d=2
.

In this case one has
G
-structure preserving isometries
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\operatorname{O}(3)
that consist of global rotations and reflections around the origin, and therefore
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
An interesting special case in the current context is that of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions that map between scalar fields, for which the kernel constraint reads

\displaystyle K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=K({v})\quad\ \forall\ \ {v}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\ g\in\operatorname{O}(2)\,.

(422)

This seems like a stronger constraint than that in Eq. (
421
) above:
instead of only demanding kernels to be rotationally invariant, it requires them additionally to be invariant under reflections.
However, since rotation invariant kernels are already invariant under reflections, this leads again to zonal kernels, and therefore exactly the same kernel space as for
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
112
112

112

More formally, we are searching for kernels that satisfy
K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=K({v})\ \ \forall g\in G
, that is, which are invariant on the
orbits

G.{v}=\{g\mkern 1.0mu{v}\,|\,g\in G\}\in G\backslash\mathbb{R}^{d}
of points
{v}
in
\mathbb{R}^{d}
.
As the orbits
\operatorname{O}(2).{v}=\operatorname{SO}(2).{v}
agree for any
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}
, the resulting kernel spaces are the same.

This implies that the model by
Ramasinghe et al. 2019
is actually not only
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant, as claimed by the authors, but more generally
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant, which justifies our classification in row (29) of Table
,
Note that this is a special case that applies only for scalar fields – the spaces of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
- and
\operatorname{O}(2)
-steerable kernels differ for general group representations.

How does the model by
Ramasinghe et al. 2019
relate to that of
Esteves et al. 2018b
, which relies on the
G
-structure shown in Fig.
51
?
A key difference between the two approaches is that the
G
-structure in Fig.
51
consists of frames whose outward pointing axes grow with the radial distance from the origin, which is not the case for the
G
-structure in Fig.
52
.
If we modify the latter to consist of frames whose radial axes grow linearly with the frames’ distance from the origin, one would have
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)\!\times{S}
(instead of
\Isom_{G\mkern-1.4muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
).
The corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution would therefore additionally be scale equivariant.
In an implementation, this could easily be realized by spacing the discrete spherical shells considered by
Ramasinghe et al. 2019
exponentially instead of uniformly (corresponding to a uniform spacing of the logarithmized radius).

Lastly, we briefly discuss the convolution by
Boomsma and Frellsen 2017
that is listed in row (30) of Table
.
It relies on a radial projection of the signal on spherical shells to a circumscribing cube.
To define a convolution on the cube, the authors cut it open at some of its edges and flatten it out; see Fig. 2 in their work.
Subsequently, they perform a conventional two-dimensional convolution on the flattened cube faces.
Extending this operation with a third, radial dimension, defines a convolution on
\mathbb{E}_{3}\backslash\{0\}
.
As the radial shells are in the discretized implementation again spaced equidistantly, this operation corresponds to a
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution on an
\{e\}
-structure that varies radially as shown in Fig.
52
.
The projection from the spherical shells to the cube implies a distortion of the frames on each of the cubes faces, and thus to a distortion of the metric on the spherical shells.
The
\{e\}
-structure is discontinuous at most of the cuts and does therefore not allow the convolution to preserve the continuity of feature fields.
Since
S^{2}
is not parallelizable, this issue can not be resolved without assuming a non-trivial structure group
G
.
The
\{e\}
-structure as a whole is not preserved by any isometries, implying that the model’s global equivariance group
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\{e\}
is trivial.
However, as the restriction of the
\{e\}
-structure to the four “vertical” faces of the cube is invariant under rotations by multiples of
\pi/2
, the model is in practice partially equivariant w.r.t. global
\operatorname{C}_{4}
-rotations around the vertical axis.
For datasets whose samples are centered around the origin
\{0\}
and are rotationally symmetric in distribution, this property is empirically shown to lead to an improved performance in comparison to conventional convolutions on
\mathbb{E}_{3}
.
The authors are furthermore investigating the effect of different weight sharing schemes over the radial dimension, finding that full weight sharing works best in practice.

11
Spherical coordinate independent CNNs

Figure 54:
Visualization of the 2-sphere’s isometry group
\Isom(S^{2})=\operatorname{O}(3)
and its various subgroups.
The isometry group can be thought of as being composed of the orientation preserving rotations in
\Isom_{+}(S^{2})=\operatorname{SO}(3)
and reflections
{R}
via the direct product
\operatorname{O}(3)=\operatorname{SO}(3)\times{R}
.

\operatorname{SO}(3)
, in turn, is generated by
\operatorname{SO}(2)
rotations around any two non-parallel axes, which is used in the Euler angle parametrization.
See the main text for more relevant subgroups and their relations.

Beyond convolutions on Euclidean spaces, convolutions on the 2-sphere
S^{2}
are of great practical relevance.
Applications include omnidirectional vision tasks, global weather forecasting, or the analysis of the cosmic microwave background.
Instead of being translation equivariant, spherical convolutions are typically required to be rotation equivariant.
The isometry group
\Isom(S^{2})=\operatorname{O}(3)
of the sphere and its decomposition in the most relevant subgroups is visualized in Fig.
54
.

A major difference between Euclidean spaces
\mathbb{E}_{d}
and the sphere
S^{2}
is that the latter is not parallelizable, i.e. does not allow for a global, continuous frame field.
Reductions of the structure group beyond
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
are topologically obstructed, which means that spherical convolutions require at least
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernels if they should preserve the continuity of feature fields.
The corresponding
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure, which is fully determined by the sphere’s metric and orientation, is shown in Fig.
55(a)
.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on this globally rotation invariant
G
-structure are guaranteed to be
\Isom_{\mkern 1.0mu\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant.

Despite the unavoidable topological obstruction, many authors proposed spherical CNNs that do not apply
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernels.
The most prevalent choice of
\{e\}
-structure corresponding to such convolutions is the frame field shown in Fig.
55(b)
, whose orthonormal reference frames (Eq. (
428
)) are aligned with the coordinate grid of spherical coordinates.
Note that this frame field comes with singularities at the poles, where the convolutions becomes discontinuous.
To reconcile such models with our theory, in particular the smoothness assumption of the
G
-structures, they need to be described as convolutions on a topological cylinder with sphere-like metric.
The isometry group of this punctured sphere
S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}
without poles
n,s\in S^{2}
is the subgroup
\operatorname{O}(2)
(Fig.
54
(middle and right)) of the sphere’s full isometry group
\operatorname{O}(3)
.
The visualized
\{e\}
-structure is preserved by azimuthal rotations in
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\operatorname{SO}(2)
, i.e. rotations around the axis through the poles.

From an engineering perspective, both approaches have their justification:
fully isotropic applications like the analysis of the cosmic microwave background require fully
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant models on
S^{2}
.
Learning tasks that come with a preferred rotation axis, which is for instance the case for the earth or panoramic images with a distinguished “up” and “down” direction, might benefit from the additional geometric information encoded in the
\{e\}
-structure.
Empirical results suggest that it is in such cases often useful to work with a combination of both approaches:
initial layers with fully equivariant convolutions can exploit local symmetries in the data, while subsequent layers with only azimuthal equivariance can learn to discriminate based on the preferred axis; see Section 2.7 in
[
235
]
.

We start by describing the sphere’s geometry in Section
11.1
.
Section
11.2
discusses fully
\operatorname{SO}(3)
and
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant spherical
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, which rely on
\operatorname{SO}(2)
or
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structures as shown in Fig.
55(a)
.
Globally
\operatorname{SO}(2)
and
\operatorname{O}(2)
-equivariant spherical CNNs, corresponding to the
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
55(b)
or the corresponding
{R}
-structure, respectively, are reviewed in Section
11.3
.
Section
11.4
focuses on icosahedral approximations of spherical convolutions, which allow for compute-efficient implementations since the icosahedron is piecewise flat and admits regular sampling grids; see Fig.
59
.
The
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure and
\{e\}
-structure in Figs.
55(a)
and
55(b)
are hereby approximated by the
\operatorname{C}_{6}
-structure and the
\{e\}
-structures in Figs.
60(c)
and
60(a)
or
60(b)
, respectively.

(a)
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure
\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM
on the 2-sphere
M=S^{2}
, preserved by general three-dimensional rotations in
\Isom_{\mkern 1.0mu\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
.

(b)
\{e\}
-structure
\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.5mue\mkern-0.9mu\raisebox{0.4pt}{\scalebox{.8}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM
on a punctured 2-sphere
M=S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}
, preserved by azimuthal rotations in
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\operatorname{SO}(2)
.

Figure 55:
Common
G
-structures underlying spherical CNNs.
Topological obstructions prevent a reduction of the 2-sphere’s structure group beyond
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
Fig.
55(a)
shows the standard
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure on
S^{2}
, which is in agreement with the embedding metric (Eq. (
431
)) induced from the inner product of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
It is invariant under rotations in
\Isom_{\mkern 1.0mu\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
, implying the rotation equivariance of the corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution.
Note that the fibers
G_{\mkern-1.3mup}\mkern-1.2muM
and
G_{\mkern-1.3muq}\mkern-1.3muM
at different points
p
and
q
are isomorphic but not canonically so – frame colors in the visualization seem to suggest such an isomorphism, however, they are randomly chosen and carry no meaning.
Fig.
55(b)
shows a sphere that is punctured at two antipodal poles.
This turns the sphere into a topological cylinder
S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}\cong S^{1}\times(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})
with sphere like metric – which allows for a complete reduction to a trivial structure group.
The figure shows the most prominent choice of
\{e\}
-structure, which corresponds to orthonormal frames that are aligned with the coordinate grid of spherical coordinates; cf. Fig.
57
.
As this
\{e\}
-structure is invariant under azimuthal rotations around the polar axis, the corresponding
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are
\Isom_{\scalebox{.85}{$\raisebox{0.2pt}{$\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\{$}}\mkern-1.3mue\mkern-1.1mu\raisebox{0.5pt}{\scalebox{.75}{$\}$}}$}\mkern-2.0muM$}}=\operatorname{SO}(2)
-equivariant.
Note that the puncturing of the sphere is just a means of hiding the models’ discontinuity at the poles.

11.1
Geometry of the 2-sphere
\bm{S^{2}}

As a basis for our discussion of spherical CNNs, this section discusses the differential geometry of the (unit) sphere
M=S^{2}
.
It is usually defined as the subset

\displaystyle S^{2}\,:=\,\big\{p\in\mathbb{E}_{3}\,\big|\,\lVert p\rVert=1\big\}

(423)

of those points in Euclidean 3-space
\mathbb{E}_{3}
that have unit distance from the origin.
As an embedded surface, it inherits a Riemannian metric (first fundamental form) from the embedding space
\mathbb{E}_{3}
.
In the following, we will for simplicity model
\mathbb{E}_{3}
by the vector space
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
When interpreting the tangent spaces
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
literally as those two-dimensional subspaces of
\mathbb{R}^{3}

that contain all tangent vectors at
p\in S^{2}
, then the metric, exponential maps, parallel transporters, frames and gauges can all be expressed in terms of usual vector space operations in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Before coming to these concrete expressions, which come handy when implementing spherical CNNs,
we discuss some properties of the sphere from a more abstract angle.

The isometry group of the sphere is given by

\displaystyle\Isom(S^{2})=\operatorname{O}(3)\,,

(424)

i.e. three-dimensional rotations and reflections, which are visualized in Fig.
54
.
The action of any isometry
\phi\in\operatorname{O}(3)
coincides with its usual action on
\mathbb{R}^{3}
via matrix multiplication, restricted to the embedded sphere
S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Note that this yields indeed a well defined action on
S^{2}
since
\operatorname{O}(3)
consists by definition of all distance and angle preserving linear maps, and thus preserves the sphere.
As the sphere is orientable, it comes with a subgroup of orientation preserving isometries

\displaystyle\Isom_{+}(S^{2})=\operatorname{SO}(3)\,,

(425)

consisting of all three-dimensional rotations.
Further subgroups that are relevant in the deep learning context are the following:
any choice of rotation axis determines a subgroup of two-dimensional rotations, isomorphic to
\operatorname{SO}(2)
, and all of these subgroups are conjugated to each other.
Similarly, any choice of two-dimensional subspace of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
corresponds to a subgroup of reflections over this plane, which is isomorphic to
{R}
.
The subgroups of two-dimensional rotations around two non-parallel rotation axes generate
\operatorname{SO}(3)
, which relates to the Euler angle parametrization of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.
A choice of reflection plane and any rotation axis within this plane generates the semidirect product subgroup
\operatorname{O}(2)=\operatorname{SO}(2)\rtimes{R}
.
If the rotation axis is instead chosen to be orthogonal to the reflection plane, the two-dimensional rotations and reflections commute, and generate therefore subgroups isomorphic to the direct product
\operatorname{SO}(2)\times{R}
.

\operatorname{O}(3)
has furthermore discrete subgroups, the most practically relevant of which are the symmetry groups of the platonic solids, for instance of the icosahedron, shown in Fig.
59
.
113
113

113

An exhaustive list of all finite subgroups of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
can be found at
nLab
.

\operatorname{O}(3)
acts transitively on the sphere, that is, for any two points
p
and
q
of
S^{2}
, there exists at least one isometry
\phi\in\operatorname{O}(3)
such that
q=\phi(p)
.
The actions of
\operatorname{O}(3)
on
S^{2}
are not fixed point free:
any point
p\in S^{2}
is stabilized by the subgroup
\operatorname{Stab}_{p}\cong\operatorname{O}(2)<\operatorname{O}(3)
, consisting of rotations and reflections around the axis spanned by
p
in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Together, these two properties imply that the sphere is a homogeneous space of
\operatorname{O}(3)
and is algebraically realized as the quotient space

\displaystyle\operatorname{O}(3)/\operatorname{O}(2)\,\cong\,S^{2}\,,

(426)

which consists of cosets of the form
{\phi\mkern 1.0mu.\mkern-4.0mu\operatorname{O}(2)}
.
A similar statement holds for
\operatorname{SO}(3)
, which has stabilizer subgroups
\operatorname{Stab}_{p}\cong\operatorname{SO}(2)<\operatorname{SO}(3)
and thus

\displaystyle\operatorname{SO}(3)/\operatorname{SO}(2)\,\cong\,S^{2}\,.

(427)

With these relations, Theorem
8.14
proves that any
\operatorname{O}(3)
or
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant kernel field transform on
S^{2}
is equivalent to a
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution with
G
being
\operatorname{O}(2)
or
\operatorname{SO}(2)
, respectively.
This result is in line with the classical viewpoint of group equivariant CNNs on homogeneous spaces
[
37
]
– the precise relation between the two is clarified in Theorem
11.2
below.
Recall that isometries preserve the Riemannian metric by definition.
That
\operatorname{O}(3)
acts transitively on
S^{2}
with stabilizer
\operatorname{O}(2)
implies therefore that the Riemannian geometry of
S^{2}
“looks similar” at each point and in each direction and orientation –
S^{2}
is a maximally symmetric space.

As a Riemannian manifold,
S^{2}
comes by design with an
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structure.
A restriction to right-handed frames, which is possible since the sphere is orientable, yields the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure in Fig.
55(a)
, which is preserved by rotations in
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.
One can show that these two
G
-structures
\operatorname{O}\mkern-3.6muM
and
\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM
are as principal bundles isomorphic to
\operatorname{O}(3)
and
\operatorname{SO}(3)
, respectively.
The specific isomorphism is hereby given by a choice of frame from the
G
-structure, that is to be identified with the identity group element.

The hairy ball theorem states that no continuous vector field exists on
S^{2}
, which implies in particular that no (continuous)
\{e\}
-structure can exist.
A reduction of the structure group beyond
\operatorname{SO}(2)
requires therefore a change in the topology of the manifold.
For example, puncturing the sphere at an arbitrary point
p\in S
yields a surface that is homeomorphic to the Euclidean plane, and is therefore parallelizable.
114
114

114

This process corresponds for instance to the stereographic projection of the sphere.

Puncturing the sphere at two arbitrarily chosen antipodal points, as shown in Fig.
55(b)
, turns the topology of the sphere into that of a cylinder and thus allows for
\{e\}
-structures.
The most common choice of
\{e\}
-structure on the punctured sphere
S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}
is the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-invariant
\{e\}
-structure in Figs.
55(b)
and
57
.
Its frames

\displaystyle\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta},\;\frac{1}{\cos(\theta)}\frac{\partial}{\partial\varphi}\right]

(428)

are aligned with the usual spherical coordinates, which are in physics conventions
(i.e. with
\varphi
and
\theta
denoting the azimuthal angle and inclination against the
xy
-plane, respectively)
given by the following surjective,
2\pi
-periodic map:

\displaystyle\chi:\,\big({\textstyle\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}}\big)\times\mathbb{R}\>\to\>S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}\,,\quad(\theta,\varphi)\,\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta)\cos{\varphi}\\
\cos(\theta)\sin{\varphi}\\
\sin(\theta)\end{pmatrix}

(429)

Some
\{e\}
-steerable CNNs are implemented by representing feature fields on
S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}
in spherical coordinates; see Section
11.3
below.
As the coordinate map
\chi
is
\emph{not}
isometric, these methods require an alternative metric (or
\{e\}
-structure) on the coordinates
{(\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\pi/2,\;\pi/2)\times\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}}
; see the stretched frames in Fig.
57
(right).

Since
S^{2}
is compact, it is geodesically complete.
The geodesics are given by the great circles of the sphere, i.e. those circles that correspond to the intersection of the sphere with a plane through the origin of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
The exponential maps
\exp_{p}(v)
follow these great circles through
p
in direction of
v
for a distance of
\lVert v\rVert
.
Logarithmic maps
\log_{p}(q)
are therefore for all points
q\in S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mup
, which are not antipodal to
p
, given by the unique vector in the shorter direction along the great circle through
p
and
q
, with
\lVert\log_{p}(q)\rVert
given by the arc-length along this path.
Geodesics between antipodal points
p
and
-p
are not unique, such that the logarithmic map does not exist.

Explicit geometry of
\bm{S^{2}}
as embedded surface in
\bm{\mathds{R}^{3}}

As stated above, the tangent spaces of
S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
are in the classical differential geometry of surfaces defined as two-dimensional subspaces of the embedding space
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
A specific tangent space
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
at
p\in S^{2}
is in this interpretation given by

\displaystyle T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\,=\,\big\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\,\big|\,\langle p,v\rangle=0\big\}\ \subset\ \mathbb{R}^{3}\,,

(430)

i.e. the space of all vectors that are orthogonal to the surface normal at
p
, which coincides for the sphere with
p
itself.
Note that, despite being expressed relative to the standard frame of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
, these tangent vectors are coordinate free object in the sense that they are not described by 2-tuples of coefficients
v^{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}
relative to some gauge
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}
of
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
The identification of tangent spaces with subspaces of the embedding space allows to express many of the abstract algebraic relations in terms of vector space operations on
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
In the remainder of this section we will state such expressions for the metric, exponential and logarithmic maps, frames, gauges, Levi-Civita transporters along geodesics and induced gauge transformations.

By definition,
S^{2}
inherits its Riemannian metric from the embedding space.
This induced metric is for any
v,w\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
given by

\displaystyle\eta_{p}(v,w)\,:=\,\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\,,

(431)

i.e. the standard inner product of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
, restricted to
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
To reduce clutter, we drop the subscript
\mathbb{R}^{3}
in the notation
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}
in the remainder of this section.

The exponential map
\exp_{p}
maps vectors
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
to points
q=\exp_{p}(v)\in S^{2}
at a distance of
\lVert v\rVert
along the great circle in direction of
v
.
Lying on the same great circle,
p
and
q
relate via a rotation by an angle of
\alpha=\lVert v\rVert/r=\lVert v\rVert
around the rotation axis
a=\frac{p\times v}{\lVert p\times v\rVert}=\frac{p\times v}{\lVert v\rVert}
,
where the equations simplify since the sphere has unit radius
r=\lVert p\rVert=1
and the vectors
p
and
v
are orthogonal in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Using Rodrigues’ rotation formula,
q=p\cos(\alpha)+(a\times p)\sin(\alpha)+a\langle a,p\rangle\big(1-\cos(\alpha)\big)
,
together with the orthogonality
\langle a,p\rangle=0
and

a\times p=\frac{1}{\lVert v\rVert}(p\times v)\times p=\frac{1}{\lVert v\rVert}\big(\langle p,p\rangle v+\langle p,v\rangle p\big)=\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}
,
this leads to the explicit expression

\displaystyle\exp_{p}:\,\mathbb{R}^{3}\supset T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3},\quad v\mapsto\exp_{p}(v)=p\mkern 1.0mu\cos\big(\lVert v\rVert\big)+\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}\sin\big(\lVert v\rVert\big)

(432)

for the exponential map.

An explicit expression of the logarithmic map is found along the same line of reasoning:
the norm of
\log_{p}(q)
, where
q\in{S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mup}
, coincides with the rotation angle
\alpha=\arccos\!\big(\langle p,q\rangle\big)
.
Its direction is given by the direction tangent to the great circle, which may be expressed in terms of the normalized projection

\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}=\frac{q-\langle p,q\rangle p}{\lVert q-\langle p,q\rangle p\rVert}

of
q
on
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
Overall, the logarithmic map is therefore instantiated as

\displaystyle\log_{p}:\,S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mup\to B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,\pi),\quad q\mapsto\log_{p}(q)=\arccos\!\big(\mkern-1.0mu\langle p,q\rangle\mkern-1.0mu\big)\,\frac{q-\langle p,q\rangle p}{\lVert q-\langle p,q\rangle p\rVert}\,,

(433)

where
B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,\pi)\subset T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
denotes the open ball of injectivity-radius
\pi
around the origin of
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.

Reference frames on
S^{2}
are by definition just
2
-tuples of linearly independent tangent vectors.
When expressing the axes of a reference frame explicitly as vectors in the embedding space
\mathbb{R}^{3}
, this frame can be identified with the
3\times 2
rank
2
matrix

\displaystyle\big[e_{1}^{A},\,e_{2}^{A}\big]\ =\ \left[\!\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{A}_{1,1}&e^{A}_{2,1}\\
e^{A}_{1,2}&e^{A}_{2,2}\\
e^{A}_{1,3}&e^{A}_{2,3}\end{array}\!\right]\;=:E^{A}_{p}\ \ \in\,\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2}.

It defines the vector space isomorphism

\displaystyle E^{A}_{p}=\big[e_{1}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\big]:\,\mathbb{R}^{2}\to T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM,\ \ \ v^{A}\mapsto E^{A}_{p}v^{A}=v^{A}_{1}e^{A}_{1}+v^{A}_{2}e^{A}_{2}

(437)

from vector coefficients to coordinate free tangent vectors.
The tangent spaces
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
are therefore exactly the image of
E^{A}_{p}
.

The corresponding gauges
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to\mathbb{R}^{2}
are technically just the inverses of the frames, when being interpreted as maps
E^{A}_{p}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.
In contrast, when being interpreted as
3\times 2
matrices that map
\mathbb{R}^{2}
non-surjectively to
\mathbb{R}^{3}
,
E^{A}_{p}
is non-invertible but only admits a pseudo-inverse

\displaystyle\big(E^{A}_{p}\big)^{+}\,:=\,\big((E^{A}_{p})^{\top}E^{A}_{p}\big)^{-1}(E^{A}_{p})^{\top}\ \in\,\mathbb{R}^{2\times 3}.

(438)

Geometrically, this matrix acts by
1) projecting vectors in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
to the image of
E_{p}^{A}
, which is just
E_{p}^{A}(\mathbb{R}^{2})=T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
, and
2) applying the inverse of the isomorphism
E_{p}^{A}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
on this subspace.
This means that the pseudo-inverse is indeed the inverse of
E_{p}^{A}
on the tangent space, implying that the gauge map is given by

\displaystyle\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to\mathbb{R}^{2},\ \ v\mapsto\big(E_{p}^{A}\big)^{+}v\,.

(439)

Written out, the gauge map acts according to

\displaystyle\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}(v)\ =

\displaystyle\ \Bigg(\mkern-9.0mu\begin{array}[]{cc}\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle&\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle\\[4.0pt]
\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle&\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle\end{array}\mkern-9.0mu\Bigg)^{\!-1}\Bigg(\mkern-9.0mu\begin{array}[]{cc}\langle e_{1}^{A},v\rangle\\[4.0pt]
\langle e_{2}^{A},v\rangle\end{array}\mkern-9.0mu\Bigg)

\displaystyle\ =

\displaystyle\ \frac{1}{\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle-\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle}\Bigg(\mkern-9.0mu\begin{array}[]{cc}\phantom{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle&\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\rangle\\[4.0pt]
\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\langle e_{2}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle&\phantom{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}\langle e_{1}^{A},e_{1}^{A}\rangle\end{array}\mkern-9.0mu\Bigg)\Bigg(\mkern-9.0mu\begin{array}[]{cc}\langle e_{1}^{A},v\rangle\\[4.0pt]
\langle e_{2}^{A},v\rangle\end{array}\mkern-9.0mu\Bigg)\,.

Note that, in general,
\langle e_{i}^{A},v\rangle\neq v^{A}_{i}
.
However, if (and only if)
E^{A}_{p}
is an orthonormal frame, i.e. for
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)
, the gauge map is simply given by the projection of the tangent vector on the frame axes:

\displaystyle\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}(v)\ =\ \big(E^{A}_{p}\big)^{\!\top}v\ =\ \Bigg(\mkern-9.0mu\begin{array}[]{cc}\langle e_{1}^{A},v\rangle\\[4.0pt]
\langle e_{2}^{A},v\rangle\end{array}\mkern-9.0mu\Bigg)\qquad\textup{for \emph{orthonormal} frames, i.e.}\ \langle e_{i}^{A},e_{j}^{A}\rangle=\delta_{ij}

The explicit expression for the coordinate free Levi-Civita transporters
along geodesics
is similar to that of the exponential map, with the difference that Rodrigues’ rotation formula is not applied to rotate the source to the target point but tangent vectors between source and target.
Let
\gamma
be the shortest geodesic between
p\in S^{2}
and
q\in{S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mup}
.
The rotation from
p
to
q
along this geodesic is then given by the axis
a=p\times q
and angle
\alpha=\arccos\!\big(\langle p,q\rangle\big)
.
In terms of these quantities, the Levi-Civita transport of an embedded tangent vector
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
along the geodesic
\gamma
is given by the rotated vector

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mkern-2.0mu\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\!T\!M$}\mkern-2.0mu,\gamma}}(v)\ =\ v\cos(\alpha)+(a\times v)\sin(\alpha)+\big(a\langle a,v\rangle\big)\big(1-\cos(\alpha)\big)

(450)

in
T_{\mkern-1.5muq}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Relative to gauges
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}
and
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$q$}}^{\widetilde{A}}
at the start point
q
and end point
q
of the geodesic, this transporter is expressed by the group element

\displaystyle g_{\gamma}^{A\widetilde{A}}\ =\ \psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\circ\mathcal{P}_{\mkern-2.0mu\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\!T\!M$}\mkern-2.0mu,\gamma}}\circ\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$q$}}^{\widetilde{A}}\big)^{-1}\ =\ \big(E_{p}^{A}\big)^{+}\circ\mathcal{P}_{\mkern-2.0mu\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\!T\!M$}\mkern-2.0mu,\gamma}}\circ E_{q}^{\widetilde{A}}\,.

(451)

Isometry induced gauge transformations are relative to the explicit reference frames similarly given by the following matrix multiplication:

\displaystyle g_{\phi}^{A\widetilde{A}}(p)\ =\ \psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$\phi(p)$}}^{A}\circ\phi\circ\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{\widetilde{A}}\big)^{-1}\ =\ \big(E_{\phi(p)}^{A}\big)^{\!+}\phi\>E_{p}^{\widetilde{A}}

(452)

11.2
Fully rotation equivariant spherical CNNs

This section discusses the fully
\operatorname{SO}(3)
or
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant spherical convolutions that are listed in rows (31-33) of Table
.
They can all be understood as specific instances of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions on either the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure in Fig.
55(a)
or the corresponding
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structure, which is additionally closed under frame reflections.

Instead of organizing this discussion in terms of the considered structure groups and group representations, we assort the models by the theoretical frameworks in which they are developed:

Kicanaoglu et al. 2019
define a pixel grid on the sphere and formulate the convolution directly as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution, that is, in terms of gauges, steerable kernels and feature vector transporters.
An alternative framework is that of graph convolutions on spherical pixel meshes
[
169
,
245
]
.
Such graph convolutions correspond to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions with isotropic kernels.
They map therefore between (directionally insensitive) scalar fields.
Lastly, we come to implementations that consider (steerable) convolution kernels on
S^{2}
instead of our kernels on the tangent spaces
[
61
,
35
,
122
,
64
]
.
Theorem
11.1
proves that such spherical steerable kernels can be identified with
G
-steerable kernels on the tangent spaces, when being expressed in geodesic normal coordinates.
Based on this result, we prove in Theorem
11.2
that convolutions with spherical kernels are equivalent to our
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
For completeness, we need to mention that such models are typically implemented in the spectral domain.
We do not focus on this viewpoint but refer the interested reader to the review by
Esteves 2020
.

Spherical
GM
-convolutions:

We start with the spherical CNN by
Kicanaoglu et al. 2019
since its formulation agrees precisely with our more general theory when being applied to the spherical geometry.
The authors assume the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure from Fig.
55(a)
, and therefore
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable feature fields and convolution kernels.
Feature fields are discretized in terms of feature vectors that are assigned to a sampling grid on the sphere.
While the method is in principle independent from the particular sampling scheme, the authors propose to discretize the spherical geometry by an icosphere mesh.
This mesh is constructed by taking an embedded icosahedron, repeatedly subdividing its faces as shown in Fig.
59
, and finally projecting the grid vertices radially to the sphere, i.e. to unit norm.
The sampled feature fields are numerically represented by a set of coefficient vectors
f^{A}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{c}
at the grid vertices
p
, which are expressed relative to some arbitrarily chosen right-handed orthonormal frames
\big[e_{1}^{A},e_{2}^{A}\big]
at the vertices.
115
115

115

This corresponds to an independent choice of gauge
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A_{p}}
on any open neighborhood
U^{A_{p}}
of each vertex
p
.

In practice, the frames are represented by a single tangent vector of unit norm, from which the second frame vector follows uniquely since the frames are right-handed.

To compute the coordinate independent convolution
[K\star f](p)
from Eq. (
87
),
Kicanaoglu et al. 2019
need to contract the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernel
K
with the transporter pullback
[\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{A}
of the feature field
f
, Eq. (
4.2.1
).
As usual in deep learning,
K
is hereby assumed to be compactly supported, such that it covers only a few vertices in a one-ring or two-ring neighborhood
\mathcal{N}_{p}
around a center vertex
p
.
In the continuous theory, the transporter pullback takes features from all points
\exp_{p}(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A})^{-1}({v})
for
{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}
and transports them back to
p
.
In practice, the feature fields are only sampled at the grid vertices
q
, which correspond to the tangent vector coefficients
v^{A}_{pq}=\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$p$}}^{A}\log_{p}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}
relative to gauge
A
at vertex
p
.
116
116

116

If the exponential map is not restricted to the injectivity radius, each vertex
q
is represented by multiple tangent vectors.
This is in practice no issue since the kernel is assumed to be locally supported within the injectivity radius.

The logarithmic maps
\log_{p}(q)
are thereby computed as defined in Eq. (
433
).
The Levi-Civita transporters
\rho\big(g_{p\leftarrow q}^{A\widetilde{A}}\big)
along the geodesics from
q
to
p
are in principle given by Eq. (
451
).
Since the frames are all right-handed and orthonormal, and since the transport corresponds to the Levi-Civita connection on
S^{2}
, the group elements
g_{p\leftarrow q}^{A\widetilde{A}}
are
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-valued.
They are therefore fully determined by the angle between the transported first frame axis
\mathcal{P}_{\mkern-2.0mu\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{$\!T\!M$}\mkern-2.0mu,\gamma}}\big(e_{1}^{\widetilde{A}}\big)
from
q
and the first frame axis
e_{1}^{A}
at
p
.
With these ingredients at hand, the authors propose to approximate the continuous convolution integral by the discrete sum

\displaystyle\big[K\star f\big]^{A}(p)\ =\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}K({v})\,\big[\!\operatorname{Exp}^{*}_{p}\mkern-2.0muf]^{A}({v})\,\ d{v}\ \approx\ \sum_{q\in\mathcal{N}_{p}}K\mkern-1.5mu\big(v^{A}_{pq}\big)\,\rho\big(g^{A\widetilde{A}}_{p\leftarrow q}\big)\,f^{\widetilde{A}}(q)

(453)

over neighboring mesh nodes.
The missing normalization factor can be thought of as being absorbed in the learnable parameters
w_{i}\in\mathbb{R}
of the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable convolution kernel
K=\sum_{i}w_{i}K_{i}
.
As an alternative to this naive approximation, the authors propose an optimized quadrature integration scheme, which is empirically shown to improve the model’s
\operatorname{SO}(3)
isometry equivariance.

The model is in Table
listed as processing feature fields that transform according to the regular representation of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
In their implementation,
Kicanaoglu et al. 2019
consider irrep fields of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
in the convolutions.
A change of basis before and after the convolutions transforms these feature fields to regular feature fields, which are then acted on by pointwise nonlinearities like e.g. ReLU.
The infinite-dimensional regular representation of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
is hereby approximated by regular representations of discrete cyclic subgroups
\operatorname{C}_{\!N}
, whose irreps are just the irreps of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
up to a bandlimiting frequency of
\lfloor N/2\rfloor
; see e.g. Appendix F.2 of
[
234
]
.
The change of basis between the representations is in this specific case just the usual discrete Fourier transform.

Spherical graph convolutions:

The spherical CNNs by
Perraudin et al. 2018
and
Yang et al. 2020a
, which are listed in row (33) of Table
, are based on conventional graph convolutions
[
114
]
.
Pixel meshes on the sphere are hereby interpreted as graphs.
The graph convolutional networks process signals on the sphere by multiplying them with degree
\kappa
polynomials
\sum_{k=0}^{\kappa}w_{k}L^{k}
of the graph’s Laplacian matrix
L
, where
w_{k}\in\mathbb{R}
are trainable parameters.
Since the Laplacian matrix has non-zero entries only for adjacent nodes, the
k
-th order term affects only the
k
-hop neighborhood around each node.
On a regular mesh with unweighted graph edges, the contribution of a neighboring node
q
to the accumulated feature at
p
depends only on their graph distance (“radius”), but not on the particular neighbor (“direction”).
The graph convolution applies therefore in such cases
isotropic
kernels on the graph.
The considered pixel graph on the sphere satisfy these properties approximately.
As their
embedding
on the sphere is furthermore such, that the nodes are geodesically approximately equidistant, the topological isotropy of the graph convolution kernels corresponds to their metric isotropy on the sphere.

The isometry group
\operatorname{O}(3)
of the sphere induces
\operatorname{O}(2)
-valued gauge transformation, that is, it acts by moving patterns to a new location and in a new orientation.
Due to the convolutional weight sharing and the isotropy of the kernels, the graph convolutions are trivially isometry equivariant.
As already argued in Eq. (
422
), isotropic kernels are in our framework recovered as
\operatorname{O}(2)
-steerable kernels that map between
scalar fields
.
The
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariance of the convolution is in our theory explained by the
\operatorname{O}(3)
-invariance of the sphere’s
\operatorname{O}(2)
-structure.

Spherical convolutions with kernels on
\bm{S^{2}}
:

As a homogeneous space, the sphere admits group (or quotient space) convolutions
[
121
]
and more general steerable convolutions on homogeneous spaces
[
37
]
.
117
117

117

A more general review of convolutions on homogeneous spaces is found in Appendix
D
.

Instead of defining the convolution kernels on the tangent spaces or on graph neighborhoods, these approaches define kernels immediately as matrix-valued function on the sphere, that is, as

\displaystyle\kappa:\,S^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,.

(454)

Cohen et al. 2019a
showed that these kernels are required to satisfy a symmetry constraint in order to guarantee the equivariance of the convolution.
We argue in the following that such kernels on
S^{2}
are equivalent to
G
-steerable kernels on the tangent spaces (Theorem
11.1
), which implies that the spherical CNNs covered in
[
37
]
and
[
121
]
can be viewed as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions (Theorem
11.2
).
The identification between the two kinds of kernels is hereby made by pulling the spherical kernels via the exponential map back to the tangent spaces.
Before explaining this operation, we briefly discuss the models proposed in
[
35
,
61
,
64
,
122
]
as specific instances of spherical convolutions with spherical kernels.
For a more details on these models, specifically on their formulation in Fourier space, we refer the reader to the comprehensive review by
Esteves 2020
.

We start our discussion with the group convolutional spherical CNN by
Cohen et al. 2018a
, listed in row (32) of Table
.
This model processes stacks of
{c_{\textup{in}}}

scalar
fields

\displaystyle f:\,S^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}

(455)

on the sphere by matching them with spherical kernels, Eq. (
454
), in any
\operatorname{SO}(3)
transformed pose.
In equations, this operation is defined as

\displaystyle\big[\kappa\star_{\mkern-2.0muS^{2}}\!f\big](\phi)\

\displaystyle:=\,\int_{S^{2}}\kappa(\phi^{-1}(p))\,f(p)\ dp\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\phi\in\operatorname{SO}(3)\,.

(456)

Note that the resulting feature map is viewed as a stack of
{c_{\textup{out}}}
scalar functions on the symmetry group
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.
Such feature maps of the form
f:\operatorname{SO}(3)\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{in}}}}
(with the new number of input channels corresponding to the previous layer’s output channels) are processed further by group convolutions of the form

\displaystyle\big[\kappa\star_{\operatorname{SO}(3)}\!f\big](\phi)\

\displaystyle:=\,\int_{\operatorname{SO}(3)}\!\kappa(\phi^{-1}\omega)\,f(\omega)\ d\omega\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\phi\in\operatorname{SO}(3)\,,

(457)

where
\kappa:\operatorname{SO}(3)\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
is now a matrix-valued function on
\operatorname{SO}(3)
and
d\omega
is the Haar measure on
\operatorname{SO}(3)
.
From the viewpoint of steerable CNNs on homogeneous spaces
[
37
]
and
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, scalar functions on
\operatorname{SO}(3)
are viewed as feature fields on
S^{2}\cong\operatorname{SO}(3)/\operatorname{SO}(2)
, that transform according to the
regular representation
of the fibers (stabilizer subgroups)
\operatorname{SO}(2)
.
The initial convolution in Eq. (
456
) applies in this interpretation
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernels between scalar and regular fields, while the group convolution in Eq. (
457
) applies
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernels between regular fields on
S^{2}
.

Esteves et al. 2018a
apply spherical convolutions as in Eq. (
456
) with the additional assumption that the kernels are
zonal
, that is, invariant under
\operatorname{SO}(2)
rotations around the polar axis; cf. Fig.
53
.
While the integral technically still gives responses in
\operatorname{SO}(3)
, the kernel symmetry implies that these responses are constant on the fibers
\operatorname{SO}(2)
of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
, when being interpreted as bundle over
S^{2}
.
The resulting feature fields are therefore identified as scalar fields on
S^{2}
, which allows for a repeated application of this type of convolution.
Note that the zonal symmetry of the kernel is consistent with the steerability kernel constraint between scalar fields (trivial representations) that we encountered before in Eq. (
421
).
As already discussed in the previous Section
10
, this constraint is equivalent to the
\operatorname{O}(2)
-steerability constraint between scalar fields in Eq. (
422
), which implies that the model of
Esteves et al. 2018a
is actually
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant.
It is in spirit similar to the spherical graph convolutions discussed above, but is derived from a different viewpoint and is discretized differently in the implementation.

Esteves et al. 2020
generalize this model from scalar fields to general
spin weighted spherical functions
.
These functions depend not only on the position
p\in S^{2}
on the sphere, but in addition on the particular choice of right-handed, orthonormal reference frame at that point.
They are associated to the
irreps

\rho_{s}
of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
, where the integer
s\in\mathbb{Z}
is denoted as the functions’ spin weight.
118
118

118

One can generalize this concept to spin representations, labeled by half-integer spin weights.

Their values for the different frames
\operatorname{SO}_{\mkern-1.1mup}\mkern-3.2muM
of the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-structure
\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM
are constrained such that gauge transformations of the frame by
g\in\operatorname{SO}(2)
lead to a transformation of the function value by
\rho_{s}(g)
.
In equations, they are therefore defined by
119
119

119

A real-valued implementation would instead consider spin weighted functions of the form
\prescript{}{s}{f}:\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM\to\mathbb{R}^{\dim(\rho_{s})}
, where
\rho_{s}
are the irreps of
\operatorname{SO}(2)
over the real numbers.

\displaystyle\prescript{}{s}{f}:\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM\to\mathbb{C}\ \ \ \textup{such that}\ \ \ \prescript{}{s}{f}\big([e_{1},e_{2}]\lhd g\big)=\rho_{s}(g)\prescript{}{s}{f}\big([e_{1},e_{2}]\big)\ \ \ \forall\ [e_{1},e_{2}]\in\operatorname{SO}_{\mkern-1.1mup}\mkern-3.2muM,\ g\in\operatorname{SO}(2)\,;\!

(458)

see
[
16
]
for more details and alternative definitions.
Note the similarity of this symmetry constraint to the equivalence relation

\displaystyle\big[[e_{i}]_{i=1}^{2}\lhd g,\,{f}\big]\ \sim_{\rho_{s}}\ \big[[e_{i}]_{i=1}^{2},\,\rho_{s}(g){f}\big]

(459)

from Eq. (
172
), which is underlying the definition of associated bundles.
Spin weighted spherical functions are indeed equivalent to sections of the associated bundles

(\operatorname{SO}\mkern-3.6muM\times\mathbb{C})/\!\sim_{\rho_{s}}
;
see for instance Proposition 1.6.3 in
[
237
]
.
They appear in our theory simply as
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-irrep fields, including scalar fields for
s=0
and vector fields for
s=1
.
The neural networks proposed by
Esteves et al. 2020
convolve spin weighted features with spin weighted kernels on the sphere.
This operation corresponds to a convolution with
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable kernels where
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}
and
\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}
are irreps.

The models in
[
35
,
61
,
64
]
are initially formulated in the spatial domain, i.e. as processing functions on
S^{2}
as discussed above.
They are, however, implemented in the spectral domain, which is possible thanks to generalized convolution theorems on
S^{2}
and on
\operatorname{SO}(3)

[
141
,
121
,
116
]
.

Kondor et al. 2018
generalize these approaches, proposing a model that is based on learned linear combinations of all feature fields’ Fourier modes of the same frequency.
The authors argue that this approach covers the full space of
\operatorname{SO}(3)
-equivariant linear maps between feature fields on the sphere.
On the other hand,
Cohen et al. 2019a
show that any such map can in the spatial domain be written as a convolution with
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-steerable spherical kernels.
A notable property of the model proposed by
Kondor et al. 2018
is that it operates fully in Fourier space:
instead of transforming back to the spatial domain and applying pointwise nonlinearities like ReLUs there, as done in the previous approaches, the authors compute the tensor product between all feature fields and decompose them subsequently via the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition back into irreducible features (Fourier modes).
This is computationally beneficial, however, comes at the expense of losing the locality of the nonlinearities.
Certain learning tasks, especially in the natural sciences, might benefit from such nonlinearities since physical interactions are often described by tensor products.

As argued in
[
37
,
36
]
, all of these models can be viewed as applying steerable kernels on
S^{2}
that map between scalar fields
[
61
]
, regular feature fields
[
35
]
or irrep fields
[
64
,
122
]
.
In the remainder of this section and Appendix
F
we show that they can as well be viewed as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions.
The claim that spherical convolutions with steerable kernels on
S^{2}
are equivalent to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions is thereby made precise in Theorem
11.2
.
This theorem relies crucially on Theorem
11.1
, which establishes an isomorphism between the spherical steerable kernels and
G
-steerable kernels on the tangent spaces.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be any transitive isometry group of the sphere, i.e.
\mathcal{I}=\operatorname{O}(3)
or
\mathcal{I}=\operatorname{SO}(3)
.

Cohen et al. 2019a
describe
\mathcal{I}
-equivariant spherical convolutions in terms of
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
-steerable spherical kernels
{\kappa:S^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}}
, where
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}<\mathcal{I}
is the stabilizer subgroup of any point
n\in S^{2}
, e.g. the north pole.
As these kernels are defined on the sphere, which is topologically distinct from
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, it is not directly possible to define an isomorphism between them and
G
-steerable kernels.
However, as the south pole
-n
is a set of measure zero, we can replace the integration domain
S^{2}
of the spherical convolutions with
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
without changing the result.
With this adaptation, the spherical steerable kernels of
Cohen et al. 2019a
are defined as

\displaystyle{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}:=\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\{$}}}}}\kappa:S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\displaystyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\textstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}{\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\resizebox{291272}{786432}{\hbox{\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big|$}}}}}\ \kappa\big(\xi(p)\big)=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}\big(g_{\xi}^{NN}(n)\big)\mkern-1.5mu\cdot\mkern-1.5mu\kappa(p)\mkern-1.5mu\cdot\mkern-1.5mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{\xi}^{XP}(p)\big)^{-1}\qquad

(460)

\displaystyle\forall\,\ p\in S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun,\ \ \xi\in\operatorname{Stab}_{n}\mathchoice{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\displaystyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\textstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{\resizebox{360448}{655360}{\hbox{\raisebox{2.5pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\Big\}$}}}}}\,,

when being translated to our notation.
Since the kernels are globally defined on the sphere, their values in
\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}
are expressed relative to potentially different gauges
N
at
n
, where the kernel is centered,
P
at
p\in S^{2}
, where the kernel contracts a feature
f^{P}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{\textup{in}}}
and
X
at
\xi(p)
, where this feature moves under the action of
\xi\in\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
.
This kernel constraint relates all kernel values that lie on the orbits
{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}\mkern-4.0mu.\mkern 1.0mup}=\{\xi(p)\,|\,\xi\in\operatorname{Stab}_{n}\}
via their isometry induced gauge transformations
g_{\xi}^{XP}(p)
and
g_{\xi}^{NN}(n)
; see Eqs. (
301
) and (
304
).
120
120

120

Cohen et al. 2019a
denote the isometry induced gauge transformations by
\operatorname{h}(p,\xi)
instead of

, assuming that the gauges

at
\xi(p)
and

at

Their definition of

is similar to our Eq. (

Our equivalent
G
-steerable kernels, where
G\cong\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
, is given by

\displaystyle{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}:=\Big\{K\!:B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)\to\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}}\mkern 1.5mu\Big|\,K(g\mkern 1.0mu{v})=\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}(g)\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\mkern-2.0muK({v})\mkern-2.0mu\cdot\mkern-2.0mu\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}(g)^{-1}\ \ \ \forall\ {v}\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi),\,\ g\in G\Big\}.

(461)

The kernel domain is hereby restricted from
\mathbb{R}^{2}
to the open ball
B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi):=\{{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,|\,\lVert{v}\rVert<\pi\}
of radius
\pi
around the origin of
\mathbb{R}^{2}
– which can via the exponential map be identified with
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
.
Note that
{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
is well defined since
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}\cong G
contains isometries, implying
G=\operatorname{O}(2)
or
G=\operatorname{SO}(2)
, under whose action
B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)
is closed.
We furthermore dropped the determinant factor from the more general
G
-steerability constraint in Eq. (
86
) since
{|\!\det g|=1}
for
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)
.
Our kernel constraint is considerably simpler than that of
Cohen et al. 2019a
since it describes the kernel locally relative to a single gauge, instead of globally relative to an atlas of gauges.
Note further that we dropped the smoothness assumption on the kernels, since the smoothness or continuity of feature fields is not discussed by
Cohen et al. 2019a
.
This property could easily be added by demanding that the
G
-steerable kernels converge to the same value for
\lVert{v}\rVert
going to
\pi
, corresponding via the exponential map to the south pole.

The spaces of
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
-steerable kernels on
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
and
G
-steerable kernels on

are isomorphic, that is, their kernels are identified by an invertible map
\Omega
that respects the kernel constraints:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{-1}}

(462)

This isomorphism (or rather its inverse
\Omega^{-1}
) can be viewed as the analog of the
transporter pullback
of feature fields:
it pulls the kernel values from points
\exp_{n}\!\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\big)^{\!-1}{v}
in
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
back to
geodesic normal coordinates

{v}\in B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)
.
To express the kernel values from all points
p\in S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
relative to the same gauge, it applies Levi-Civita transporters
\rho\big(g_{n\leftarrow p}^{NP}\big)
from
p
along the geodesics to the north pole
n
.
In addition, it rescales the kernel values by the Riemannian volume element

\sqrt{\big|\eta_{p}^{\partial\mkern-2.0mu/\mkern-2.0mu\partial{v}}\big|}:={\sqrt{\big|\!\det\!\big(\eta_{p}\big(\frac{\partial}{\partial{v}_{i}}\mkern-2.0mu\big|_{p},\frac{\partial}{\partial{v}_{j}}\mkern-2.0mu\big|_{p}\big)_{ij}\big)\big|}}

relative to the geodesic normal coordinate system (coordinate chart)

{v}:S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun\to B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi),\ \ p\mapsto{v}(p):=\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\log_{n}p
.
121
121

121

Note that the coordinate bases

\big[\frac{\partial}{\partial{v}_{1}}\mkern-2.0mu|_{p},\,\frac{\partial}{\partial{v}_{2}}\mkern-2.0mu|_{p}\big]

that are induced by the geodesic normal coordinates

{v}:S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun\to B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)

are for
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)

not
contained in
G\mkern-1.4muM
.
These bases play no role for the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution but appear only to correct for the Riemannian volume when integrating in geodesic normal coordinates over the sphere.

The following theorem defines and proves the kernel space isomorphism formally.

Theorem 11.1
(Spherical steerable kernels in geodesic coordinates).

Let
\mathcal{I}
be any transitive isometry group of
S^{2}
and let
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
be its stabilizer subgroup at the north pole
n\in S^{2}
.
Given any choice of gauge
\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}
at this pole, let
G\leq\operatorname{GL}(2)
be the isomorphic structure group that represents
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
in coordinates according to

\operatorname{Stab}_{n}\xrightarrow{\sim}G,\ \xi\mapsto\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\circ\xi_{\overset{}{\mkern-1.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muT\mkern-3.0muM$}}}\circ\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\big)^{-1}
.
The space
{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
of
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
-steerable kernels on
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
by
Cohen et al. 2019a
(Eq. (
460
)) is then isomorphic to the space
{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
of
G
-steerable kernels on the open ball
B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)
(Eq. (
461
)).
The kernel space isomorphism

\displaystyle\Omega:\ {K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}\xrightarrow{\,\sim\,}\,{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}

(463)

is given by

\displaystyle\Omega(K)\!

\displaystyle:

\displaystyle\,\ S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun\,

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\,\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}},\quad p\,

\displaystyle\mapsto\,\big[\Omega(K)\big](p)\

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\ K\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\log_{n}p\big)\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{n\leftarrow p}^{NP}\big)\,\sqrt{\big|\eta_{p}^{\partial\mkern-2.0mu/\mkern-2.0mu\partial{v}}\big|}^{\,-1}

(464)

if the kernel is expressed relative to (potentially independent) gauges
N
at
n
and
P
at
p
.
Its inverse is given by

\displaystyle\Omega^{-1}(\kappa)\!

\displaystyle:

\displaystyle\,\ B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu(0,\pi)

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\mathbb{R}^{{c_{\textup{out}}}\times{c_{\textup{in}}}},\quad{v}\,

\displaystyle\mapsto\,\big[\Omega^{-1}(\kappa)\big]({v})\

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\ \kappa\big(\!\exp_{n}\!\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\big)^{\!-1}{v}\big)\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{n\leftarrow p}^{NP}\big)^{\!-1}\sqrt{\big|\eta_{p}^{\partial\mkern-2.0mu/\mkern-2.0mu\partial{v}}\big|},

(465)

where we abbreviated
p:=\exp_{n}\!\big(\psi_{\scalebox{.6}{$T\!M,$}\scalebox{.7}{$n$}}^{N}\big)^{\!-1}{v}
.

Proof
:

By inserting the two expressions, one can easily see that
\Omega^{-1}
is a well defined inverse of
\Omega
since

\Omega\circ\Omega^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}}

and

\Omega^{-1}\circ\Omega=\mathrm{id}_{{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}}
.
The technical part of the proof is to show that the two kernel constraints imply each other, which is done in Appendix
F.1
.

\Box

Note that the volume scaling factor is not necessary to establish the isomorphism between the kernel spaces but is required to make the spherical convolution integral over
S^{2}\backslash\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\mkern 1.0mun
equivalent to the

-convolution integral over

.

Cohen et al. 2018b
define the convolution
{[\kappa\star_{\mkern-2.0muS^{2}}\!f]}
of a feature field

with spherical steerable kernels
\kappa\in{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
in coordinates.
Given gauges
P
at
p
and
q
at
Q
, let
\phi_{p}\in\mathcal{I}
be the unique isometry that moves the north pole to
p
, i.e.
\phi_{p}(n)=p
, and that maps the frame at

to the frame at
p
, that is,
(\phi_{p})_{\overset{}{\mkern-2.0mu*\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.55}{$,\mkern-2.0muG\mkern-2.0muM$}}}\sigma^{N}(n)=\sigma^{P}(p)

.

The spherical convolution is then in
[
36
]
relative to these gauges pointwise defined by

\displaystyle\big[\kappa\star_{\mkern-2.0muS^{2}}\!f\big]^{P}(p)\ :=\ \int\limits_{S^{2}}\kappa\big(\phi_{p}^{-1}q)\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{\phi_{p}^{-1}}^{XQ}(q)\big)\,f^{Q}(q)\ dq\ =\int\limits_{S^{2}\backslash\mkern-2.0mu-p}\mkern-8.0mu\kappa\big(\phi_{p}^{-1}q)\,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\big(g_{\phi_{p}^{-1}}^{XQ}(q)\big)\,f^{Q}(q)\ dq\,,

(466)

where we removed the antipodal point

in the second step without changing the result.
122
122

122

This formulation is more general than that in Eq. (
456
).
The latter is recovered for kernels that map scalar fields to regular feature fields.

Intuitively, this operation computes an output feature at
p
by
1) taking both the kernel and the input field,
2) rotating them via
\phi_{p}^{-1}
such that
p
moves to the north pole (via the induced gauge transformation for the feature vector) and
3) integrating their product over the sphere.
Instead of sharing weights directly over the tangent spaces, as we do, this operation is therefore sharing weights via the isometry action.
By the definition of
\phi_{p}
, both definitions of weight sharing orient the kernel at the target location
p
such that it is aligned with the chosen frame
\sigma^{P}(p)
at this location.
The following theorem proves that the
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution with a kernel
K\in{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
is equivalent to the spherical convolution with the corresponding spherical kernel
\Omega(K)\in{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
.

Theorem 11.2
(Spherical steerable convolutions as
GM
-convolutions).

Let
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
be the stabilizer subgroup of any transitive isometry group
\mathcal{I}
of
S^{2}
and let
G\leq\operatorname{GL}(2)
be any isomorphic structure group.
Let furthermore
K\in{K}^{G,B_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0,\pi)}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
be any
G
-steerable kernel on the open ball

of radius
\pi
(Eq. (
461
))
and let
\Omega(K)\in{K}^{\operatorname{Stab}_{n}}_{\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{in}}}}\mkern-1.0mu,\rho_{\overset{}{\scalebox{.6}{\;\!\!{out}}}}}
be its corresponding
\operatorname{Stab}_{n}
-steerable kernel on

(Eqs. (

) and (

The
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution (here for clarity denoted by

with the spherical kernel

, that is,

\displaystyle\Omega(K)\star_{\mkern-2.0muS^{2}}\!f\ =\ K\star_{\mkern-1.0mu\scalebox{.64}{$G\mkern-1.4muM$}}f

(467)

holds for any spherical feature field

.

Proof
:

The proof is given in Appendix
F.2
.

\Box

This proof justifies our claim that the models from
[
35
,
61
,
64
,
122
]
, discussed in this section, are all special cases of

-convolutions.

11.3
Azimuthal rotation equivariant spherical CNNs on cylindrical topologies

Besides fully
\operatorname{SO}(3)
or
\operatorname{O}(3)
-equivariant spherical convolutions, many spherical CNNs are designed to be equivariant w.r.t. azimuthal rotations around a specified polar axis.
All of the models discussed in this section rely either on the
\operatorname{SO}(2)
-invariant
\{e\}
-structure
that is shown in Figs.
55(b)
and
57

or, alternatively, that in Fig.
58
.
Due to the triviality of the structure group
G=\{e\}
, the kernel spaces remain unconstrained (
\{e\}
-steerable).
Features are transported according to the unique
\{e\}
-compatible trivial connection which differs from the usual spherical Levi-Civita connection.
With this information, and with the explicit exponential maps in Eq. (
432
), the spherical
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions in this section are in theory fully specified.
In practice, the implementations, listed in row (34) of Table
, differ in their numerical implementations, which we discuss in the following.

Figure 56:
Gnomonic projection
{{G}_{p}\!:T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to H_{p}^{2}}
of the tangent space at
p
to the upper hemisphere
H_{p}^{2}\subset S^{2}
around
p
.
When interpreting the sphere as being embedded in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
, the gnomonic projection
{G}_{p}(v)
(blue) is given by the sum of
{p\in S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}}
(purple) and
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
(yellow) in ambient space, followed by a normalization back to the sphere.
Theorem
11.3
proves that this operation is equivalent to a projection of a radially warped vector
\omega(v)=\arctan(\lVert v\rVert)\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}\in B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,{\textstyle\frac{\pi}{2}})
(red) via the exponential map (green).
The gnomonic projection based spherical convolutions in

[
39
,
254
,
222
,
55
,
149
]

are therefore special cases of spherical
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions with radially warped kernels.

G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions are more general since they allow for kernel projections over the whole sphere instead of the upper hemisphere only.

Concurrent with our definition of convolutional weight sharing, the models in
[
39
,
254
,
222
,
55
,
149
]
share a given template kernel over the tangent spaces by orienting it relative to the frames of the considered
\{e\}
-structure in Fig.
55(b)
.
However, contrary to
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions, the matching of these kernels with the feature field is not done via exponential maps (or transporter pullbacks), but via the gnomonic projection.
This gnomonic projection is at any point
p
defined by

\displaystyle{G}_{p}:\,T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to H_{p}^{2},\quad v\mapsto\frac{p+v}{\lVert p+v\rVert}\,,

(468)

which is visualized in Fig.
56
.
The summation of
p\in S^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
with tangent vectors
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
is hereby performed in the embedding space
\mathbb{R}^{3}
and the normalization projects the result back to the sphere. The codomain of the gnomonic projection is the “upper” hemisphere

\displaystyle H_{p}^{2}:=\big\{q\in S^{2}\,\big|\,\langle p,q\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}>0\big\}\,\subset S^{2}

(469)

centered around
p
.
Given this difference in the kernel projections, it might seems like the models in
[
39
,
254
,
222
,
55
,
149
]
are not (or only approximately) explained as
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution.
The following theorem proves, however, that the gnomonic projection is equivalent to a projection via the exponential map after applying a
radial warp

\displaystyle\omega:\ T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM\to B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,{\textstyle\frac{\pi}{2}}),\quad v\mapsto\arctan\!\big(\lVert v\rVert\big)\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}

(470)

to the tangent spaces, which contracts tangent vectors to an open ball of radius
\pi/2
around the origin:

Theorem 11.3
(Gnomonic projections as warped exponential maps).

The gnomonic projection
{G}_{p}
of
T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
to the upper hemisphere
H_{p}^{2}\subset S^{2}
, defined in Eq. (
468
), is equivalent to a projection of its radial warp
\omega(T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM)=B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,{\textstyle\frac{\pi}{2}})
, Eq. (
470
), via the exponential map, that is, the following diagram commutes:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces H_{p}^{2}\subset S^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM}(0,{\textstyle\frac{\pi}{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G}_{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\omega\,}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\exp_{p}}

(471)

In equations,

\displaystyle{G}_{p}(v)\,=\,\exp_{p}\circ\,\omega(v)

(472)

holds for any
p\in S^{2}
and any
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
.

Proof
:

The proof is given by the following simple calculation, which holds for any
p\in S^{2}
and any
v\in T_{\mkern-1.5mup}\mkern-0.5muM
:

\displaystyle\exp_{p}\circ\mkern 2.0mu\omega(v)\

\displaystyle\overset{(1)}{=}\ p\cdot\cos\!\big(\lVert\omega(v)\rVert\big)\,+\,\frac{\omega(v)}{\lVert\omega(v)\rVert}\cdot\sin\!\big(\lVert\omega(v)\rVert\big)

\displaystyle\overset{(2)}{=}\ p\cdot\cos\!\big(\!\arctan(\lVert v\rVert)\big)\,+\,\frac{v}{\lVert v\rVert}\cdot\sin\!\big(\!\arctan(\lVert v\rVert)\big)

\displaystyle\overset{(3)}{=}\ \frac{p+v}{\sqrt{1+\lVert v\rVert^{2}}}

\displaystyle\overset{(4)}{=}\ \frac{p+v}{\lVert p+v\rVert}

\displaystyle\overset{(5)}{=}\ {G}_{p}(v)

(473)

The first two steps make use of the explicit definition of the embedded sphere’s exponential map, Eq. (
432
), and the radial warp, Eq. (
470
).
The third step follows since
\cos\circ\arctan(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}
and
\sin\circ\arctan(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}
.
In the fourth step we used that
\lVert p\rVert=1
and
\langle p,v\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}=0
, while the last step identified the gnomonic projection, Eq. (
468
).

\Box

This theorem implies that the gnomonic projection based convolutions in

[
39
,
254
,
222
,
55
,
149
]

are indeed specific
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions after identifying the kernels via the radial warp
\omega
.
123
123

123

Technically, the equivalence of both convolutions requires furthermore a radially dependent change of the kernel amplitude to account for the change in the volume measure when warping the kernel.

Note that this identification holds not only for
\{e\}
-steerable kernels but for any subgroup
G\leq\operatorname{O}(2)
since the corresponding
G
-steerability constraints affect only the kernels’ angular parts but are independent from the warped radial parts.
We furthermore want to mention that the exponential map based projection of
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolutions is insofar more general than the gnomonic kernel projection that it can describe kernels that extend beyond the upper hemisphere
H_{p}^{2}
around
p
.
Note that both kernel projections become in the practically relevant limit of small kernels even without the radial warp equivalent since
\arctan\big(\lVert v\rVert\big)=\lVert v\rVert+\mathcal{O}\big(\lVert v\rVert^{3}\big)
.

The implementations in
[
39
,
254
,
222
,
55
,
149
]

are in the continuum all equivalent to each other and to our
G\mkern-1.4muM
-convolution, however, their numerical discretizations differ.

Coors et al. 2018
,
Eder and Frahm 2019
and
Martin et al. 2020
discretize feature fields on (approximately) uniform sampling grids on the sphere.
Specifically,
Coors et al. 2018
and
Martin et al. 2020
use the “generalized spiral set on
S^{2}
” from
[
189
]
as sampling points, while
Eder and Frahm 2019
use the vertices of an icosphere.
Since the gnomonic projections of kernel sampling grids on the tangent spaces do not match the spherical sampling grid, the authors interpolate bilinearly between them.
The kernel sampling coefficients can hereby be precomputed in an offline step.
The actual convolution computes then an output feature field by contracting the projected, interpolated kernels at each point with the input field.

\operatorname{SO}(2)

The spherical coordinate map

(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})\times\mathbb{R}

Since
\chi

\{e\}

1/\cos(\theta)
, which diverges towards the poles.
The spherical convolution on this
\{e\}

[

,

implemented by projecting and interpolating a kernel sampling grid on the tangent spaces to a feature field sampling grid on the sphere.
If the feature fields are instead sampled on the equirectangular projection, the kernel sampling grid is in a second step mapped further from the sphere to a deformed sampling grid on
(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})\times\mathbb{R}

[

,

.
Note that regular sampling grids on the equirectangular projection oversample the signal (relative to the spherical metric) towards the poles.

Zhao et al. 2018
and
Tateno et al. 2018
discretize their spherical feature fields
f:S^{2}\backslash\{n,s\}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
instead in form of a regular pixel grid on an equirectangular projection of the sphere.
Mathematically, the equirectangular projection, visualized in Fig.
57
, is formalized as the pullback

\chi^{*}f=f\circ\chi:\big(\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\big)\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}
,
of the image by the spherical coordinate map
\chi
from Eq. (

):

In an additional step, they map it via

Since the deformation incurred by the equirectangular projection is independent from the longitude
\phi\in\mathbb{R}
, it is sufficient to compute it only once for each latitude
\theta\in{\textstyle\big(\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\big)}
